READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Daniel chapter 2 sets the stage for the interpretation of the second dream in chapter 4 and the visions of Daniel 7-12 by the prophecy about four (idiom for all the earth) coming world empires. Daniel is a unified literary document.
    1. Daniel 2 reveals that the Messianic kingdom (i.e., Jesus' incarnation, life, death, resurrection) will come in the time of the fourth world empire (Rome).
    2. Daniel 7:2-8 describes all four coming kingdoms, but the emphasis of the chapter is on the fourth kingdom ("the little horn," who I think is Nero, cf. 2 Thessalonians 2; see SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTICHRIST).
    3. Daniel 8 focuses on the second (Persia) and third (Greece) kingdoms, but the emphasis is on the third kingdom ("little horn" = Antiochus IV Epiphanies, 175-163 B.C.) of the Selucid Empire (i.e., Syria).
    4. Daniel 9:24-27 focuses in detail on the fourth kingdom, the Roman Empire (also possibly Dan. 11:36-45).
    5. Daniel 10 introduces the message of chapters 11-12, which refer to the third kingdom, particularly the conflict between Babylon/Syria (Seleucids) and Egypt (Ptolomies).
      SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE #2

  2. The inter-relatedness of these chapters shows the unity of Daniel 1-6 and 7-12.

  3. Daniel's gift of interpreting dreams and visions parallels Joseph's gift in Genesis 41. Many of the terms used are similar except Genesis 41 is Hebrew and Dan. 2:4-7:28 is Aramaic.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Daniel 2:2 "the king gave orders to call in the"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:2 "the king gave orders to call in the" This is a series of royal counselors, which implies that Nebuchadnezzar called in the entire group of those who claimed to know the will of the gods.

▣ "magicians" This is from the Hebrew word "engraving tool" (BDB 355). Possibly an Egyptian loan word (cf. Gen. 41:8; Exod. 7:11,22; 8:7,18-19; 9:11; Dan. 1:20; 2:2,10,27; 4:7,9). See note at Dan. 1:20. A good discussion of these different kinds of wise men is found in Robert B. Girdlestone's Synonyms of the Old Testament, pp. 296-302.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

▣ "the conjurers" See note at Dan. 1:20.

▣ "sorcerers" The general term for "magic" in Hebrew is kšp (BDB 506).

  1. male witch, wizard ‒ kaššāp
  2. sorcery ‒ kešep
  3. witchcraft ‒ kešāpîm

These people tried to know and manipulate current and future events by the use of natural and supernatural powers through physical means, divination, magic charms, and occult potions.

For a good general discussion of all the terms see New International Dictionary of Old Testament Theology and Exegesis, vol. 3, pp. 945-951. Also look at my exegetical commentary on Deuteronomy 18 online (www.freebiblecommentary.org).

▣ "Chaldeans" This seems to refer to astrologers. However, the term in Gen. 11:28 has a racial connotation (cf. 1:4; 2 Kgs. 24:2; Jer. 35:11; and also in Assyrian documents relating to Nabopolassar). Some have dealt with this changing meaning by asserting a misunderstanding in the Sumerian root, "master-builders," instead of racial lineage. The fifth century B.C. historian, Herodotus, in his Persian Wars, mentions a class of priests whose origins went back to Cyrus' day.

Here and in Dan. 2:10 it occurs last in a list of wise men, but in Dan.4:7; 5:7,11 it occurs within the list. It is obvious this term had several connotations (BDB 505, KB 501-502). It seems to be a collective term for wise men (cf. Dan. 2:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

2:3
NASB, NKJV   "my spirit is anxious"
NRSV   "my spirit is troubled"
TEV   "I'm worried"
NJB   "my mind is troubled"

This Hebrew term "anxious" (BDB 821, KB 952, Niphal IMPERFECT with waw) originally meant strike or hit. It is also used of Pharaoh in Gen. 41:8, who was disturbed by his dreams (both in Niphal).

entries.title: Daniel 2:4 "in Aramaic"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:4 "in Aramaic" At this point the text of Daniel changes from Hebrew to Aramaic and will continue through chapter 7. Aramaic was the governmental and commercial language from the Assyrian to the Persian Empires. At this point in the text Daniel begins to quote Nebuchadnezzar's fearful warning of judgment on his wise men (i.e., royal counselors). Therefore, a change to Aramaic fits.

The problem is why it continues through chapter seven. H. C. Leupold even makes chapter 7 a part of the literary unit starting in chapter one. The truth is no one knows why Hebrew starts, Aramaic continues, and Hebrew concludes the book of Daniel. Some compare the structural pattern of Job (prose, poetry, prose) or Hammurabi's law code following the same pattern, but these are not in two languages, rather writing styles. Aramaic is a cognate Semitic language to Hebrew. Both are written in the same characters. It was known early in the Bible by its use in Gen. 31:47 (two words) and it appears as the language of diplomatic dialogue in 2 Kgs. 18:26. Imperial Aramaic was used from 600 to 330 B.C.

For a good discussion of the ancient use of Aramaic see R. K. Harrison, Introduction to the Old Testament, pp. 201-210,1125.

▣ "O king, live forever" This was a common honorific hyperbolic idiom for addressing Near Eastern potentates, (cf. Dan. 3:9; 5:10; 6:6,21; 1 Kgs. 1:31; Neh. 2:3).

2:5
NASB  "The command from me is firm"
KJV  "The thing is gone from me"
NKJV, REB  "My decision is firm"
NRSV  "This is a public decree"
TEV  "I have made up my mind"
NJB  "This is my firm resolve"
LXX  "your houses confiscated"
Peshitta  "the word that I have spoken is true"

Nebuchadnezzar II had fully made up his mind about this issue and made his decision public.

The KJV translation often is based on (see note at Dan. 2:2, third item)

  1. a textual change in the Aramaic
  2. an opinion from Josephus (cf. Antiq. 10.10.3)

▣ "torn limb from limb" This was a common method of capital punishment in the Ancient Near East. Whether they were

  1. cut with a knife
  2. torn by means of bended trees
  3. being tied between two or more animals is uncertain
▣
NASB, REB  "your houses shall be made a rubbish heap"
NKJV  "and your houses shall be made an ash heap"
NRSV  "and your houses shall be laid in ruins"
TEV  "and make your houses a pile of ruins"
NJB  "and your houses turned into dunghills"
Peshitta  "your houses shall be plundered"

Some translations follow the rabbinical interpretation of the Targums, making this "dung-hill," (NJB, cf. 2 Kgs. 10:27). The reducing of criminals' homes and possessions to rubbish (cf. Ezra 6:11) was a common practice in the empires of the Fertile Crescent. To further humiliate these people, these rubbish heaps were often turned into public latrines (developed idiomatic usage from the Targums).

entries.title: Daniel 2:4-6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:4-6 It may be that Nebuchadnezzar II was going to

  1. test the interpretation of his wise men by also demanding that they reveal the contents of his dream first
  2. simply forgot his dream (see note at Dan. 2:1, third item)

entries.title: Daniel 2:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:9 This verse implies that Nebuchadnezzar did not trust his own wise men. This may be because

  1. their interpretation had been false in the past
  2. he saw true insight by means of the four Jewish youths (cf. Dan. 1:19-20, but this seems unlikely because of Dan. 2:13b)

Whatever the reason this king is about to completely eliminate the entire group of wise men through violent means (cf. Dan. 2:12-13).

entries.title: Daniel 2:10 "Chaldeans answered"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:10 "Chaldeans answered" There is a series of three alibis:

  1. no man on earth can do this
  2. no king has ever asked this of the wise men before
  3. only the gods can answer this question (cf. Dan. 2:11)

This heightens the significance of Daniel's interpretation from YHWH's revelation!

entries.title: Daniel 2:11 "difficult"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:11 "difficult" This Aramaic ADJECTIVE (BDB 1096, KB 1893) normally means "precious," "costly," "valued," "honored" (cf. Ezra 4:10). It can mean "rare" (cf. KJV and marginal note in NASB) but only here, translated "difficult" (JPSOA).

However, in this text it has an unusual idiomatic meaning. The word can have a royal or kingly connotation which fits this context, but "difficult" is a most unusual translation. The Bible: An American Translation by Smith and Goodspeed, has "hard thing," while The Living Bible by Taylor, has "an impossible thing."

▣ "flesh" This term (BDB 1088) is imagery for the transitoriness and frailty of human beings. Here it does not denote sinfulness, but weakness.

entries.title: Daniel 2:12 "the king became indignant and very furious"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:12 "the king became indignant and very furious" The king's response to their alibi was extreme anger (BDB 1084). The second term, "very furious" (BDB 1111) is used of YHWH's wrath. He ordered that all the wise men of Babylon be killed.

The term "Babylon" can refer to

  1. the city
  2. the province
  3. the whole empire

Knowing how superstitious and fearful the ancient world was, it is amazing that a king would totally destroy all his diviners, astrologers, soothsayers, and wise men. In a sense he was cutting himself off from the spiritual realm. For some reason Nebuchadnezzar II had lost all respect and confidence in his wise men.

Many times in Daniel the author uses hendiadys, where two words are given, but express the same idea:

  1. Dan. 2:6, "gifts and a reward"
  2. Dan. 2:12, "indignant and very furious"
  3. Dan. 2:14, "with discretion and discernment"
  4. Dan. 2:23, "wisdom and power"
  5. Dan. 3:13, "rage and anger"
  6. Dan. 4:2, "signs and wonders"
  7. Dan. 5:11, "illumination, insight, and wisdom"
  8. Dan. 5:18, "sovereignty, grandeur, glory, and majesty"
  9. Dan. 5:19, "feared and troubled"
  10. also the last four paralleled phrases of Dan. 2:19

entries.title: Daniel 2:13 "the decree went forth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:13 "the decree went forth" It seems that the wise men were to be rounded up and killed at one public execution. This would give Daniel time to seek God.

2:14
NASB  "descretion and discernment"
NKJV, LXX  "counsel and wisdom"
NRSV  "prudence and discretion"
TEV  "choosing his words carefully"
NJB  "shrewd and cautious words"
REB  "discreet and tactful"
Peshitta  "meditated and took counsel"

These two NOUNS (BDB 1096, 1094) characterize the way these four Hebrew youths dealt with Babylonian court intrigue and political pressure. God's wisdom enabled them to fit in, but also stand out!

The term NASB translates "discernment" (BDB 1094) was used in two senses (NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 379).

  1. eat ‒ 1 Sam. 14:24,29,43; 2 Sam. 3:35; Jonah 3:7
  2. discern, test ‒ Ps. 34:8; Prov. 31:18

In this context, "discernment" fits best.

▣ "Arioch" This proper name (BDB 1082) is also found in Gen. 14:9 as the name of one of the kings who took Lot captive (i.e., different person).

▣ "the captain of the king's bodyguard" This person has several things said about him in this phrase.

  1. captain (BDB 1112) ‒ This ADJECTIVE denotes a person of leadership (NIDOTTE, vol. 3, pp. 1028-1032)
  2. The term "bodyguard" (BDB 1094) is literally "the chief slaughter" (KB 368, possibly from "butcher") or "executioner." In Dan. 2:15 he is called "the King's commander" (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:8,11; Jer. 39:9). This term, like "eunuch" may have become an official title for a royal servant. This person was a successful military leader, now working at the palace.
  3. "of the king" (BDB 1100) denotes a royal servant
    1. military
    2. now at court
2:15
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, LXX, Peshitta, JPSOA  "urgent"
TEV, NJB  "harsh"
REB  "preemptory"

This Aramaic word is used only here and in Dan. 3:22. Its basic meaning is "harshness" (BDB 1093), but it can mean suddenly or urgently (Davidson, Analytical Hebrew and Chaldee Lexicon, p. 272).

entries.title: Daniel 2:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:16 The king is more patient with Daniel's request for time than he was with the group of wise men's request (cf. Dan. 2:8).

entries.title: Daniel 2:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:17 Notice that the Hebrew names (see note at Dan. 1:8) for these young men are used here (i.e. among themselves), while in Dan. 2:49 the new Babylonian names are used at court (cf. Dan. 1:7).

2:18
NASB  "they might request compassion"
NKJV  "they might seek mercies"
NRSV  "seek mercy"
TEV  "to pray. . .for mercy"
NJB  "to beg. . .to show mercy"

Notice again YHWH is in control! These Hebrew youths have no power apart from Him.

The Aramaic term (BDB 1113) "compassion" is used only here. Its Hebrew parallel also means "compassion" or "mercy." They both come from the term "womb" denoting a mother's care, love, and protection. YHWH's love is often denoted as female (cf. Exod. 19:4; Deut. 32:11; Isa. 31:5; 40:31; 49:15; 66:9-13, also note Matt. 23:37; Luke 13:34). YHWH is not a male or a female, but an eternal Spirit.

If you would like to hear my sermon, "The Femininity of God," go to the second dark green box on my home page, click on "A. God the Father," tape #111.

▣ "the God of heaven" Some see this as a common title for the high god in both Babylon (Marduk) and Persia (Ahura Mazda) patheon. However, it is possible that it was used by the Jews to show the supremacy of YHWH (cf. Gen. 24:7; Ezra 1:2; 6:10; 7:12,21; Neh. 1:5; 2:4). The exiled Jews often took the common title for the high god of their captors and applied it to YHWH.

▣ "mystery" This Aramaic word (BDB 1112) , raz, means "to hide," "to keep a secret." It is used several times in Daniel (cf. Dan. 2:18,19,27,28,29,30,47; 4:9). It becomes a central theme in apocalyptic literature and is mentioned often in the Dead Sea Scrolls. God reveals His hidden counsel to His prophets (cf. Gen. 18:17; Jer. 23:18; Dan. 9:22; Amos 3:7).

In the Dead Sea Scroll community God's revelation was mediated through

  1. the OT prophets' message (raz)
  2. but also, the interpretation (pesher) of "the teacher of righteousness"

This two-fold pattern of revelation and interpretation characterizes apocalyptic literature.

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

entries.title: Daniel 2:19 "a night vision"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:19 "a night vision" There is a distinction between a "vision" and "dream" (cf. Dan. 1:17) in the OT, but not in Daniel. This revelation was at night (cf. Dan. 7:2,7,13), but Daniel was conscious and the revelation was visual and auditory. In context Nebuchadnezzar II had the dream, but Daniel received the vision needed to interpret it. Both were from God.

This same term (BDB 1092) is often associated with God speaking to the prophets. Its root is "behold" and it became the earliest designation for prophets (i.e. seer, cf. 2 Sam. 24:11; 2 Kgs. 17:13; Amos 7:12; Micah 3:7; for a parallel term see 1 Sam. 9:9; Isa. 30:10).

Again the emphasis in on God's control, God's revelation, God's provision and protection (cf. Dan. 2:20-23).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHET (the different Hebrew terms)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

entries.title: Daniel 2:20 "the name of God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:20 "the name of God" This phrase stands for the character of God. Daniel 2:20-23 have been called "Daniel's prayer of praise" or the "Song of Daniel."

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

▣ "God" This is Eloah (BDB 43, KB 52), which is the SINGULAR form of Elohim. The general name for deity in the ANE was El. Daniel is using vocabulary Gentiles would understand.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, A. and C.

▣ "forever and forever" This is the term 'olam repeated twice, which surely denotes eternity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

▣ "For wisdom and power belong to Him" God is the only source of

  1. life
  2. wisdom
  3. power

Human wisdom is fallen wisdom, earthly wisdom, fleeting wisdom. Verses 21-23 expand this thought.

entries.title: Daniel 2:20-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:20-23 Daniel seems to thank God for four major things:

  1. God's control of history (i.e., all peoples, cf. Job 12:23; Ps. 47:7-8; Acts 17:26)
  2. God's freely giving wisdom to the Hebrew exiles
  3. God's knowledge compared to the knowledge of Babylonian deities and wise men
  4. God's consistency in His purpose with the Jews (i.e., Abrahamic covenant)

These are the key theological issues of Daniel, which were so needed by an exiled, defeated, and humiliated covenant people.

It must be remembered that in the ancient world people fought under the protection and power of their god. If one people defeated another it was considered that one god triumphed over another. However, in the Bible it is stated again and again that Israel and Judah's judgment was due to their sin, not YHWH's impotence. Here in this passage Daniel asserts YHWH's power and control of nations and history, as well as His wisdom.

entries.title: Daniel 2:21 "It is He who changes the times and the epochs He removes kings and establishes kings"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:21 "It is He who changes the times and the epochs
  He removes kings and establishes kings" Israel's God is the Creator and Controller of time/history. This is a recurrent theme in the Bible (cf. Deut. 32:8 [LXX]; Job 12:13-25; Ps. 22:28; 47:7-8; 66:5-7; 75:6-8; Isa. 10:5-14; Zech. 14:9; Dan. 4:17,25,32,35; 5:18-19; Acts 17:26; Rom. 8:28; 9; Eph. 1:11). All theology must start with a sovereign, unchanging, merciful Creator!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISREAL'S GOD (NT)

▣ "He gives wisdom to wise men, and knowledge to men of understanding" In this context it refers to the four Jewish youth, especially Daniel (cf. Dan. 2:23) and not at all to the guild of Babylonian wise men.

entries.title: Daniel 2:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:22 The imagery of darkness vs. light is common in the Bible. God creates both. He controls both (cf. 1 Chr. 29:11-12). But, His character is light which is imagery for goodness, knowledge, truth, and revelation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: DARKNESS

entries.title: Daniel 2:23 "God of my fathers"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:23 "God of my fathers" Daniel knows he is addressing the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (cf. Gen. 31:42; Exod. 3:15). He is the covenant God of national Israel. The God of fulfilled promises!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

▣ "You have made known to me" Daniel's national God (YHWH) has

  1. answered Daniel's prayer
  2. fully revealed the required information
  3. None of the other "wise men" nor their magic arts could do this!

entries.title: Daniel 2:25 "hurriedly"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:25 "hurriedly" This is a Hithpael INFINITIVE (BDB 1084) which normally denotes terror or confusion, but in this context, it deontes "rapid action."

▣ "Arioch. . .I have found" As all politicians, Arioch claimed credit for finding Daniel when, in reality, Daniel approached him (cf. Dan. 2:24).

▣ "among the exiles from Judah" All of the Babylonian wise men could not help, but a man from God's exiled people could! This is a way of magnifying YHWH. His people know because they know Him. Judah may seem small and insignificant, but its people are God's people. He has revealed Himself to them and now through them to Nebuchadnezzar II.

entries.title: Daniel 2:27-30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:27-30 Daniel disclaims any personal merit but gives the God of his fathers (YHWH) the credit for the revelation. This whole incident magnifies Israel's God over the Babylonian gods (Bel, Marduk).

SPECIAL TOPIC: BEL

SPECIAL TOPIC: MARDUK

entries.title: Daniel 2:28 "He has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will take place in the latter days"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:28 "He has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will take place in the latter days" Nebuchadnezzar II is used in a symbolic way to represent human government (cf. Dan. 2:36-38). This same type of imagery is found in Revelation 18 in the phrase "the whore of Babylon." Daniel, chapters 1 through 6, describes human governments, while chapters 7 through 12 discuss the coming of the kingdom of God.

Often the prophets spoke about the nations (e.g., Isa. 12-24; 46-47; Jer. 44-51; Ezekiel 25-32), but not in the presence of the leaders of the nations (with the possible exception of Amos to the leaders of Israel). In a sense it is Daniel who addresses directly on God's behalf the pagan empires of the Ancient Near East. This world order and God's purpose for creation are in opposition. God will judge the nations and fulfill His plan for creation. Daniel has a unique place in YHWH's dealing with pagan rulers and their kingdoms (much like Joseph to Pharoah).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOVERNMENT

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣
NASB, NKJV, Peshitta  "in the latter days"
NRSV, JPSOA, LXX  "at the end of days"
TEV  "in the future"
NJB  "in the final days"
REB  "at the end of this age"

The OT saw only one coming of the Messiah (i.e., the stone of Dan. 2:31-35). This climactic event of history was preceded by major events known as "the latter days" (i.e., end-times, cf. Deut. 31:29; Isa. 2:2; Dan. 10:14; Hosea 3:5; Micah 4:1; NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 362). In this context it denotes a future time, not necessarily the last days.

However, with further revelation (i.e., the progressive revelation of the NT), we realize that the term "latter days" often refers to the period between the incarnation of the Messiah at Bethlehem and His coming again in power and glory at His Second Coming (cf. Acts 2:17 quoting Joel 2:28-32). This is basically an overlapping of the two Jewish ages.

Just a brief note about how Futurists try to extend the fourth kingdom (i.e., Roman) into the far distant future by asserting that the Jews rejected Jesus so the Kingdom was postponed (i.e., so far, 2000 years plus). It is obvious to me that Daniel accurately predicts the coming of the Kingdom in the birth and life of Jesus.

How is the presumption of a 2,000 year unexpected gap in clear prophesy, seen as "taking the Bible literally"?

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KINGDOM OF GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE MESSIANIC ERA

SPECIAL TOPIC: THIS AGE AND THE AGE TO COME

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE LAST DAYS

entries.title: Daniel 2:29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:29 Predictive prophecy is one of the greatest evidences that the Bible really is the only inspired self-revelation of the one true God (cf. Dan. 2:45,47). The Bible is the only world holy book that has predictive prophecy.

God is above time. All history is present before Him. He is not limited by past, present, and future time sequence. This foreknowledge does not remove human free will. We are responsible for our choices. The Bible does not teach determinism (Islam), but covenant!

This is such a foundational truth that I have included several video sermons on this crucial issue in the first paragraph on my homepage (light blue box), www.freebiblecommentary.org

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BIBLE (its uniqueness and inspiration)

2:30
NASB, NRSV  the thoughts of your mind"
NKJV  "the thoughts of your heart"
TEV  "the thoughts that have come to you"
NJB  "your inmost thoughts"

The term "heart" is an OT way of referring to the entire person.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

entries.title: Daniel 2:31
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:31 The statue is described as:

  1. "large" (BDB 1112) ‒ used
    1. of the statue (Dan. 2:31)
    2. of the tree (Dan. 4:7)
    3. of honor (Dan. 2:6)
    4. of gifts (Dan. 2:48)
  2. "of extraordinary splendor" (BDB 1096) ‒ possibly refers to the brightness of the differing metals
▣
NASB, NKJV, JPSOA  "awesome"
NRSV  "frightening"
TEV, Peshitta  "terrifying"
NJB  "terrible to see"
REB  "fearsome"

This same term (BDB 1087) describes the fourth beast in Dan. 7:7,19.

entries.title: Daniel 2:31-35 "a statue"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:31-35 "a statue" This statue of a human male of differing metals represents fallen human world governments of the ANE. Each one is inferior to the one before it (cf. v. 39).

entries.title: Daniel 2:33 "clay"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:33 "clay" This refers to baked clay ("potter's clay" or terra cotta), as do Dan. 2:34,35, first use in Dan. 2:41,42, but 2:41 and 43 seem to mean wet clay ("miry clay").

entries.title: Daniel 2:34 "a stone"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:34 "a stone" This is imagery for the Messiah. He is often spoken of in prophecy as a rock or stone.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CORNERSTONE

entries.title: Daniel 2:35 "were crushed"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:35 "were crushed" Although the stone cut out of the mountain without hands strikes only the fourth kingdom, all others are also crushed to fine powder (BDB 1089 Peal PERFECT, used three times in v. 35, cf. Dan. 2:45). This seems to symbolize the ultimate overthrow of human government and the establishment of God's universal reign (i.e., in two stages).

  1. the coming of the Kingdom of God in Jesus' life
  2. the consumation of the Kingdom at Jesus' return

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIANIC ERA

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGDOM OF GOD

▣ "became a great mountain and filled the whole earth" This may be

  1. a play on the ancient Babylonian belief that the earth was a mountain
  2. biblical imagery for God's kingdom (cf. Isa. 2:2; Mic. 4:1)

It surely does show a worldwide kingdom.

The "stone" in Dan. 2:34 is obviously a reference to the Messiah, but the use of the term in Dan. 2:35 refers to His kingdom (the church of the redeemed, cf. Rom. 9-11; Eph. 2:11-3:13). In Daniel there is often a fluidity between leaders and their kingdoms. The real interpretive issue is whether this relates to

  1. the inauguration of the kingdom of God by the incarnation, life, death, and resurrection of Jesus
  2. the consummation of the kingdom of God at Jesus' Second Coming

This unforeseen two-stage coming complicates OT prophecy.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THIS AGE AND THE AGE TO COME

entries.title: Daniel 2:36 "we"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:36 "we" This is an editorial "we."

entries.title: Daniel 2:37 "to whom the God of heaven has given"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:37 "to whom the God of heaven has given" The VERB (BDB 1095) is a Peal PERFECT. Notice the continuing emphasis on God's sovereignty (cf. Dan. 1:2,9,17). He allows kings to rise and prosper.

entries.title: Daniel 2:38
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:38 This description of Nebuchadnezzar's reign seems to mimic Gen. 1:28 (cf. Jer. 27:6; 28:14).

This verse reminds me of God's care for animals (cf. Jonah 4:11; Ps. 36:6c). Animals may be a part of the new creation (cf. Isa. 11:6-9; 65:25 and possibly Rom. 8:18-22).

▣ "You are the head of gold" The statue of four succeeding human empires mimics chapter seven (cf. Dan. 7:2-19; 8:8,22; 11:2,4).

  1. Here, the first kingdom is specifically identified (neo-Babylon, 626-539 B.C.).
  2. In Dan. 8:20-21 the second (Medo-Persian, 539-333 B.C.).
  3. The third, Greece, 333-63 B.C. is specifically identified.
  4. This makes the fourth kingdom (cf. Dan. 2:40) Rome, which was the Mediterranean government in control of Palestine at the time of the life of Jesus.

There is an interesting discussion of the use of the number in ancient cultures to describe world empires in D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Langauge of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, p. 115.

entries.title: Daniel 2:39 "After you there will arise another kingdom"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:39 "After you there will arise another kingdom" Apparently this was to ease Nebuchadnezzar's fear that his kingdom might be taken from him soon.

▣ "which will rule over all the earth" This is either imagery for the known world or a specific local use of the word "earth" (as it is in Genesis 6-9, cf. Bernard Ramm, The Christian View of Science and Scripture, pp. 158-169).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH

entries.title: Daniel 2:40 "a fourth kingdom"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:40 "a fourth kingdom" This kingdom is described in Dan. 2:40-43; 7:7-8. It is never named as are the first three. In some ways it refers to Rome, but also to a type of worldwide human government, which is opposed to God. It has a historical reference (Rome) and a future reference (end-time, anti-God world empire, cf. Dan. 9:25-27; 11:36-45; also notice Psalm 2; Ezekiel 38-39).

This second chapter sets the literary stage for the whole book.

entries.title: Daniel 2:41 "it will be a divided kingdom"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:41 "it will be a divided kingdom" This refers to the fourth kingdom and seems to imply that these will be successive kingdoms. There has been much discussion about the meaning of it being divided (BDB 1108, Peal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE):

  1. the Roman Empire would divide into the east and west
  2. it refers to the attempted political marriages with Germanic tribes (cf. Dan. 2:43 and TEV)
  3. it possibly refers to the distinction between the republic and later the dictatorship

The toes of iron and clay mentioned in Dan. 2:42 may point toward the literary meaning of "divided." This fundamental weakness will cause its destruction.

2:43
NASB  "they will combine with one another in the seed of men"
NKJV  "they will mingle with the seed of men"
NRSV, Peshitta  "as they will mix with one another in marriage"
TEV, REB  "the rulers of that empire will try to unite their families
  by intermarriage"
NJB  "the two will be mixed together in human seed"

This kingdom will attempt to save itself by human means (here probably political marriages, cf. Dan. 11:6). See #3 above.

entries.title: Daniel 2:44 "In the days of those kings"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:44 "In the days of those kings" It is very important to realize that the coming of the Messiah will be during the fourth kingdom. This is why I believe that it refers to the incarnation of Jesus at Bethlehem during Roman occupation of Palestine; therefore, "those kings" would refer to Roman Caesars of the first century and not future end-time world rulers.

▣ "set up a kingdom which will never be destroyed" This phrase is not related to the millennium which is a specific period of time (cf. Rev. 20:1-6). This looks at a far wider scope of history in which the kingdom of God will be established when the Messiah will set up a perpetual, eternal kingdom (cf. 2 Sam. 7:13,16; Ps. 45:6; 89:36-37; Isa. 9:7; Dan. 4:3; 6:26; 7:14,18,27; Micah 5:2-5a; Luke 1:33; 1 Cor. 15:24-28; 2 Pet. 1:11; Rev. 11:15).

Notice how this kingdom is characterized.

  1. set up by God (BDB 1110)
  2. never be destroyed (BDB 1091)
  3. not left for another people
  4. crush (BDB 1089) and end (BDB 1104) all previous kingdoms
  5. endure forever (BDB 1104)

This same powerful imagery describes this kingdom in Dan. 7:14,18,27. I think the brief discussion of "eternal," found in F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, pp. 202-203, is very helpful.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

SPECIAL TOPIC: IMMANUEL'S PERSON AND REIGN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KINGDOM OF GOD

entries.title: Daniel 2:45 "a stone was cut out of the mountain without hands"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:45 "a stone was cut out of the mountain without hands" This may be a veiled allusion to the virgin birth of the Messiah (cf. Gen. 3:15; Isa. 7:14) and the incarnation at Bethlehem. Even the Jewish commentators Rashi and Eben-Ezra see this as a Messianic passage.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CORNERSTONE

▣ "without hands" This is imagery for God's agency (cf. Dan. 8:25; Zech. 4:6). This is another way that God's control apart from human affect or agency is emphasized (cf. Heb. 11:10,16).

entries.title: Daniel 2:46
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:46 King Nebuchadnezzar II pays homage to Daniel as the representative of the God who has revealed this truth. This does not refer to the worship of Daniel or he would not have allowed it (i.e., the "him") refers to YHWH to which Nebuchadnezzar II offered a sacrifice (i.e., possibly drink libation) and incense.

The term "homage" (BDB 1104) is literally "bowed down." It is always used in connection to false worship (cf. Isa. 44:15,17,19; 46:6; Dan. 2:46; 3:5-28; NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 222).

entries.title: Daniel 2:47
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:47 These very high-sounding words (cf. Dan. 3:28-29; 4:1-3,34-37) do not mean that Nebuchadnezzar II became a believer in YHWH. He was a polytheist who had no problem with adding other gods to his pantheon. He was still a worshiper of Marduk and Nebo. It is astonishing that he would allow YHWH, the national deity of the Hebrews to be characterized as the revealer of mysteries, for this was the function of Nebo in the Babylonian pantheon.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEBO

SPECIAL TOPIC: MARDUK

▣ "God of gods and Lord of kings" As Daniel had described Nebuchadnezzar II as "king of kings" (cf. Dan. 2:37), now he realizes that the God of Daniel (Judah) is the supreme Deity!

entries.title: Daniel 2:48 "Daniel was promoted"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:48 "Daniel was promoted" He became a governor of the province of Babylon and the head of the wise men.

▣
NASB, NRSV, JPSOA   "chief prefect"
NKJV   "chief administrator"
TEV   "the head"
NJB   "head"

These two Aramaic terms (BDB 1112, 1104) usually denote governmental leadership (cf. Dan. 3:2,3,27; 6:8), but here they denote leadership over the guild of wise men.

entries.title: Daniel 2:49 "And Daniel made request of the king"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:49 "And Daniel made request of the king" Daniel did not forget his prayer partners and they, too, were put in places of authority. This distinction between Daniel's task and the other three Hebrew children sets the stage of Daniel 3 where Daniel apparently is not present.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Was Daniel violating his Jewish heritage by being apart of this group of wise men?
  2. What specific things does Daniel praise God for in Dan. 2:20-23?
  3. Why did God reveal this dream of four successive empires to Nebuchadnezzar?
  4. How many kingdoms does Daniel mention and who are they?
  5. Why is Dan. 2:44 so important in interpreting Daniel?
  6. Who or what does the stone symbolize?

entries.title: Daniel 3:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:1 The LXX has an added phrase which dates this event as "in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar," which would be 587 B.C. This is one of the dates for exiles being taken from Jerusalaem and the destruction of the city and the temple.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

▣ "an image of gold" The image (BDB 1109 ‒ statue, form) may have been similar to the vision of a human person made of four metals from chapter 2. It is either

  1. an elongated human form
  2. a tall obelisk of uncertain shape

The Aramaic term can mean "obelisk." The normal physical proportions of the human body is five to one, but the image's height and width would be ten to one. A large platform has been found six miles from the ruins of the ancient city of Babylon, which measures forty-five feet by forty-five feet by eighteen feet. This could have been the base of this image.

▣ "of gold" This seems to mean overlaid with gold and we have biblical and secular examples of this, such as

  1. Aaron's golden calf (Exod. 32)
  2. Isaiah 40:19; 41:7; 44:10
  3. Jeremiah 10:4,14
  4. Herodotus 1.183

▣ "sixty cubits and its width was six cubits" This would make the image about ninety feet tall by nine feet wide if we base our measurements on a cubit (BDB 1081) as being eighteen inches, which denotes the distance from the longest finger to the elbow of a normal sized human being of that period. The Colossus of Rhodes was seventy cubits high (i.e., 105 feet), so this was not out of the realm of ancient technology. See IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 735.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CUBIT

▣ "the plain of Dura" The term (BDB 1087) seems to come from the "duru" which means "an enclosing wall" or "fortress" (Akkadian). We have found several documents from Babylon which mention the Plain of Dura. However, its exact location is uncertain. With the finding of the large base several miles from the city of Babylon, this is a possibility.

entries.title: Daniel Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
DANIEL 3

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB (MT versing)

3:1-7 3:1-7 3:1-7 3:1-7 3:1-7
Worship of the Image Daniel's Friends Disobey the King   Daniel's Three Friends Are Accused of Disobedience The Denunciation and Condemnation of the Jews
3:8-12 3:8-15 3:8-12 3:8-12 3:8-23
3:13-15   3:13-15 3:13-15  
3:16-18 3:16-18 3:16-18 3:16-18  
Danielsl Friends Protected Saved in the Fiery Trial   Daniel's Three Friends Are Sentenced to Death  
3:19-23 3:19-23 3:19-23 3:19-23 The King Acknowledges the Miracle
3:24-27 3:24-25 3:24-30 3:24a 3:24-29
    (25b)
      3:24b

  Nebuchadnezzar Praises God   The Three Men Are Released and Promoted  
  3:26-30   3:26-27     (26-27) 
3:28-30     3:28  
      3:29

        Nebuchadnezzar's Proclamation
        3:31-30
(in other translations, 4:1-3)

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This chapter shows that the faith of Daniel is equally shared by his three exiled friends. There has been much speculation on why Daniel was not present that day on the Plains of Dura.
    1. he was sick
    2. he was on assignment
    3. Hippolytus supposed he was watching from a distance (NET Bible, p. 1538, #14)
    4. the Jewish Study Bible suggests chapter 3 was a separate document that circulated independantly for many years

  2. This chapter is characterized by
    1. lists
    2. the repeating of these lists
      1. names of government officials (cf. Dan. 3:2,3,27)
      2. names of musical instruments (cf. Dan. 3:5,7,10,15)
      3. names of people groups (cf. Dan. 3:4,7; 4:1; 6:25)
      4. the three Hebrew youths (cf. Dan. 3:12,13,14,16,19,20,22,23,26 [twice],28,29,30)

  3. The theological issue of God's sovereignty (i.e., Dan. 2:21; see full note there) continues. He is God and He rewards those who trust (cf. Dan. 3:28) Him.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Daniel 3:2 "the king sent word to assemble"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:2 "the king sent word to assemble" We have, from Sargon II's records, examples of this same type of royal assembly, possibly an annual "loyalty oath."

entries.title: Daniel 3:2-3,5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:2-3,5 These eight categories of governmental officials come from Persian words (NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 604). However, this by itself, does not necessitate a later date for the composition of Daniel. It is probable that the writings of Daniel were edited and compiled after his death in the Persian period (i.e., Cyrus II).

Loan words by themselves do not indicate the original date of the writing.

  1. loan words common in ANE
  2. later Jewish compilers update the terminology

SPECIAL TOPIC: SCRIBES

entries.title: Daniel 3:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:3 The repetitive nature of this chapter, both in the listing of the government officials and the musical instruments, is characteristic of

  1. Hebraic writing
  2. obelistic writing

▣ "satraps" This Aramaic governmental term (BDB 1080) reflects a Median word which means "protector of the land." In the later Persian Empire it referred to the twenty governors (Herodotus) of the provinces (cf. Ezra 8:36; Esther 3:12; 8:9; 9:3), but its exact meaning in the earlier neo-Babylonian Empire is uncertain, possibly "prince" (cf. TEV).

▣ "prefects" The meaning of this Aramaic governmental term (BDB 1104) is uncertain, possibly an Akkadian term for those who report directly to the satraps. Daniel was appointed to this position over all the wise men of Babylon in Dan. 2:48.

▣ "governors" The meaning of this Aramaic governmental term (BDB 1108) is also uncertain. The related Hebrew term denotes "governors" (cf. 1 Kgs. 10:15; 20:24; 2 Kgs. 18:24; often in Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther; Isa. 36:9; Jer. 51:23,28,57; and several times in the post-exilic prophets).

▣ "counselors" This is another Aramaic governmental term (BDB 1078) of uncertain meaning. The typical translation is "counselor," but some scholars think it refers to

  1. a military position (BDB 1078)
  2. "treasurers" (cf. Ezra 7:21)

▣ "magistrates" This Aramaic governmental term (BDB 1118) is also uncertain. William Holladay, A Concise Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, says it refers to a police official (p. 425) from a Persian loan word.

▣ "the rulers of the provinces" This refers to lesser governmental officials (BDB 1097). This event was a gathering of all governmental workers of all levels (cf. Dan. 3:4,7).

entries.title: Daniel 3:4-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:4-7 The call for "all" the peoples to bow down and worship the image must be an example of "representative government." All the peoples" (i.e., languages, nations) were not on the Plain of Dura that day, but their appointed governmental leaders were. This is similar "representative government" to Exod. 19:7, where Moses called the tribal leaders to ratify the covenant of YHWH.

entries.title: Daniel 3:5,7,10 "at the moment you hear the sound of"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:5,7,10 "at the moment you hear the sound of" This list of musical instruments refers to the Babylonian national orchestra. This may have been the Babylonian national anthem (cf. Dan. 3:10). We have a record from Babylonian documents of a similar party where 150 musicians played. It is obvious that the neo-Babylonians enjoyed music and included it in all of their festive occasions.

3:5
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NJB, JPS, NIV, NEB, LXX  "horn"
Peshitta  "trumpet"

In Daniel 7:7-8,11,20,21,24 this Aramaic word (BDB 1111) refers to an animal horn. Here, it refers to a musical instrument, possibly made from an animal horn.

▣
NASB, NKJV, NIV, Peshitta  "flute"
NRSV, NJB, JPS, NEB, LXX  "pipe"

The Aramaic term (BDB 1117) refers to some type of wind instrument.

▣
NASB, NRSV, NJB, LXX  "lyre"
NKJV, Peshitta  "harp"
JPS, NIV, NEB  "zither"

This is a Greek loan word (kitharis), which denotes a stringed instrument (harp, BDB 1111).

▣
NASB, NRSV, LXX  "trigon"
NJB  "zither"
JPS, NIV, NEB  "triangle"
Peshitta  sackbut"

This reflects another Greek loan word (sambukē), which denotes a stringed instrument with four strings (BDB 1113).

▣
NASB, JPS, Peshitta  "psaltery"
NRSV, NJB, NIV, LXX  "harp"
NEB  "dulcimer"

This (BDB 1108) denotes a triangular shaped stringed instrument with a sounding board (William Holladay, A Concise Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament, p. 418).

▣
NASB, NJB  "bagpipe"
NRSV  "drum"
NEB  "music"
LXX  "a symphony of all kinds of musical instruments"
Peshitta  "all kinds of music"

There is confusion in the English translation as to how many musical instruments are listed. The Masoretic Text and the Septuagint have only five in Dan. 3:7, but this sixth one is listed in Dan. 3:5 and 10. It may refer to a double pipe similar to a Pan flute (BDB 1104).

It is also possible that this last term means "in unison" (cf. NKJV, TEV, LXX, Peshitta).

▣ "fall down and worship" Both VERBS are Peal IMPERFECT (BDB 1103 and 1104). This shows the religious and political significance of this human image (cf. Dan. 3:12). This is the reason that the three Hebrew children refused to participate. It is uncertain if the Neo-Babylonian rulers claimed deity (the image as a representative of Nebuchadnezzar, cf. Dan. 2:38), as did the Pharaohs of Egypt and some later Caesars of Rome.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WORSHIP

entries.title: Daniel 3:6,15 "immediately"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:6,15 "immediately" Literally this is "same hour" (BDB 1116, cf. Dan. 4:30; 5:5; see note at Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 1, p. 183). This is the first use of the term "hour" in the OT. There is some discussion if the term and concept began with the Babylonians or the Greeks. We must remember that this does not refer to our precise sixty minutes because they were using more crude timing instruments.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOUR

▣ "cast into the midst of a furnace of blazing fire" Because of the description found in Daniel 3 and also because of archaeology discoveries, it seems that this was a large, domed kiln with an opening at the top and an earthen ramp leading up to it. It also had a door on the bottom for putting in charcoal and taking out ashes.

This was a common form of capital punishment during this period (cf. Code of Hammurabi 110,157 and Jer. 29:22).

entries.title: Daniel 3:8 "certain Chaldeans"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:8 "certain Chaldeans" It must be remembered that "Chaldeans" can be

  1. a racial group of the southern Tigris-Euphrates River Valley (cf. Dan. 5:30)
  2. a group of wise men and priests (cf. Dan. 2:2,4,5,10; 3:8; 4:7; 5:7,11)

In this context, #2 makes more sense. Remember, words have meaning only in sentences and sentences have meaning only in paragraphs.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

▣ "brought charges against the Jews" This is literally "chewed up the pieces of" (cf. Dan. 6:25, NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p.396, #5). This is a very strong phrase (BDB 1080, Peal PERFECT and BDB 1111) which shows the vehemence of the charges. From the text it is obvious that there was jealousy involved because these Jewish young men had been assigned a place of leadership (cf. Dan. 3:12; 6:4). Also, there was an ethnic prejudice because of the mention of their origin (cf. Dan. 3:12).

For "Jews" (BDB 1095) see SPECIAL TOPIC: JEWS

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW PEOPLE

entries.title: Daniel 3:9 "O king, live forever"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:9 "O king, live forever" See note at Dan. 2:4 and SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('OLAM)

entries.title: Daniel 3:12 "namely, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:12 "namely, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego" It is uncertain where Daniel was at this time. It could be that he was sick or on a governmental assignment. This would be unusual because all the other government officials were present.

For a summary of the possibilities related to Daniel's absence see The Expositor's Bible Commentary, vol. 7, pp. 55-56.

For the Babylonian meaning of these names, see Dan. 1:7.

▣ "have disregarded you; they do not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up" Imagine the peer pressure that there must have been on these young men who were so far from home and who were placed in such important places of leadership.

Nebuchadnezzar II must have forgotten his praise of YHWH from Dan. 2:46-47.

entries.title: Daniel 3:13 "in rage and anger"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:13 "in rage and anger" Nebuchadnezzar II was prone to anger (cf. Dan. 2:12; 3:19). Oriental kings were not accustomed to people disobeying their orders!

This phrase (BDB 1112 and 1095) is called a hendiadys, which is characteristic of Daniel writing style. See note at Dan. 2:12. The king was so angry that he physically shook!

entries.title: Daniel 3:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:14 Nebuchadnezzar II tries to give them a second chance (cf. Dan. 3:15, they were excellent administrators), but their refusal just proves to intensify his anger. He took their rejection of his gods as a personal rejection.

entries.title: Daniel 3:15 "what god is there who can deliver you out of my hands"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:15 "what god is there who can deliver you out of my hands" This is theologically similar to 2 Kgs. 18:33 and 19:12. YHWH is openly challenged to demonstrate His existence, power, and compassion to those who trust Him (cf. Dan. 3:28). YHWH reveals Himself to the nations by showing His sovereignty and love for His covenant people.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

entries.title: Daniel 3:17 "If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the furnace of blazing fire"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:17 "If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the furnace of blazing fire" Nebuchadnezzar II had made this a contest between the gods of Babylon and the God of Judah by asserting that no one could deliver them out of his hand (cf. Dan. 3:15). The descriptive title, "the God who is able," is also in Dan. 3:29 and in the NT at Rom. 16:25; Eph. 3:20; Jude 24.

The NET Bible translates this phrase as "If our God whom we are serving exists, he is able to rescue us from the furnace of blazing fire." The Anchor Bible, vol. 23, also has a translation that tries to employ the Aramaic word "exist" (BDB 1095, KB 410 [Hebrew root]) — "If there is a God able to save us, such as our God, he will save us from the white-hot furnace" (p. 155).

SPECIAL TOPIC: DESCRIPTIVE TITLES FOR GOD

entries.title: Daniel 3:18 "But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king that we are not going to serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:18 "But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king that we are not going to serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up" They believed that God was able, but they were not being presumptuous by demanding a miracle. They had faith in God, not in circumstances (i.e., Job 13:15).

entries.title: Daniel 3:19 "seven times more than it was usually heated"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:19 "seven times more than it was usually heated" This is an obvious use of figurative language (cf. v. 22). It simply means that the brick kiln was heated as hot as it possibly could be heated. The hyperbole reflects Nebuchadnezzar II's anger!

SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #4

3:20
NASB  "valiant warriors"
NKJV  "mighty men"
NRSV  "some of the strongest guards"
TEV, REB. JPSOA  "the strongest men"
NJB  "certain stalwarts from his army"

The CONSTRUCT (BDB 1086 and 1093) implies his strongest military guards. Nebuchadnezzar's anger will result in the death of these valued servants (cf. Dan. 3:22).

entries.title: Daniel 3:21 "their trousers, their coats, their caps, and their other clothes"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:21 "their trousers, their coats, their caps, and their other clothes" This was their official attire showing the high governmental level they had attained in the neo-Babylonian empire.

entries.title: Daniel 3:22 "the furnace had been made extremely hot, the flame of the fire slew those men"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:22 "the furnace had been made extremely hot, the flame of the fire slew those men" This is a graphic detail of the extreme heat into which the three Hebrew boys were thrown. The fall itself should have killed them, much less the temperature.

entries.title: Daniel 3:23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:23 After this verse is the place where the Septuagint inserts two Apocryphal writings, "The Song of the Three Youths" and "The Prayer of Assariah." These two Apocryphal writings assert that the dew of heaven brought by the angel of the Lord kept the Hebrew youths from death.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

entries.title: Daniel 3:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:24 Notice that Nebuchadnezzar, talking to his counselors, says, "did not we cast?" He wants to spread the blame.

entries.title: Daniel 3:25 "I see four men loosed and walking about in the midst of the fire"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:25 "I see four men loosed and walking about in the midst of the fire" There has been much discussion about how Nebuchadnezzar II could see these men. It seems that the brick kiln was a domed structure with a place at the bottom for the removal of ashes. Apparently, he looked through the hole in the bottom and saw the young men walking about.

▣ "the fourth is like a son of the gods" This is simply polytheistic jargon for a supernatural being. A considerable amount of speculation has been made about this fourth personage. He is an angel of the Lord (cf. Dan. 3:28 also 6:22). It is humorous to note that when Nebuchadnezzar II calls the boys out by name, he makes no mention of that fourth person!

SPECIAL TOPIC: sons of. . .

SPECIAL TOPIC: The Angel of the Lord

entries.title: Daniel 3:27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:27 In the presence of all his civil, military, and police officials Nebuchadnezzar is forced to acknowledge the God of Judah (cf. Dan. 3:28-29) for the second time (i.e., Dan. 2:46-49).

This striking evidence of God's protection is similar to Isa. 43:2 which used water and fire imagery. In Isaiah it is imagery for earthly struggles and persecution, but in Daniel it is literal (cf. Heb. 11:34).

entries.title: Daniel 3:28 "who put their trust in Him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:28 "who put their trust in Him" Not only is the One True God emphasized, but also the need for personal, active trust in Him (BDB 1113, Hithpael PERFECT, cf. Isa. 26:3-4)! Trust is crucial in biblical faith.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT

entries.title: Daniel 3:28-29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:28-29 This statement is very similar to Dan. 2:46-48. It is an outburst of a fearful polytheist in the face of the power of YHWH. It is not Nebuchadnezzar's confession of faith.

entries.title: Daniel 3:29 "shall be torn limb from limb"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:29 "shall be torn limb from limb" This was an ancient form of ANE execution, as was being burned (cf. Dan. 2:5; 1 Sam. 15:33).

▣ "their houses reduced to a rubbish heap" This was also an ancient form of punishment and shame (cf. Dan. 2:5; Ezra 6:11).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why were the Chaldeans of Dan. 3:8 out to get the Hebrew youths?
  2. Was the image political or religious?
  3. What are the implications of Dan. 3:17 and 18 for our lives?
  4. Who was the fourth person in the flames?

entries.title: Daniel 4:1 "Nebuchadnezzar"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:1 "Nebuchadnezzar" Dan. 4:1-3 is in chapter 3 in the Hebrew Bible, but this context obviously starts a new section. His name may mean "may Nebo guard the boundary" (cf. Dan. 4:8). See full note at Dan. 1:1.

▣ "all the peoples, nations, and men of every language" We must remember that the kingdom of neo-Babylon included many language groups (cf. Dan. 3:4,7,29; 6:25). This chapter seems to be a royal decree issued to praise the God of Judah for Nebuchadnezzar's restoration.

▣ "in all the earth" This, of course, refers to the known world of that day and is an example of a non-literal exaggeration (hyperbole). See G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, pp. 22,110-117,121,133,181.

▣ "May your peace abound" This is parallel to Dan. 6:25 (cf. Ezra 4:17). This was a common idiom for initial greetings, meaning "welfare," "prosperity" (BDB 1116). Nebuchadnezzar II is declaring, in a royal decree, the praises of the God of Judah, who he calls "the Most High God" (BDB 1080, 1106 both with the DEFINITE ARTICLE, see Hebrew form at BDB 43; SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.).
