READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHT

  1. The verse numbering differs from translation to translation because Dan. 4:1-3 in the NASB is 3:31-33 in the original Aramaic text.

  2. There are several recurrent themes
    1. praise of YHWH
    2. dream interpretation by YHWH
    3. sovereignty of YHWH

  3. There are many differences between the MT (Masoretic Text) and the LXX (Septuagint) in Daniel, chapters 4-6.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT (MT)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT (LXX)

  4. This chapter seems to be a very Jewish theological document. It has long been disputed that a pagan polytheist like Nebuchadnezzar II could compose a chapter like this by himself (this chapter is in the FIRST PERSON SINGULAR except for the period of Nebuchadnezzar's madness). It is obvious from the book of Esther that King Ahasuerus (Xerxes I) allowed both Haman and Mordecai to compose documents of their own in his name. Daniel is the Jewish theological influence behind this chapter.

  5. Some of the specific reasons for why Nebuchadnezzar II could not have written this chapter are
    1. theological content, Dan. 4:3
    2. the style is in line with the rest of the book of Daniel
    3. Nebuchadnezzar is spoken of in the third person, Dan. 4:25-30
    4. Dan. 4:29 seems to be written for non-Babylonian people

  6. W.A. Criswell and E. J. Young assert that Nebuchadnezzar II is converted to the worship of YHWH because of this final, great sign of Daniel 4. However, because of Dan. 4:8, it is obvious to me that although he was greatly impressed, he was not willing to convert to the monotheism of Israel. All known Babylonian documents of the period refer to him as a worshiper of Marduk.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: MARDUK

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Daniel 4:2 "the signs and wonders which the Most High God has done for me."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:2 "the signs and wonders which the Most High God has done for me." Nebuchadnezzar II has now been confronted with YHWH in chapters 2, 3, and 4. The accumulating evidence of the existence, sovereignty, and covenant loyalty of the Jewish God is overwhelming.

The book of Daniel is characterized by lists and hendiadys. See the third paragraph of Dan. 2:12. The corresponding Hebrew terms for "signs," and "wonders" are often used together (cf. Exod. 7:3; 8:23; Deut. 4:34; 6:22; 7:19; 13:1,2; 26:8; 28:46; 29:3; 34:11; Neh. 9:10; Ps. 105:27; 135:9; Jer. 32:20). What God did for Israel in the Exodus (cf. Acts 7:36) He now displays to pagan kings (Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, and Darius). The revelation continues in the life of Jesus (cf. Acts 2:22) and the gospel proclamation (cf. Acts 2:43; 4:30; 5:12; 8:13; 14:3). However, in the NT these two terms are usually associated with false Messiahs (cf. Matt. 24:24; Mark 13:22) or the Jewish people demanding evidence of Jesus' Messiahship (cf. Matt. 12:39; 16:1; John 4:48). God wants the world to know Him!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIGN

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Daniel 4:3 "His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:3 "His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom" This verse is a poetic/hymnic text extolling YHWH.

  1. "His signs. . .and wonders" (cf. Dan. 6:27). God is actively involved in the lives of these Near Eastern kings (cf. chapters 2;3;4;5;6) to demonstrate His power and presence.
  2. "everlasting kingdom" (cf. Dan. 4:34; 2:44; 6:26; 7:14,26). This is in contrast to the changing kingdom represented by the vision of chapter 2. These last two lines of poetry are very similar to the Hebrew of Ps. 145:13; also see Ps. 45:6; Lam. 5:19.
  3. "dominion is from generation to generation." God's people are safe and secure in Him in each and every generation, even amidst war and exile. Physical circumstances (destruction of Jerusalem and the temple) do not affect the peace and presence of God in the lives of His followers. These words and phrases are in a parallel relationship in Dan. 4:3. Semitic poetry must be interpreted in light of thought parallels, not rhyme.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: IMMANUEL'S PERSON AND REIGN

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGDOM OF GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

4:4
NASB  "was at ease in my house and flourishing in my palace"
NKJV  "was at rest in my house, and flourishing in my palace"
NRSV  "was living at ease in my home and prospering in my palace"
TEV  "was living comfortably in my palace"
NJB  "was living comfortably in my house, prosperously in my palace"

This is another example of Semitic parallelism (as is Dan. 4:5). Nebuchadnezzar II was experiencing the kind of prosperity that he had wished for his hearers in Dan. 4:1.

This seems to be an allusion to the up-coming dream of a glorious tree. This type of human arrogance is prophesied in Isa. 47:7,8. Isaiah 13-14 and 46-47 are oracles of judgment against Babylon, which becomes the biblical symbol of human arrogance and pride (similar to the Tower of Babel and Edom).

entries.title: Daniel 4:5 "I saw a dream. . .the visions in my mind"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:5 "I saw a dream. . .the visions in my mind" Dreams were often thought to be the gods revealing information to ANE kings. Therefore, these rulers had to have people to interpret these revelations (biblical examples would be Joseph and Daniel). For a good discussion of this cultural expectation, see John H. Walton, Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament: Introducing the Conceptual World of the Hebrew Bible, p. 243 and footnote #50.

▣ "fearful" There are two similar Aramaic roots for fear and dismay that are used often in Daniel, usually connected to the visions.

  1. בהל (BDB 1084)
    1. "in haste" caused by fear ‒ Dan. 2:25; 3:24; 6:19
    2. fear caused by vision/dream ‒ Dan. 4:5,19; 5:6,10; 7:15,28
  2. דחל (BDB 1087)
    1. fear caused by a vision/dream ‒ Dan. 2:31; 4:5
    2. fear of Nebuchadnezzar's power ‒ Dan. 5:19
    3. part of Nebuchadnezzar's decree ‒ Dan. 6:26
    4. in description of the 4th beast ‒ Dan. 7:7,19

entries.title: Daniel 4:5-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 4:5-7 Again the impotence of Neo-Babylon and its wise men is contrasted with the wise power and control of the God of Judah and her people.

entries.title: Daniel 4:6 "So I gave orders"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 4:6 "So I gave orders" Nebuchadnezzar II can make decrees (cf. Dan. 2:9,15; 3:10,29), but he could not produce the desired result (and neither could his wise men). This is in stark contrast to God's will being accomplished (i.e., Isa. 55:9-11).

entries.title: Daniel 4:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:7 For the meaning of these terms see Dan. 1:20 or 2:2.

▣ "the Chaldeans" See SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

▣ "they could not make known its interpretation" It is unusual that they did not attempt an interpretation, given the fact that Nebuchadnezzar II had revealed the dream. Possibly they would have attempted to interpret it, but were afraid to.

It is surprising that Nebuchadnezzar II calls on the same group of wise men which he previously had no confidence in (cf. Dan. 2:4-13), and also that he had forgotten his own decrees (Dan. 2:4-49; 3:29) relating to YHWH. This seems to imply that several documents about Daniel circulated separately and were later combined.

Modern Bible scholars do not know who or when the final form of the OT books was decided. Believers assume inspiration extends to editors and scribes.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

entries.title: Daniel 4:8 "Daniel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:8 "Daniel" The name means "God is my judge" (BDB 1088). See full note at Dan. 1:6.

▣ "Belteshazzar" Daniel's name implies a Babylonian deity, "may_______ protect his life" (BDB 1084). The Babylonian pantheon developed from the Sumerian pantheon. Originally deities were the patrons of specific cities. The god, Marduk, was known as "lord." Bel was originally the patron god of the city of Nippur, but came to be identified with Marduk, the pagan god of the city of Babylon (i.e. Bel, cf Isa. 46:1; Jer. 50:2; 51:44). It is uncertain exactly which god is implied by Daniel's name, but Marduk became the chief god of the city of Babylon. Although Bel looks to be a part of Daniel's Babylonian name, it is not. Daniel 4:8 functions as a parenthesis explaining the name, Belteshazzar (cf. NKJV, NRSV, TEV).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MARDUK

SPECIAL TOPIC: BEL

▣
NASB, NRSV  "a spirit of the holy gods"
NKJV  "the Spirit of the Holy God"
TEV, NJB, JPS, NEB, REB, Peshitta  "the spirit of the holy gods"

If this phrase is from a polytheist (cf. Dan. 4:8a; 5:11,14) then surely this is not a reference to YHWH or His Spirit (the textual evidence is that the qualifying ADJECTIVE "holy" is PLURAL, however, there is a Hebrew PLURAL equivalent in Josh. 24:19, although the LXX translation implies that it does refer to YHWH and that Nebuchadnezzar was a believer). The context (Dan. 4:9) implies that Nebuchadnezzar II remembered Daniel's previous help of dream interpretation in chapter 2; if so, then this could be translated like the NKJV (cf. Dan. 4:9,18). Remember the consistent theological emphasis is YHWH's power and control versus the Babylonian pantheon and government (cf. Dan. 2:20-23).

"The spirit" would be understood as YHWH's influence in Daniel's giftedness (cf. Dan. 2:27-28,30,47).

This Aramaic phrase is similar to the Hebrew phrase used of Joseph in Gen. 41:38. Both Joseph and Daniel served pagan kings and interpreted their dreams by divine revelations.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOLY

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

entries.title: Daniel 4:9 "the chief of the magicians"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:9 "the chief of the magicians" Daniel was trained in the language and traditions of the Chaldeans (cf. Dan. 1:4). He was made the leader of the Babylonian wise men (cf. Dan. 1:20; 2:48). Daniel's abilities were from YHWH, not from Babylonian magic. These Babylonian wise men failed again and again (cf. Dan. 2:1-13; 4:7,18). Daniel's position and title caused later Jewish rabbis to criticize his cooperation with pagan culture and governments.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

▣
NASB  "tell me the vision"
NKJV  "explain to me the vision"
NRSV  "hear the dream"
TEV  "this is my dream"
NJB  "this is the dream"
REB, Peshitta  "tell me its interpretation"

From these English translations it is obvious there are at least two ways to interpret the Aramaic text:

  1. Nebuchadnezzar II wanted Daniel to reveal the dream and its interpretation, like chapter 2 (NASB, NKJV)
  2. Nebuchadnezzar II told Daniel the dream (as he did the other wise men, cf. Dan. 4:7 and NRSV, TEV, NJB) and wanted him to give the interpretation. The second makes sense contextually, but demands a revocalization of the Masoretic Consonantal Text. The VOWEL markings in the MT are a later addition and not inspired.

See UBS Text Project, vol. 5, pp. 204-205.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT (MT)

entries.title: Daniel 4:10 "behold"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:10 "behold" A Handbook on the Book of Daniel, by UBS, pp. 106-107, notes that this Aramaic interjection (BDB 1080) and its Hebrew equivalent (BDB 243) are used often in Daniel, but usually not translated.

  1. Aramaic ‒ Dan. 2:31; 4:10,13; 7:2,5,7,8 (twice), 13
  2. Hebrew ‒ Dan. 8:3,5,15,19; 9:18; 10:5,10,16; 11:2; 12:5

Its literary function is to energize the narrative.

▣ "a tree" This was apparently a common symbol of the power and pervasiveness of important men in the Ancient Near East (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 374, 2. e.; cf. Ezek. 17:3,22-24; 19:10-14; 31 and Herodotus 1.108; 7.19).

See a good brief article on the concept of "A cosmic tree at the center of the earth,"

  1. IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 736
  2. John H. Walton, ANE Thought and the OT, pp. 175-176

SPECIAL TOPIC: TREES

▣
NASB. NKJV, Peshitta  "in the midst of the earth"
NRSV, REB  "at the center of the earth"
TEV  "in the middle of the earth"
NJB  "in the middle of the world"

This is an idiomatic way of showing the extent and power of the neo-Babylon empire (cf. Dan. 2:38-39; 4:20-22). As always interpreters must take this figurative (hyperbolic) language in the sense it would have been used by a king in the ancient Near East. Nebuchadnezzar II controlled the known world.

entries.title: Daniel 4:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:11 This verse has all PARTICIPLES, showing continuing action. The tree (kingdom) was still expanding.

▣"its height reached to the sky" This phrase is reminiscent of the Tower of Babel in Gen. 11:4, which also denotes human arrogance and pride (cf. Isa. 14:14).

▣ "it was visible to the end of the whole earth" This is obviously poetic hyperbole.

entries.title: Daniel 4:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 4:12 The neo-Babylonian empire provided a safe and growing economic climate.

entries.title: Daniel 4:13 "the angelic watcher"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:13 "the angelic watcher" This means "one that stays awake" (BDB 1105). The Hebrew counterpart is used of God in Ps. 121:4. This Aramaic word and concept is used only in this chapter in the entire Bible. It is SINGULAR in Dan. 4:13 but PLURAL in 4:17. The Hebrew counterpart is used

  1. of angels in the inter-testamental books of Jubilees (4:15) and I Enoch (1:5)
  2. for fallen angels (cf. I Enoch 10-16)
  3. It has been found in Cave 1 of the Qumran Text in "the Genesis Apocraphon" and is used for fallen angels (see SPECIAL TOPIC: DEMONS [fallen angels]).
  4. It is also known to be the title for the messenger of the gods in the Canaanite pantheon (Ras Shamra texts from Ugarit).

We are uncertain if this is an allusion to Babylonian mythology or simply a unique way to refer to a special type of angel who kept watch over "the cosmic tree." For a good brief article on "watchers," see IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 736.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

▣ "a holy one" Nebuchadnezzar II recognized that "the watcher" was a single being from the divine realm (hendiadys). We must be careful of putting too much weight on the words of a pagan king, who was a polytheist and wordshiped Marduk.

This "holy one" declared the divine judgment on Nebuchadnezzar II (for a period of time). Angels serve to implement God's will.

  1. revelation
  2. judgment
  3. deliverance
  4. restoration
  5. protection

It is interesting that Millard Erickson, in his Christian Theology 2nd ed., p. 462, asserts that the collective term "angels" is made up of

  1. "sons of the Elohim" (Job 1:6; 2:1,6; see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.)
  2. "sons of Elim" (Ps. 29:1; 89:6)
  3. "holy ones" (Ps. 89:5,7)
  4. "watchers" (Dan. 4:13,17,23)
  5. "the council" (Ps. 89:7)
  6. "the assembly" (Ps. 89:5)
  7. "host of heaven," used many times; see SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: godly ones, holy ones

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

▣ "descended from heaven" Since the word "heaven" is also used in Dan. 4:11b, however in a different sense, this is a good opportunity to emphasize the crucial aspect of context in interpretation. Lexicons and dictionaries do not give meaning, only literary (or verbal) contexts give meaning. In 4:11 the term refers to the sky (cf. Dan. 4:15d, see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN), but in Dan. 4:13 (cf. 4:26-31, see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN) it refers to the dwelling place of God or the gods.

entries.title: Daniel 4:14 "He shouted out"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 4:14 "He shouted out" Apparently the reader is meant to understand that one of the holy watchers cried out to the other angelic beings (cf. Dan. 4:17). Remember, however, this is a highly symbolic and figurative dream, not time-space reality.

entries.title: Daniel 4:15 "a band of iron"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:15 "a band of iron" There has been much discussion about the band.

  1. Most commentators assume that it was for the protection of the stump.
  2. Although some see it as being related to the restraints that bound Nebuchadnezzar II during the time that he was deranged.
  3. The LXX sees it as referring to the king himself as a symbol of his restoration to the throne.

The tree stands for the kingship of Nebuchadnezzar II. God cuts down/brings down his kingdom (cf. Isa. 10:33-34; Ezek. 17:22-24). However, the stump remains and will regenerate.

This imagery is also used of the stump of Jesse (i.e., the Messiah, cf. Isa. 11:1; 53:2; Jer. 23:5; 33:15). This is the origin of the Messianic term "Branch" (i.e., netzer, cf. Isa. 4:2; Zech. 3:8; 6:12).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BRANCH OF THE LORD

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS THE NAZARENE

▣
NASB  "let him share with the beasts in the grass of the earth"
NKJV  "let him graze with the beasts on the grass of the earth"
NRSV  "let his lot be with the animals of the field in the grass of the earth"
TEV  "let him live with the animals and the plants"
NJB  "have its lot with the animals, eating grass"

As you can tell by these English translations, there are two ways to understand this ambiguous phrase.

  1. The king will live outdoors in the royal gardens with the domestic animals (NASB, NRSV, TEV).
  2. The king will eat grass like the domestic animals (NKJV, NJB).

entries.title: Daniel 4:16 "Let his mind"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:16 "Let his mind" This word is literally "heart," which in Hebrew was imagery for the mental processes and choices of the person.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

▣
NASB  "And let seven periods of time pass over him"
NKJV, NRSV  "let seven times pass over him"
TEV  "for seven years"
NJB, REB  "seven times shall pass over him"
Peshitta  "and let seven seasons change over him"

This phrase becomes theologically significant because

  1. the term "seven" is used both literally and figuratively in the Bible (see SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #4). In Hebrew thought it is the perfect number going back to the consummation of creation week of Genesis 1 (i.e., the day God rested).
  2. the term "time" is used in several of the prophecies of Daniel. Is it referring to a specific period of time or a full or perfect period of time? These possibilities must be answered from context, not philology or lexicology.

The LXX has "seven years," but the term implies "seasons," "annual seasons." The time element is divinely set and known but recorded for us in a purposefully ambiguous way.

entries.title: Daniel 4:17 "This sentence is by the decree of the angelic watchers, And the decision is a command of the holy ones"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:17 "This sentence is by the decree of the angelic watchers,
  And the decision is a command of the holy ones" This seems to imply that the angels made the decision on their own, but Dan. 4:24 shows the ultimate source of this decision was the Most High God. Again, it is important to realize that the Jews were uncertain at this time about their covenant relationship with YHWH because the temple and Jerusalem (cf. Deut. 12:10) had been destroyed and the Davidic king taken into exile (cf. 2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17). They needed Him to show them that He was in control of all of world history.

The concluding part of this verse is very similar in theological emphasis to Dan. 2:20. The entire book of Daniel makes this assertion again and again. To the Ancient Near East the historical situation looked as if YHWH had been defeated by the Babylonian gods, but in reality YHWH was using the empires of the Fertile Crescent (Assyria, Babylon, Persia) to execute His will related to His people (cf. Isa. 10:5; Jer. 51:20). God's people were reaping the consequences of idolatry and rebellion (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-29). God needed to reassure His people and inform the pagan empires (Dan. 4:25) of the source of their current political and military prowess (i.e., Dan. 2:21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: godly ones, holy ones

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

entries.title: Daniel 4:18 "This is the dream. . .tell me its interpretation"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:18 "This is the dream. . .tell me its interpretation" In the ANE dreams and visions were often used to communicate divine messages to humans. Two good articles are:

  1. John H. Walton, ANE Thought and the OT, p. 243
  2. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, pp. 721-724

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣ "inasmuch as none of the wise men of my kingdom is able" This is a recurrent theme (cf. Dan. 1:20; 2:4-13; 4:7; 5:7-8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVINATION

entries.title: Daniel 4:19 "Daniel. . .was appalled for a while"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:19 "Daniel. . .was appalled for a while" Daniel was apparently very loyal to Nebuchadnezzar II and regretted having to reveal this judgment. Several times in the book of Daniel, Daniel is spiritually and physically affected by the revelations he receives (cf. Dan. 7:15,28; 8:27; 10:16,17).

It seems that "appalled" and "alarmed" are parallel grammatical structures so characteristic of the book of Daniel.

▣ "do not let the dream or its interpretation alarm you" Nebuchadnezzar II had himself been alarmed by this dream (cf. Dan. 4:5).

▣ "those who hate you. . .to your adversaries" This is another of many parallel phrases. This literary style characterizes the entire book (cf. Dan. 4:21c,d, and e,f; 22a,b; 23c,d).

entries.title: Daniel 4:22 "it is you, O king"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 4:22 "it is you, O king" The king himself as the representative of his empire is the focus of the dream, as in Daniel 2 (2:38b, "you are the head of gold").

entries.title: Daniel 4:25 "until you recognize that the Most High is ruler over the realm of mankind, and bestows it on whomever He wishes"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:25 "until you recognize that the Most High is ruler over the realm of mankind, and bestows it on whomever He wishes" See full note at Dan. 4:17. This is the central and recurrent theme of Daniel (cf. Ps. 83:18; 97:9; Jer. 27:5; Romans 9-11).

The LXX adds a temporal note at the beginning of this chapter and chapter 3 ("in the eighteenth year"). This would designate the year that Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed. Nebuchadnezzar II needed to recognize YHWH's permission for his apparent victory (i.e., Dan. 2:21).

4:26
NASB  "it is Heaven that rules"
NKJV  "Heaven rules"
NRSV  "Heaven is sovereign"
TEV  "God rules all the world"
NJB  "the Most HIgh rules over human sovereignty"
Peshitta  "that authority is from heaven"

This is a circumlocution, a way of referring to deity without using a title/name (cf. Matt. 3:2, "kingdom of heaven"; and Luke 15:18,21, "sinned against heaven").

entries.title: Daniel 4:27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:27 Daniel's advice to Nebuchadnezzar recognizes the biblical worldview (OT) that there is a holy God who requires righteousness. These words to a proud eastern monarch shows the basic ethical nature of reality. Kings were meant to act for the welfare of the people.

Sin and rebellion are the problem, but God is a God of mercy (cf. Isa. 55:6-7; Ezek. 18:21-22). These words to Nebuchadnezzar II show Daniel's understanding that pagans are loved by God and can respond to Him by faith and life. However, these kings will be judged for their actions.

These revelatory words of potential judgment to the Neo-Babylonian King who destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, would have encourage the exiled covenant people. World empires are subject to Israel's God (cf. Dan. 2:21). Even pagan rulers are called on to show mercy and fairness to their subjects.

The parallelism of "sins" and "iniquities" is obvious, but also "righteousness" and "mercy to the poor" are parallel. This reflects the Jewish understanding of almsgiving (in the LXX translation as well as usage in the Aramaic Targums and Talmud, cf. Ps. 112:3,9; Isa. 33:15; Matt. 6:1; 2 Cor. 9:6-11) as an expression of "righteousness" (i.e. God's character, cf. Isa. 58:6-11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALMSGIVING

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

▣
NASB  "break away"
NKJV  "break off"
NRSV  "atone for"
NJB  "break with"
LXX  "redeem"
Peshitta  "get rid of"

This is literally "tear off" or "break off" (BDB 1108, Peal IMPERATIVE, cf. Gen. 27:40). Humans have been given a free will. They must exercise it for righteousness, not self. There are pivotal moments of appropriate choices and accompanying actions. Seize the moral moment! Current choices determine future conditions.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "in case there may be a prolonging of your prosperity" YHWH is warning a proud ANE king to change his ways. The hope would be that he would be spared from judgment. This is very similar to the revelatory word by Jonah that changed the King of Niveveh's ways.

Repentance and faith make a difference! This was even true for the evil King Manassah, who repented and believed at the very end of a terrible reign (cf. 2 Chr. 33:18-20).

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT

entries.title: Daniel 4:28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:28 This summary verse is placed first, similar to Dan. 4:1-3. This verse asserts a great biblical truth—what God says comes to be (cf. Numbers 23:19c; Isa. 40:8; 45:23; 55:11). When all is said and done, humanity's only hope is in the unchanging merciful character of God (cf. Mal. 3:6, see SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD [OT]). His promises are an extension of His character.

The theological difficulty of God's Sovereignty and human free will meet in the concept of covenant. As far as God's promises of redemption, the covenant promises are "unconditional" (one example, "Gen. 15:12-21).

However, on an individual basis, His promises are "conditional" (see Deut. 30:15,19). Often Scripture clearly expresses this by "If. . .then," but if when it is not stated it is implied.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ELECTION/PREDESTINATION AND LTHE NEED FOR A THEOLOGICAL BALANCE

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Daniel 4:29 "he was walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 4:29 "he was walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon" The people of the ANE used the roof in the summertime as a cool place to rest and sleep.

entries.title: Daniel 4:30 "The king reflected and said"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:30 "The king reflected and said" Pride has always been the major problem of fallen humanity (cf. Genesis 3; Isaiah 14; Ezekiel 28; see SPECIAL TOPIC: LIFTED UP). This king had much to be proud of, as he is known from the Babylonian Archives as a great builder. Babylon's Hanging Gardens were one of the Seven Wonders of the World. The city itself had huge double walls. The inner wall of the city was 21 feet thick, 50 cubits high with towers every 60 feet. The outer wall was 11 feet thick, 42 miles in circumference, and 6 feet beyond the outer wall was a man-made moat, which channeled the waters of the Euphrates around the city for protection.

The LXX is very different from the MT in Daniel, chapters 4-6. At this point in the LXX the arrogant king walking on the walls of his palace in the city of Babylon is King Nabonidus, Belshazzar's father (cf. Dan. 5). The Dead Sea Scrolls 4Q242 records Nabonidus' illness and recovering after 7 years. It is entitled "Prayer of Nabonidus."

▣ "by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty" Several of these words are used in Dan. 2:37, where Nebuchadnezzar's possession of these is directly attributed to the God of Judah. All he has is a gift from God, but he thinks it is all from himself (cf. Dan. 4:26,31,32; 2:37,44). Israel is warned of this very attitude in Deuteronomy 8.

entries.title: Daniel 4:31 "a voice came from heaven"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 4:31 "a voice came from heaven" The rabbis assumed that this is the Bath-kol of the inter-biblical period, God's way of confirming His will during that time when there were no prophets in Israel. But, in context, it seems to refer to the decree of the angelic watchers (cf. Dan. 4:13,23).

entries.title: Daniel 4:32-33 "Immediately the word concerning Nebuchadnezzar was fulfilled"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:32-33 "Immediately the word concerning Nebuchadnezzar was fulfilled" If we see this as a psychological illness, his malady is called lycantrophy or boanthrophy (cf. R. K. Harrison's Introduction to the OT, pp. 1115-1117).

There is even some historical documentation supporting Nebuchadnezzar's period of madness.

  1. Berossus (priest of Bel who wrote three history books about Babylon in Greek in the fourth and third centuries B.C.). This tradition is recorded by Josephus (Against Apion 1.19-20).
  2. Eusebius, Praep. Evang. IX.41, preserves the testimony of Abydenus (second century B.C.) that Nebuchadnezzar, in his last days, was possessed by some god or other (cf. R. K. Harrison, Introduction to the Old Testament, p. 1115).

It is also possible to try to connect this imagery to Sumerian myths related to the physical conditions of primative humans (i.e., no regular food, shelter, or other privileges of civilization).

The exact time and nature of Nebuchadnezzar's condition is the fact God set the conditions of his judgment. YHWH controls world events and powers!

▣ "his body was drenched with the dew of heaven" The temperature range in this part of the earth is 120 degrees in summer to below freezing in winter. One can imagine the physical changes which occurred in this man's body as he lived outdoors the year round.

entries.title: Daniel 4:34 "at the end of that period"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:34 "at the end of that period" This refers to the specific time mentioned in Dan. 4:16, "seven periods of time." Most commentators think it refers to years, but this is speculation. However, the specificity confirms that God is in control of Nebuchadnezzar's condition and healing.

The phrase "at that time" of v. 36, also denotes a specific time appointed by the Most High God. Israel's God is in control of history!

▣ "I, Nebuchadnezzar, raised my eyes toward heaven" This is a symbolic way of referring to his acknowledging Israel's God (cf. Dan. 4:36) and His sovereignty (cf. Dan. 4:34-35). As Nebuchadnezzar II "honored" YHWH, the opposite is true of Belshazzar in Dan. 5:22-23.

▣ "Him who lives forever" This seems to be a play on the name "YHWH" from the Hebrew VERB "to be" (cf. Exod. 3: 14). This theological affirmation is made several times in Daniel (cf. Dan. 4:34; 6:26; 12:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

▣ "His dominion" This poetic theological affirmation is parallel to Dan. 4:3, as well as 2:44; 6:26-27. YHWH's Kingdom is eternal (cf. Dan. 7:14). The four kingdoms of Daniel 2 will pass away, but not the Kingdom of the Most High!

entries.title: Daniel 4:35
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:35 This chapter has several poetic hymnic affirmations (cf. Dan. 4:3,34-35,37).

▣ "All the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing" This is not asserting that God does not love humanity (i.e., John 3:16 and Special Topic below), but that no human individual or nation can compare with God's power, authority, and longevity (cf. Isa. 40:17; Jer. 10:10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "the host of heaven" This phrase can have two orientations

  1. in texts relating to faithful Israel it refers to YHWH, the commander of the heavenly army of angels (cf. Josh. 5:14-15; 1 Kgs. 22:19; Ps. 103:20-21)
  2. in texts which relate to Mesopotamian empires, particularly Babylon, who advocate and use astrology or to idolatrous Israel, then it refers to YHWH as creator (cf. Gen. 1:14-19) and controller of the heavenly bodies (sun, moon, stars, etc., e.g. Deut. 4:19; 17:3; 2 Kgs. 17:16; Ps. 33:6; Isa. 34:4; 40:26; Jer. 8:2-3; 19:13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

▣ "And no one can ward off His hand" This word refers to child training or discipline. It is a strong emphasis on God's sovereignty over all humans and nations (cf. Dan. 2:21; Isa. 43:13).

▣ "Or say to Him, 'What have You done'" This is another possible allusion to Isaiah (cf. Isa. 10:15; 45:9-13). The phrase is imagery often related to making pottery (cf. Isa. 29:16; Jer. 18; Rom. 9:19-22). God's total sovereignty is a recurrent theme (i.e., 2 Chr. 20:6; Job 9:12).

entries.title: Daniel 4:37 "praise, exalt and honor"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:37 "praise, exalt and honor" As is characteristic of Daniel several synonymous terms are used to make a strong emphasis.

▣ "the King of heaven" This is a title related to the concept of YHWH as king of the universe (cf. Jdgs. 8:23; 1 Sam. 8:7; Ps. 5:2; 29:10; 44:4; 47:6-8; 48:2; 68:24; 74:12; 84:3; 95:3; 97:1; 99:4; 146:10; Isa. 41:21; 43:15; 44:6; 52:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KINGDOM OF GOD

▣ "all His works are true and His ways just" Truth and justice are twin characteristics of YHWH (cf. Deut. 32:4; Ps. 33:4-5). The one true God reveals knowledge and acts fairly. He wants His people to emulate His character.

▣ "to humble those who walk in pride" This first refers to Nebuchadnezzar II (and Belshazzar, cf. Dan. 5:20), but also to all Gentile empires represented by the image of four metals in chapter 2 (cf. Exod. 18:11). This is another common biblical theme (cf. Job 40:11-12; James 4:6,10; 2 Pet. 5:5-6).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Who wrote this decree? The king or Daniel or both?
  2. Why didn't Nebuchadnezzar call Daniel first to interpret his dream?
  3. What or who was the tree a symbol of?
  4. What or who are the watchers?
  5. What is the purpose of the band around the tree (Dan. 4:15)?
  6. How long are the seven periods of time?
  7. Does this prophecy have any significance outside the life of Nebuchadnezzar?
  8. What was Nebuchadnezzar's disease and is it an uncommon medical problem?
  9. How would you entitle this chapter?
  10. Was Nebuchadnezzar converted?

entries.title: Daniel 5:1 "Belshazzar"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:1 "Belshazzar" In Babylonian Bel-shar-usur means "Bel, protect the king" (BDB 1084). Bel means lord" and is another name for Marduk.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MARDUK

SPECIAL TOPIC: BEL

▣ "the king" Although his name was not found initially on any of the cuneiform lists of Babylonian kings, further archaeological studies have found him on cuneiform lists which call him the "son of the king" (i.e. Nabonidus' cylinder, see J. B. Pritchard, ANET, pp. 315-316)). Because he is called the son of Nebuchadnezzar in vv. 2,11,18,22, there has been much discussion about his true ancestry. Some possible theories are:

  1. He was the adopted son of Nabonidus.
  2. Family terms have a wide latitude of meanings, as is common in Semitic languages.
  3. Nabonidus may have married a daughter of Nebuchadnezzar II (Nitocris) in order to legitimatize his reign because he may not have been of the royal line (cf. R. P. Dougherty, Nabonidus and Belshazzar, pp. 63-80).
  4. Some even assert that he married Nebuchadnezzar's queen.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BIBLE (its uniqueness and inspiration)

▣ "held a great feast" Possibly it was a state or religious holiday. In the face of the approaching Medo-Persian army it may have been a way of taking their minds off of the impending battle.

▣ "a thousand of his nobles" History gives many examples of large festivals given by eastern monarchs (cf. Daniel 3 [neo-Babylonian]; Esther 1 [Persian]).

entries.title: Daniel Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
DANIEL 5

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

5:13-16 5:13-16 5:13-16 5:13-16 5:13-16

    (25b)

5:30-31 5:30-31 5:30-31   5:30-6:1

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHT

  1. There seems to be an extended period of time (at least 23 years) between Daniel 4 (Nebuchadnezzar, 605-562 B.C.) and 5 (fall of the city of Babylon in 539 B.C.). In this period there were several Babylonian kings who reigned for a short time.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

  2. Belshazzar has been the source of great controversy because his name does not appear in many of the cuneiform lists of Babylonian kings. However, new archaeological finds have found him listed as the son of Nabonidus, the last Babylonian King (from Nabonidus' cylinder, see J. B. Pritchard, ANET, pp. 315-316). Apparently Nabonidus became devotedly involved in the worship of the moon god, Sin (Sumerian Nanna). His mother (Adadguppi) was involved in the worship of the moon god at Haran, while his daughter was high priestess at Ur. He spent most of his time in Tema (Arabic for "desert") in northern Arabia and was absent from the city of Babylon for an extended period (i.e. about ten years). The cities of Ur, Haran, and Tema were centers for the worship of the moon. Some historians assert that his absence was due to his commanding the army which was in an extended battle with Egypt.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: MOON WORSHIP

  3. This chapter is included as another example of the arrogance of world rulers and their confrontation with YHWH who is the controller of history (cf. Dan. 2:21).

  4. Belshazzar had confidence the fortifications of the city of Babylon could not be overcome. For a good discussion of the city see La Moine F. DeVries, Cities of the Biblical World, Hendrickson Publishers, 1997, pp. 13-21.

    For a good brief discussion of neo-Babylon see Jack Finegan, Archaeological History of the Ancient Middle East, Westview Press, 1979, pp. 123-133.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Daniel 5:2 "When Belshazzar tasted the wine"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:2 "When Belshazzar tasted the wine" This either refers to (1) his beginning the traditional drinking period after the dinner or (2) the fact that he was already intoxicated.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL ATTITUDES TOWARD ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

▣ "he gave orders to bring the gold and silver vessels" Nebuchadnezzar II carried off the vessels from the house of YHWH in Jerusalem (cf. 2 Kings 24:13; 25:15), as he did from all the national temples of conquered people groups. Why Belshazzar would choose to specifically desecrate YHWH's sacred temple vessels is uncertain. Possibly, since there were hundreds of guests present plus his wives and concubines (cf. Dan. 5:3), all of the vessels from all of the conquered peoples' temples were procured for the drinking, but more probably because Jerusalem is mentioned specifically in 5:2 and 3. Belshazzar knew how YHWH had humbled Nebuchadnezzar II (cf. Daniel 4), and he was simply acting out of spite (cf. Dan. 5:22).

▣ "his father" This could be literal (cf. Gen. 31:42), but probably it is used in the sense of "ancestor," "descendant" (cf. Ezra 5:12), or "previous royal leader" (BDB 1078, also the black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III calls Jehu "son of Omri"). Some examples show the term being used as grandfather (cf. Gen. 28:13; 32:9) and great grandfather (cf.1 Kgs. 15:11).

▣ "the temple" The Jewish temple in Jerusalem was built by Solomon and is described in 1 Kings 6-8. It reflects the ancient portable tabernacle described in Exodus 25-27; 35-38.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TABERNACLE OF THE WILDERNESS

▣ "his wives, and his concubines might drink from them" The Medes and the Persians did not allow women at state banquets (cf. Esther 1), but apparently the Babylonians did, at least on this occasion (Xenophon, Cyropaedia 5.2.28). To the Jewish mind of later scholars the presence of wives, and particularly concubines, would have been an aditional offense to YHWH. Most always men and women were segregated in the Ancient Near East. This was a wild and extravagant party (cf. James M. Freeman, Manners and Customs of the Bible, p. 203).

In the Hebrew Bible the distinction between "wives" and "concubines" has to do with the inheritance rights of the children. Both are legally married to the king and live in the harem. The children of "wives" have full inheritance rights, while the children of "concubines" have only limited inheritance rights.

This is the Aramaic section of Daniel and the term "concubines" (BDB 1099) is possibly from an Arabic root for "time," "note," or "song," therefore, the NJB translates it as "and the women who sang for him." But, the term can denote a female consort, not a concubine.

entries.title: Daniel 5:4 "praised the gods of gold and silver, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:4 "praised the gods of gold and silver, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone" These are the same metals involved in the statue of Daniel 2. From v. 23 we realize that these were idols (cf. Exod. 20:23; Deut. 4:28; 28:36,64; 29:17; Ps. 115:4-8; 135:15-18; Isa. 40:18-20; 44:9-20; 46:1-7). This phrase may imply that this banquet had religious or ritual connotations.

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

entries.title: Daniel 5:5 "the fingers of a man's hand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:5 "the fingers of a man's hand" This may be an ANE idiom for the activity of God (i.e., "the finger of God," cf. Exod. 8:19; 31:18; Deut. 9:10; Ps. 8:3). Here, it mentions "a man" but it is in a supernatural context.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE GOD

▣ "the lampstand" Bible readers are familiar with the lampstands of both the tabernacle (seven branched, cf. Exod. 25:31-40) and Solomon's temple (ten branched, cf. 2 Chr. 4:19-22). It is uncertain if this lamp from YHWH's temple (cf. Jer. 52:19) was brought to the party room along with the bowls or if this refers to one of the lamps, which normally lit the room. If it is YHWH's lampstand then the supernatural hand of revelation from heaven wrote its riddle right above this special holy item. Whichever is true the writing was placed in a conspicuous place where it was easily seen!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAMPSTAND

▣ "plaster of the wall of the king's palace" This is also the Aramaic word for "lime," "quicklime," or "plaster" (BDB 1086 and 162). From current archaeology we have learned that the main throne room in Neo-Babylon had white plaster on two walls (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 889).

▣ "the king saw the back of the hand that did the writing" Whether everyone saw the hand or just the king is uncertain. The word "hand" (BDB 1094) can mean "arm," "palm," or "finger." It was a human hand with an arm, possibly to the elbow (cf. Peter-Contesse, Ellington, A Handbook On The Book of Daniel, p. 134) or just to the wrist (cf. The Anchor Bible, vol. 23, p. 184).

The IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 737, mentions that this may reflect a defeated army. The body count of dead soldiers was calculated by adding up the severed right hands.

entries.title: Daniel 5:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:6 This is an eyewitness account of the physical deterioration of the king in light of his drunkenness and the supernatural appearance of the hand (cf.Dan. 5:9,10). This same term is used of Daniel's response to God's revelations in Dan. 7:15,28.

▣ "his hip joints went slack" This is imagery describing fear (cf. Nahum 2:10; Ps. 69:23; Isa. 21:3), as is "knees began knocking together" (cf. Ezek. 7:17; 21:7; Nahum 2:10).

entries.title: Daniel 5:7 bring in the conjurers; the Chaldeans and the diviners"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:7 bring in the conjurers; the Chaldeans and the diviners" Again the impotence of Babylon's wise men (i.e., royal counselors) is emphasized (cf. Dan. 2:2-13; 5:8,15). Apparently Daniel had retired from active service (cf. Dan. 5:11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVINATION

▣ "purple" The King James Version has "scarlet" and we must remember that the names of ancient colors varied greatly. Purple was the color of royalty (cf. Xenophon, Anabasis 1:5,8). Purple was very expensive cloth worn only by the very wealthy. The dye was obtained from certain shells found off the coast of Phoenicia (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 498).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE SACRED COLORS

▣ "necklace of gold" Necklaces were symbols of rank and authority in the Ancient Near East (cf. Gen. 41:42; Song of Songs 4:9; Ezek. 16:11). However, the Aramaic phrase (BDB 1090 and 1087) might refer to a solid gold collar, designating rank, not a necklace at all.

▣ "third ruler of the kingdom" This word (BDB 1118) is very ambiguous. It can mean

  1. simply a high official
  2. an army official
  3. it may fit in with Belshazzar's co-reign with his father, Nabonidus

He could only give third place to someone.

entries.title: Daniel 5:8 "they could not read the inscription"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:8 "they could not read the inscription" It is uncertain if the writing was in Aramaic or Hebrew. It seems that they should have been able to read the words, but possibly did not understand their meaning. The words may have been written in consonants only or, as the rabbis say, not horizontally, but vertically. It is obvious that Daniel was needed to interpret the words.

entries.title: Daniel 5:10 "the queen"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:10 "the queen" The Septuagint adds a phrase that says that Belshazzar called the queen. This is because it was highly unusual for anyone to enter the king's presence without being summoned (cf. Esther 4:11). However, the queen-mother had a unique position in the royal court and could probably come and go at will. There has been much debate as to her identity:

  1. Nebuchadnezzar's queen
  2. Nebuchadnezzar's daughter
  3. Nabonidus' mother (Adad-Guppi)
  4. Nabonidus' queen, the mother of Belshazzar (Nitocris)
  5. one of Nabonidus' wives

Options #1 or 2 seem most likely because she knew of Daniel and his gifts.

entries.title: Daniel 5:11 "There is a man in your kingdom"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:11 "There is a man in your kingdom" Daniel 5:8 is an example again of the failure of the Neo-Babylonian wise men to accurately know the heart and mind of the one true God. God did, however, provide a source of revelation, even to these Neo-Babylonian monarchs. That source was Daniel, one of the captives of Judah (cf. 5:13).

▣ "a spirit of the holy gods" See note at Dan. 4:8.

▣ "your father. . .your father, your father the king" This is a strange triple use of "father" (BDB 1078, NKJV). The last one is omitted by the Peshitta and LXX (NRSV, REB, NET Bible).

▣
NASB, JPSOA  "illumination, insight, and wisdom"
NKJV, Peshitta  "light and understanding and wisdom"
NRSV  "enlightment, understanding and wisdom"
TEV  "good sense, knowledge, and wisdom"
NJB  "perception, intelligence and wisdom"
REB  "clean insight and godlike wisdom"
LXX  "prudent and wise"

These three characterizations are meant to reflect Daniel's God-given abilities to know and interpret visions, dreams, etc. (cf. Dan. 5:14). The next phrase, "the wisdom of the gods" accentuates Daniel's God-given gifts (cf. Dan. 5:12; 1:17,20).

▣ "appointed him chief of the magicians, conjurers, Chaldeans and diviners" This list refers to the royal advisors. See note at Dan. 1:20; 2:48, and 4:9.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVINATION

entries.title: Daniel 5:13 "Are you that Daniel who is one of the exiles from Judah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:13 "Are you that Daniel who is one of the exiles from Judah" Notice that the king addresses him by his Hebrew name, not his Babylonian name. Also notice that it is mentioned that he is from Judah, the location of the very God that Belshazzar had offended (cf. Dan. 5:22).

▣ "one of the exiles from Judah" This phrase functions in two ways:

  1. Belshazzar is asserting that Daniel is a captive Jewish person
  2. Daniel is a member and representative of YHWH's people; the YHWH who controls history and the destiny of kings (cf. Dan. 2:20-23; 4:17,32)!

entries.title: Daniel 5:14 "Now I have heard"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:14 "Now I have heard" This refers to Dan. 5:10-12. See notes there and at Dan. 4:8.

entries.title: Daniel 5:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:17 Daniel forcibly (JUSSIVE and IMPERATIVE), but politely, rejects the king's offer of gifts, rewards, and position. Daniel can read the prophetic words. He knows the Babylonian kingdom is at an end! Daniel knew Belshazzar would be giving everything to Cyrus' army very soon.

entries.title: Daniel 5:17-21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:17-21 This is a summary of God's sovereign dealings with Nebuchadnezzar II recorded in Daniel 4.

entries.title: Daniel 5:18 "Nebuchadnezzar your father"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:18 "Nebuchadnezzar your father" The term "father" can refer to descendants in Hebrew (Semitic) usage. See note at Dan. 5:2.

entries.title: Daniel 5:19 "all the peoples, nations, and men of every language"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:19 "all the peoples, nations, and men of every language" This is hyperbole used to show the extent of the Neo-Babylonian empire under Nebuchadnezzar II (cf. Dan. 3:4,7; 4:1; 5:19; 6:25).

Nebuchadnezzar II exercised total control over a large part of the ancient Near East. He thought he was in a position of authority until the God of Judah stepped in (cf. 5:20-21)!

entries.title: Daniel 5:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:20 This verse describes not only Nebuchadnezzar, but all of the Near Eastern potentates whom Daniel served and prophesied about (cf. Dan. 2:7,8; 9:24-27; 11:12), including Belshazzar (cf. 5:22-23).

entries.title: Daniel 5:22-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:22-23 The NIV Study Bible (p. 1308) notes that Belshazzar is condemned for three things.

  1. He acted irreverently toward YHWH, not out of ignorance, but spite (Dan. 5:22).
  2. He desecrated YHWH's name by using the holy vessels from the temple in Jerusalem for a drunken party.
  3. He praised manmade idols instead of YHWH (Dan. 5:23b).

entries.title: Daniel 5:23 "but you have exalted yourself against the Lord of heaven"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:23 "but you have exalted yourself against the Lord of heaven" As Nebuchadnezzar II was humbled by YHWH (cf. Daniel 4) so too, his descendant, Belshazzar, who had purposely violated the sanctity of YHWH's temple vessels.

▣ "you have praised the gods of silver and gold, of bronze, iron, wood and stone, which do not see, hear or understand" This contrasts the only living, ever-living God with the dead, dumb, and nonexistent idols (see note at Dan. 5:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

▣ "the God in whose hand are your life-breath and your ways" The only source for life is YHWH (from the Hebrew VERB "to be," cf. Exod. 3:14). He is the controller of events, kings, and nations. This truth is mentioned in the Prophets (e.g., Jer. 10:23), but most often in Wisdom Literature (cf. Job 31:4; Ps. 139; Prov. 20:24).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

entries.title: Daniel 5:25 "MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:25 "MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN" These NOUNS were apparently the names for ancient weights and measures. Daniel turns them into VERBS to interpret their meaning. The term MENE (BDB 1101) is a word which means "to number." Literally, it is a particular weight called a "mina," (cf. 1 Kings 10; 17; Ezra 2:69; Neh. 7:71, 72).

The second term, TEKEL (BDB 1118), is the Hebrew "shaqal" which means "to weigh" and is apparently the Aramaic form of the Hebrew weight "shekel."

The word UPHARSIN (BDB 1108) means "to break or divide." The "U" is simply the connective "and." We have found from archaeological discovery that the basic root word "peres" means a half-weight. Therefore, these terms are of descending weights. However, Daniel interprets them as VERBS, Dan. 5:26-28. This last one may be a play on the word "Persian," (i.e. paras, cf. Dan. 5:28).

Scholarship of the past century thought that the title Darius the Mede (cf. Dan. 5:31) demanded a separate Median Empire and that the order of the four kingdoms in Daniel should be Babylon, Media, Persia, and Greece (e.g. Milton S. Terry, Biblical Hermeneutics, pp. 418-426). However, the term "divided" (cf. Dan. 5:28) could refer to the third empire as being a combination of Medo-Persia with Persia being the dominant one (cf. Dan. 8:20). This would then make Rome the fourth empire with the coming of the Messiah to set up a kingdom during this period. This scenario fits history and Scripture much better.

entries.title: Daniel 5:28 "the Medes and the Persians"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:28 "the Medes and the Persians" This shows the historicity of the book of Daniel. Once Cyrus II became the monarch of the Fertile Crescent, the order was changed to the Persians and the Medes instead of the Medes and Persians (cf. J. C. Whitcomb, Darius the Mede, p. 127). This phrase also shows that these two empires are seen as one entity in Daniel.

entries.title: Daniel 5:29 "he now had authority as the third ruler in the kingdom"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:29 "he now had authority as the third ruler in the kingdom" These three (triumvir) would be: Nabonidus (absent), Belshazzar (co-regent), and Daniel.

entries.title: Daniel 5:30 "That same night"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:30 "That same night" From the histories of both Herodotus (1.190-191) and Xenophon (Cyropaedia 7.5) we know the date was October 12, 539 B.C.

▣ "the Chaldean king" The term "Chaldean" is used

  1. here, in an ethnic sense (cf. Dan. 9:1 and Herodotus) in this text
  2. as a class of wise men or astrologers in Dan. 2:2,4,5,10 (twice); 3:8; 4:7; 5:7,11
  3. The Babylonians themselves never used the term in an ethnic sense in their own documents, but the Assyrians did.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

entries.title: Daniel 5:31 "Darius the Mede"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:31 "Darius the Mede" This person is unknown to extra-biblical history. There have been two predominant theories.

  1. Darius means "royal one" (in the Avesta "dar," which may be a throne name like "Hadad" for Syria, "Pharaoh" for Egypt, and "Abimelech" for Philistia) and is another name for Cyrus II (the Great), who was also about sixty years of age. For the first year of their reign eastern monarchs often used a throne name (i.e. Tiglath Pileser III was known as Pul and Shalmaneser V was known as Ululai, cf. Joyce G. Baldwin, Daniel, The Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries, p. 127, footnote #5). Cyrus was half Median by race and took the title "king of the Medes" at his defeat of Astyages (Cyrus' father-in-law), king of Media, in 549 B.C. (D. J. Wiseman, Darius" in The New Bible Dictionary, p. 293 and Notes on Some Problems in the Book of Daniel, pp. 12ff). The Septuagint in Dan. 11:1 substitutes "Cyrus" for "Darius the Mede."
  2. The Nabonidus Chronicle mentions two Medo-Persian military leaders active in the fall of the city of Babylon—Ugbaru and Gubaru (cf. J. C. Whitcomb, Darius the Mede, pp. 5ff). Ugbaru was a military leader of Cyrus' forces who captured the city of Babylon (539 B.C..), but in the campaign he was wounded and died several weeks later. Another person with a similar name, Gubaru, was also a military leader. It was he, not Ugbaru, who was appointed by Cyrus as governor of the city (maybe province) of Babylon, an office he held for many years (The Zondervan Pictorial Encyclopedia of the Bible, vol. 2, p. 17 and R. K Harrison, Introduction to the Old Testament, pp. 341-347). He may have been given the title "Royal One" by Cyrus himself.

▣ "received the kingdom" It is uncertain if this means that he received (BDB 1110, Pael PERFECT) the kingdom from God or from Cyrus II (cf. Dan. 9:1).

▣ "the age of sixty-two" It is quite obvious that Daniel is attempting to identify Darius, both with his racial lineage and his age. We know more about Darius than we do about many other persons mentioned in the Book of Daniel. Obviously, he was an historical person.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why is there such a historical problem with the name Belshazzar?
  2. How is Belshazzar related to Nebuchadnezzar II?
  3. Why did Belshazzar choose YHWH to make sport of?
  4. Who is the queen mentioned in Dan. 5:10?
  5. Why could not the wise men of Babylon read the handwriting on the wall?
  6. Explain the meaning of the words written on the wall in Dan. 5:25.
  7. Who is Darius the Mede?

entries.title: Daniel 6:1 "Darius"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:1  "Darius" See note at Dan. 5:31.

▣ "120 satraps over the kingdom" When compared with later Persian documents the number of these satraps is inappropriately large. In Persia there were usually only 20 to 30, but in the book of Esther there is also a large number (compare Dan. 1:1 with 8:9) of governmental officials.

We know so little about the different types or levels of governmental officials at this time that any kind of dogmatism is unwise and inappropriate.

▣ "satraps" This word (BDB 1080) is used often in later Persian documents and many commentaries have used it to support a later date for the writing of Daniel (i.e. the Maccabean period). However, the word is an old Persian term, kshathrapan, which becomes satarpanu in some cuneiform texts (cf. The Zondervan Pictorial Encyclopedia of the Bible, vol. 2, p. 18). Therefore, its usage cannot be used as evidence for a late date.

▣ "of the whole kingdom" If Darius (cf. Dan. 5:31) refers to Cyrus, then "the whole kingdom" refers to the entire Medo-Persian Empire and 120 satraps is not unusual. But if it refers to Gubaru (a Median general in Cyrus' army which captured the city of Babylon), then the kingdom would refer to the province of Babylon; also, "satrap" would refer to lesser governmental officials, not the word's later usage in Persian documents.

6:2
NASB  "three commissioners"
NKJV  "three governors"
NRSV, NJB, Peshitta  "three presidents"
TEV     -------
REB, JPSOA  "three chief ministers"
LXX  "three tacticians"

Brown, Driver, and Briggs Lexicon (BDB 1104) says the origin of the term is dubious, but that it refers to "overseer" or "chief" (from a Persian word for "head").

The term "three" may be related contextually to Dan. 5:7,16,29. At this point these three chief overseers are unknown to secular history.

▣ "and that the king" This could refer to (1) Cyrus or (2) Gubaru whom Cyrus appointed governor of Babylon. However, the title "king" fits Cyrus much better (cf. Joyce G. Baldwin, Daniel IVP, p. 127, note #5). The main problem of this identification is that Cyrus was not a son of Astyages, but of Cambyses, king of Anshan. On this issue scholars must await more archaeological evidence.

▣ "might not suffer loss" This is the use of the Aramaic word for "injury," used as imagery for political interest (cf. Ezra 4:22; Esther 7:4).

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Daniel 6:3 "this Daniel began distinguishing himself"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:3 "this Daniel began distinguishing himself" This phrase begins with the DEMONSTRATIVE PRONOUN "this" (cf. Dan. 6:5,28), which is typical of Persian style, but also is a way to accentuate Daniel's giftedness (cf. Dan. 1:17,20; 2:21,23).

▣ "the king planned to appoint him over the entire kingdom" This parallels what Pharaoh did to Joseph in Gen. 41:40. There are many similarities between Joseph and Daniel.

This imminent promotion of an exiled Hebrew slave over Median and Persian administrators will cause the actions of Dan. 6:4.

entries.title: Daniel 6:4 "trying to find grounds of accusation against Daniel in regard to government affairs"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 6:4 "trying to find grounds of accusation against Daniel in regard to government affairs" The same motives that led the Chaldean officials to accuse the three Hebrew youths in Daniel 3 are apparently the same motives that caused these officials to try and find accusations against Daniel (cf. Dan. 6:13).

entries.title: Daniel 6:5 "unless we find it against him in regard to the law of his God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:5 "unless we find it against him in regard to the law of his God" These administrators were wise enough to realize that the only area in which Daniel could be accused was in his loyalty to the Hebrew faith.

6:6
NASB  "came by agreement"
NKJV, JPSOA  "thronged"
NRSV  "conspired"
TEV  "went to see"
NET  "collusion"

The VERB (Haphel PERFECT, BDB 1112) is rare both in Aramaic and Hebrew. It can mean

  1. "in harmony"
  2. "thronged" (NKJV, JPSOA, BDB 1112)
  3. as in the Psalms (Ps. 2:1) the Hebrew counterpart (BDB 921, KB 1189, Qal PERFECT) is used for a treacherous conspiracy, which seems to be the implication here (NRSV, NET)

▣ "live forever" This is a standard hyperbole addressing the king (cf. Dan.2:4; 3:9; 5:10; 6:6,21). In Dan. 4:34; 6:26; and 12:7 the phrase is used in a theological sense of YHWH, the "I Am" (cf. Exod. 3:14 from the Hebrew VERB "to be"). He is the ever-living, only-living One (cf. Dan. 6:20)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

entries.title: Daniel 6:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:7 These government officials appealed to the egotism and pride of the king. Quite often leaders are susceptible to this trickery.

▣ "that anyone who makes a petition to any god or man besides you, O king" This was highly unusual for a Persian monarch to assume the status of deity because the Persian religion (Zoroastrians) believed in two deities, an eternal dualism existed between good and evil, between the Ahura Mazda and the Angra Mainyu. So how this king could possibly usurp divine attributes is historically uncertain. The plotters may have used the first ascension year of Cyrus as an opportunity to impose a loyalty-type oath (hyperbole).

▣ "the lions' den" See note at Dan. 6:17 and SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT.

entries.title: Daniel 6:8 "the law of the Medes and Persians"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:8 "the law of the Medes and Persians" This same binding legal status of the decrees of the Medo-Persian kings as being unchangeable is found in Dan. 6:12,15,17; Esther 1:19; 8:8; and Diodorus Siculus 17:30.

The Medes are mentioned first here as in Dan. 8:20. Persia was the dominant partner and very soon after Cyrus' defeat of Babylon he began to be called King of Persia. The order of these terms shows the historicity of Daniel. The order is reversed in Esther 1:19.

The prophets also combined Media and Persia as one entity as the parallelism of Isa. 21:2 (Elam and Media) clearly shows. Some scholars refer to Isa. 13:17 and Jer. 51:11,28 as an attempt to show that the prophets falsely saw Media as a separate empire (cf. NAB p. 1096), an error which they assert that Daniel followed.

Also note that Darius the Mede is subject to the laws of the Medes and Persians, which would not be true if Media was a separate, independent empire.

entries.title: Daniel 6:10 "Now when Daniel knew the document was signed"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:10 "Now when Daniel knew the document was signed" Daniel was not taken off guard, but he was more loyal to his lifestyle faith (cf.Dan. 6:15,20) than to the comings and goings of these jealous political leaders and their schemes.

▣ "(now in his roof chamber he had windows open toward Jerusalem)" These roof chambers were used as summer sleeping quarters (cf. James M. Freeman, Manners and Customs of the Bible, pp. 171-172). Apparently for Daniel it was a place of where he prayed three times a day facing the ancient, destroyed city of Jerusalem (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:44,48; 2 Chr. 6:34,38; Ps. 28:2; 138:2).

The tradition of praying towards the temple may have begun in 1 Kgs. 8:35.

▣ "he continued kneeling on his knees" The normal position of Jewish prayer is standing with the hands and head lifted to heaven with the eyes open (in dialog with God). Sometimes kneeling was done for urgency (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:54; 2 Chr. 6:13; Ezra 9:5; Ps. 95:6: Isa. 45:23).

▣ "three times a day" This phrase reflects the daily times of prayer in the temple in Jerusalem (cf. Ps. 55:17; Judith 9:1). Traditionally Jews prayed at the time of the morning (Psalm 5) and evening (cf. Dan. 9:21; Psalm 4) sacrifice (called the Continual, Exod. 29:39; Num. 28:1-8,10,15,23-24), as well as at noon (cf. Ps. 55:17). Daniel commemorated the ritual moments of the destroyed temple's schedule in his private prayer.

Just an added note that the Persian religion, Zoroastrianism, also advocated prayer three times a day, and even increased it to five times (The IVP Bible Background Commentary [OT], p. 739).

entries.title: Daniel 6:11 "came by agreement"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 6:11 "came by agreement" This is the same Aramaic word used in Dan. 6:6 and 15 for their coming before the King, apparently with evil motives against Daniel.

entries.title: Daniel 6:13 "who is one of the exiles from Judah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 6:13 "who is one of the exiles from Judah" Racial and religious prejudices are used to attack Daniel.

entries.title: Daniel 6:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:14 The King realizes that he has been used in a scheme to destroy Daniel (cf. Dan. 6:24), but is powerless (cf. Dan. 6:16,18,19) in the legal circumstances to forestall his own royal edict (cf. Dan. 6:12,15).

6:16
NASB, NKJV  "Your God. . .will Himself"
NRSV, NASB margin, NAB, Peshitta, LXX  "May your God. . .deliver you"
TEV  "May your God. . .rescue you"
NJB, REB  "Your God. . .will have to save you"

Aramaic grammar determines that this phrase is INDICATIVE, not JUSSIVE (NASB, NAB), with an emphasis on "your God" (cf. Anchor Bible, vol. 23, p. 195). Again, the impotence of earthly monarchs is contrasted with the power and authority of the God of Judah (cf. Dan. 3:17,18).

entries.title: Daniel 6:17 "A stone was brought and laid over the mouth of the den"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:17 "A stone was brought and laid over the mouth of the den" Lions were kept for the hunting pleasure of near Eastern royalty. Death by being thrown to wild animals was a common method of execution by the royal courts of the Ancient Near East and East. Apparently the den was an underground pit with two entrances, one from the top (cf. Dan. 6:23) and one from the bottom. Again, the fall should have killed the elderly man (cf. Dan. 3:20), much less the hungry lions.

▣ "sealed it" See SPECIAL TOPIC: SEAL.

entries.title: Daniel 6:18 "the king went off to his palace and spent the night fasting"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:18 "the king went off to his palace and spent the night fasting" This was not necessarily religious fasting, but simply the anxious worrying of a man who knew he had been tricked into doing evil to an innocent (cf. Dan. 6:22) faithful (and a very effective) servant.

6:18
NASB  "no entertainment was brought before him"
NKJV  "no musicians"
NRSV, Peshitta  "no food"
TEV  "nor any form of entertainment"
NJB, REB  "refused to receive any of his concubines"
JPSOA, NET  "no diversions"
LXX  "grieving"

There has been much discussion about this Aramaic word (BDB 1087). There are several theories:

  1. Eben-Ezra, John Calvin, and NKJV believe it means "play music" from the root "to strike"
  2. the Hebrew counterpart means "to thrust," therefore, possibly "dancers"
  3. the Peshitta has the word "food" (from dining table)
  4. Martin Luther and the RSV have "diversions "or "pleasure"
  5. the NJB, from a possible Arabic root, has "sexual pleasure" or "concubines"

▣ "his sleep fled from him" This is an Aramaic idiom (cf. Esther 6:1).

entries.title: Daniel 6:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 6:19 This verse shows the King's anxiety!

entries.title: Daniel 6:20 "servant of the living God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:20 "servant of the living God" This is a play on the root word "YHWH," which is the a form of the Hebrew VERB "to be," which implies the "ever-living, only-living God" (cf. Exod. 3: 14). See note at Dan. 6:6.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "been able to deliver you from the lions" Here is that wonderful play on the title for God "the God who is able" (cf. Dan. 3:17,29; Rom. 16:25; Eph. 3:20; Jude 24). Nothing is too difficult for YHWH (cf. Jer. 32:17). This whole book is about God's sovereignty and willingness to respond to those who trust Him (e.g., Dan. 3:28). Chapters 3 and 6 are lexically and theologically parallel. They may represent independant pieces of literature later combined into the book of Daniel. Baba Bathra (a book of the Talmud) says, "the men of the Great Synagogue wrote Daniel" (i.e., Ezra's day), but this means they compiled it or edited it.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

entries.title: Daniel 6:22 "my God sent His angel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:22 "my God sent His angel" The Bible seems to teach the existence of guardian angels

  1. national, cf. Num. 20:16; Isa. 63:9
  2. individual, cf. Gen. 48:16; Dan. 3:28; 6:22; Matt. 18:10; Acts 12:15; Heb. 1:14
  3. as well as the indwelling Holy Spirit (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; John 14:23; Rom. 8:9,11; 1 Cor. 3:16; 6:19; 2 Cor. 6:16; 2 Tim. 1:14)

SPECIAL TOPIC: GUARDIAN ANGELS

▣ "shut the lions' mouths" This is both literal (cf. Heb. 11:33 and I Maccabees 2:59-60), but also figurative (cf. Ps. 22:21; 2 Tim. 4:17).

▣ "inasmuch as I was found innocent before Him" The Semitic concept of "innocence" denotes living in the light of what one understands is the will of God. It involves knowledge and action (see SPECIAL TOPIC: BLAMELESS, INNOCENT, GUILTLESS, WITHOUT REPROACH). Daniel acknowledges the OT concept of "merit" (cf. Deuteronomy 27-30). Daniel was faithful; God was faithful. Yet Judah and Israel had long experienced God as faithful even when they were not. However, God's longsuffering came to an end in the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles. Yet YHWH would restore them to the Promised Land (Cyrus' edict of 538 B.C.). The New Covenant of Jer. 31:31-34 (cf. Ezek. 36:22-38) acknowledges humanity's inability to keep the covenant. The New Covenant will be based, not on human innocence or merit, but on YHWH's gracious character and His Messiah's innocence and merit!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Daniel 6:23 "no injury whatever was found on him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:23 "no injury whatever was found on him" This is parallel to Dan. 3:27.

▣ "because he had trusted in his God" It was not Daniel's innocence (cf. Dan. 6:22) that brought about his deliverance, but his faith ("trusted" BDB 1081, Haphel PERFECT; Hebrew root BDB 52, KB 63) in YHWH (cf. Dan. 3:28). This same truth is recurrent throughout the OT (cf. 1 Chr. 5:20; 2 Chr. 20:20; Ps. 9:10; Isa. 26:3). This great truth becomes the key to Paul's emphasis on justification by faith in Rom. 4:3 and Gal. 3:6, which he anchors in Gen. 15:6.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS (OT)

entries.title: Daniel 6:24 "those men who had maliciously accused Daniel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:24 "those men who had maliciously accused Daniel" The LXX states there were "two." This may imply that the bad actors were the other two leaders mentioned in v. 2 (i.e., "three supervisors").

▣ "and they cast them, their children and their wives into the lions' den" This type of family-wide punishment is known in Persia from Herodotus 3.119. This is the Hebrew concept of corporality:

  1. Adam and Eve's sin affects all humans (cf. Genesis 3)
  2. Korah's rebellion in Num. 16:25-33
  3. Achan's sin in Joshua 7 affected the whole Israeli army and the death of his family and cattle

This same idea of corporality can be seen in Esther 9:10-14. The NT counterpart is Rom. 5:12-21.

▣ "the lions overpowered them" Daniel's deliverance was not attributable to lions that were not hungry!

▣ "crushed" This Aramaic VERB (BDB 1089) is used of several things being crushed or destroyed in Daniel.

  1. the metal statue of a man ‒ Dan. 2:34,35,44,45
  2. the bones of Daniel's accusers ‒ Dan. 6:24
  3. the destruction caused by the fourth terrible beast ‒ Dan. 7:7,19,23

entries.title: Daniel 6:25 "all the peoples, nations, and men of every language"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:25 "all the peoples, nations, and men of every language" This is parallel to Nebuchadnezzar's edicts in Dan. 3:29; 4:1 and Daniel's comment in 5:19 and his vision in 7:14.

It is interesting that the unchangeable edict of the Medo-Persian ruler is obviously modified in honor of YHWH's sovereignty.

entries.title: Daniel 6:25-27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:25-27 The kingdoms of this world (symbolically pictured in the statue of a man in Daniel 2) will come to a violent end, but the Messianic Kingdom (the stone that crushes the statue) will never be defeated or end (cf. Dan. 7:14)! This Kingdom is based on the will and plan of the One True, Eternal God.
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KINGDOM OF GOD
SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM
SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

This is very similar to Nebuchadnezzar's words in Dan. 2:46-48; 3:28,29 and 4:3,34-35. See full note at Dan. 4:3. All of these texts were probably penned by one of the four Jewish exiles. They do not imply personal faith on the part of Nebuchadnezzar or Darius, but the overwhelming sense of the power of God which these polytheists experienced!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIGN (OT)

entries.title: Daniel 6:26 "to fear and tremble"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:26 "to fear and tremble" These are idioms of awe and respect for Judah's God.

▣ "For He is the living God and enduring forever" This descriptive phrase highlights the aspects of the nature of YHWH.

  1. He is the only true God
  2. He is the only eternal God

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D. (YHWH)

▣ "His Kingdom is one which will not be destroyed" Earthly kingdoms will come and go, but YHWH's Kindgom is eternal because He is eternal (cf. Dan. 2:44; 4:3,34; 6:26; 7:14,27; Ps. 10:16; 29:10; Isa. 9:7; Jer. 10:10; Micah 4:7; Heb. 12:28; 2 Pet. 1:11.

entries.title: Daniel 6:27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:27 Notice how YHWH's reign is characterized.

  1. He delivers
  2. He rescues
  3. He performs signs and wonders

He is actively involved in the lives of His people!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIGNS (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WONDERFUL THINGS (OT)

entries.title: Daniel 6:28 "in the reign of Darius and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:28 "in the reign of Darius and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian" The footnote reading in the NIV Study Bible, "of Darius, that is, the reign of Cyrus," clearly shows that the Aramaic text (as well as the explicative waw usage in an epexegetical way, i.e., understood as "even") is capable of seeing these two kings as one in the same person (cf. Joyce G. Baldwin, Daniel, IVP, p. 132 and D. Winton Thomas, ed. Documents From Old Testament Times, p. 83).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF PERSIA

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Was Darius a believer?
  2. What lessons do we learn for our lives from Daniel 6?
  3. Discuss the issue of guardian angels.
  4. Discuss the concept of corporality.
  5. Explain the theological significance of Dan. 6:26.
