entries.title: Daniel 7:1 "In the first year of Belshazzar"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:1 "In the first year of Belshazzar" This shows that the book is not written in chronological order (cf. Daniel 5, which is the fall of the city of Babylon with Belshazzar in charge in October of 539 B.C.). The date mentioned in the text would be about 552-551 B.C., which is fourteen years before chapter 5. This was when Belshazzar's father, King Nabonidus, moved his official residence to Teima in Arabia. It is uncertain exactly when Belshazzar became co-regent, but 552 B.C. is a good guess.

The Aramaic section of Daniel goes from Dan. 2:4 through 7:28, which marks it as a literary unit. Therefore, we must relate chapter 7 with what goes before, as well as with what follows.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NE0-BABYLON

▣ "Daniel saw" It is interesting that chapters 1-6 are written in the third person, as is Dan. 7:1, but the first person predominates chapters 7-12 (e.g., Dan. 7:2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11[twice], 13, 15, 16, 19, 21, 28).

▣ "a dream and visions" In chapters 1-6 the divine dreams were given to Gentile rulers, which is rare in the OT (cf. Pharaoh and Joseph), but in chapters 7-12 the revelations from YHWH come to Daniel personally.

The apparent distinction between dreams and visions is not the level of inspiration, but whether one is asleep or awake, unconscious or conscious. In this context Daniel is obviously in bed, but it is unspecified if he was asleep. In this context the two terms are synonyms of God's special revelations to Daniel about how these Gentile empires will affect the people of God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣
NASB  "the following summary of it"
NKJV  "the main facts"
NRSV    ——
TEV  "a record of"
NJB    ——
NIV  "substance"
REB  "and here his account begins"
JPSOA  "beginning the account"
LXX  " a summary of the account"
Peshitta  "and told the sum of the matter"

This is an idiom from the Aramaic word for "head" (BDB 1112; see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAD) used twice in this verse, once literally and once idiomatically. The footnote of NKJV has "literally ‘head' (or chief) of the words." This Aramaic term is used in several senses in the OT.

  1. head of
    1. head of man, Dan. 3:27
    2. head of the image, Dan. 2:32,38
    3. head of beast, Dan. 7:6,20
  2. visions of my head, Dan. 2:28; 4:2,7,10; 7:1,15
  3. chief, Ezra 5:10
  4. summary, essential context, Dan. 7:1
  5. The Anchor Bible Commentary, vol. 23, p. 205, speculates that this may mean "beginning" since Dan. 7:28 uses an idiom for the conclusion (cf. E. J. Young, The Prophecy of Daniel, p. 141, who says this is possible, but not likely).

From Daniel's style of writing the two phrases in Dan. 7:1b ("wrote" and "related") are parallel with no distinction. Notice the next verse, "answered and said," typifies the repetitive style of Daniel.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

TEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Daniel, chapters 2; 7; and 8 are related as they reveal a sequence of four coming Gentile kingdoms and a fifth eternal divine kingdom. See chart at Contextual Insights, Daniel 8.

  2.  Daniel 2   Daniel 7   Daniel 8
    1.
    2.
    3.
    4.
    5.     		gold, Dan. 2:32
    silver, Dan. 2:32

     ram, Dan. 8:3-4

    Many scholars want the order to be Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece. This is usually because they identify the blasphemous Little Horn to be Antiochus Epiphanes IV, who the Jews named Epimames ("the mad"), But, Media was never a separate world empire. It is always linked to and subservient to Persia.


  3. The kingdoms seem to be:
    1. Neo-Babylonian (Dan. 2:37-38, Nebuchadnezzar II)
    2. Medo-Persia (Dan. 8:20, Cyrus II, the Great)
    3. Greece (Dan. 8:21, Alexander the Great)
    4. Rome
    5. the Eternal Kingdom of God (Dan. 2:45, Messianic, Son of Man, Dan. 7:13)

  4. These Gentile kingdoms became progressively anti-God. It is surprising that these kingdoms, which seem to be in chronological order (cf. Dan. 7:17, are crushed simultaneously (cf. Dan. 2:35,45). This crushing represents God's ultimate and complete victory (cf. Dan. 2:44; 7:14,18,27), not that all these empires have to be in power or in existence at the same time (cf. Dan. 7:11-12).
     God's complete control and sovereignty of all historical events, both individual and national is the theological theme of the book of Daniel (i.e., Dan. 2:21; 4:17,32).

  5. This chapter continues the Aramaic section, which unites the two obvious literary divisions (chapters 1-6 and 7-12) of Daniel. Chapters 2-7 are addressed to Gentile rulers and deal with Gentile nations so they are addressed in Aramaic. The remaining chapters are addressed specifically to God's people and are in Hebrew.

  6. This begins the visions of Daniel which overlap the events of Daniel 1-6. These visions have an affinity in genre to both Hebrew prophecy and apocalyptic literature (which began in Isaiah, but is fully developed in Daniel 7-12 and Zechariah).
    SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

    SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

  7. The poetic sections of this chapter (Dan.7:9-10; 13-14) are the theological heart of the book. They capsule God's eternal purpose and plan for human redemption—the Messiah! They speak of victory through suffering for the saints of the Highest One (cf. Dan. 7:21-22,25,27).
     This text (especially Dan. 7:13-14) is the origin of Jesus' use of the phrase "Son of Man," which reveals His true humanity and divinity (cf. John 1:1-14; Phil. 2:6-11; Col. 1:15-18; Heb. 1:1-3;1 John 4:1-3).
    SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

    SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Daniel 7:2 "the four winds of heaven"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:2 "the four winds of heaven" Four is the biblical symbolic number for the world (i.e., the four corners of the earth, cf. Dan. 8:8; 11:4; Zech. 2:6; 6:5; see SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #2). This has been interpreted as

  1. universal divine knowledge (cf. Zech. 1:8-11; 6:1-8)
  2. a gathering of angels (cf. Isa. 11:12; Matt. 13:41; 24:31; Mark 13:27)
  3. destroying angels (cf. Jer. 49:36; Zech. 2:6; Rev. 7:1; 9:14-15)

This and similar phrases are imagery for God's activity in the world (where "four" is combined with "winds," "corners," "angels"). God knows and allows/controls all activity on planet earth (i.e., Dan. 2:21; 4:17,32).

"Heaven" refers to the atmosphere of this planet.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN

▣ "were stirring up" God was active in sending the "four winds of heaven" to disrupt earthly activities. This chapter is yet another emphasis on God's sovereign control of history and the nations (i.e., all humanity).

entries.title: Daniel 7:2-3 "the great sea. . .the sea"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:2-3 "the great sea. . .the sea" There have been several theories of the meaning of this phrase:

  1. it refers literally to the Mediterranean Ocean (cf. Num. 34:6, 7; Joshua 9:1)
  2. it is imagery for all the nations of the earth (cf. Dan. 7:17; Ps. 65:7; Isa. 17:12-13; 57:20; Rev. 17:15)
  3. it refers to the initial watery chaos which was part of creation (cf. Gen. 1:2; 7:11; 49:25; Ps. 36:6; Isa. 51:10; Amos 7:4; see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE WATERS and also IVP Bible Background Commentary [OT], p. 740)

As always context determines meaning. Here it refers to the known world of the Ancient Near East, that part of the world which affects the people of God and the Promised Land.

▣ Just an added note about "the sea." It seems theologically significant. It is used regularly in ANE mythology related to creation (see SPECIAL TOPIC: CREATION AND FLOOD ACCOUNTS IN THE ANE).

In the Bible the imagery, after the fall of mankind in Genesis 3, is directed toward a way of referring to "rebellious" mankind. This fits this text and the one in the book of Revelation where it mentions

  1. a beast that comes out of the sea, Rev. 13:1 (similar to Daniel)
  2. a sea of glass before the throne in heaven, Rev. 4:6, which symbolizes the holiness of God
    1. sinners cannot approach
    2. the saved can, Rev. 15:2
  3. one day the sea that "separates" will be removed, Rev. 21:18

See exegetical notes at Rev. 4:6 and 21:1 online.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE WATERS

SPECIAL TOPIC: LEVIATHAN

entries.title: Daniel 7:3 "And four great beasts were coming up from the sea, different from one another"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:3 "And four great beasts were coming up from the sea, different from one another" This seems to imply simultaneous kingdoms (cf. Dan. 7:12 and 2:44), but the extended contexts of chapters 2 and 8 demand sequential kingdoms.

There are several aspects to this description that would have intensified a negative Jewish reaction to this vision.

  1. The great surging ocean would have been fearful to those accustomed to the semi-arid life of Palestine. Jews never were extensively involved in maritime trade. Even Solomon's fleet was manned by foreigners (Phoenicians).
  2. Predatory, Levitically unclean animals were attacking humanity.
  3. Animals of composite types would violate the "after their kind" of Genesis 1 and Leviticus laws.
  4. The inhumanity of these pagan empires (especially the fourth empire, cf. Dan. 7:7,23).
  5. The blasphemy of the little horn against God (cf. Dan. 7:8,11,20,25).

entries.title: Daniel 7:4 "The first was like a lion"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:4 "The first was like a lion" Notice the word "like" used here is from an Aramaic PREPOSITION. This same idea is repeated in Dan. 7:5, but with the Aramaic word demah (cf. Dan. 3:25). In Dan. 7:6 the PREPOSITION is used again. The whole point is that what Daniel saw was not real earthly animals, but similar to known animals with different physical attributes (i.e., winged lion, winged leopard). These are apocalyptic symbols of rulers and empires.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

▣ "which had the wings of an eagle" The Babylonian army is described as a swooping eagle (cf. Jer. 49:22; Ezek. 17:3; Hab. 1:8). This was imagery to describe the speed of their advance.

▣ "its wings were plucked" This is imagery for a military defeat. These powerful, national armies seemed invincible, but in reality they were still just human armies.

Notice how often in this verse divine action is directed toward the Gentile empire:

  1. "wings were plucked" (BDB 1101, Piel PERFECT)
  2. "it was lifted up" (BDB 1102, Piel PERFECT)
  3. "made to stand" (BDB 1110, Hoph PERFECT)
  4. "human mind also was given to it" (Piel PRESENT) [this is true of "was raised up on one side," Dan. 7:5]

God is in complete control (cf. Dan. 2:21). Some commentators believe that these actions reflect Nebuchadnezzar's madness in chapter 4. Although this is possible, again interpreters must be careful of trying to find a historical referent to all the details of Daniel's visions.

▣ "made to stand on two feet like a man; a human mind also was given to it" Some commentators think this refers to

  1. Nebuchadnezzar's madness and restoration of chapter 4
  2. the barbaric Chaldeans becoming more civilized and cultured after their initial conquest (i.e., affected by Sumerian culture)

However, the phrase is very ambiguous and may simply be an apocalyptic detail which was never meant to have a historical fulfillment. This powerful empire existed and was destroyed, making room for the next empire from the Ancient Near East.

entries.title: Daniel 7:5 "a bear"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:5 "a bear" This is another powerful predator of the Near East, which is used often in the OT paralleled with lion (cf. 1 Sam. 17:34,36,37; Prov. 28:15; Amos 5:19; Rev. 13:2). Several Scriptures describe the fierceness of a bear with cubs (cf. 2 Sam. 17:8; Prov. 17:12; Hosea 13:8).

This refers to the Medo-Persian Empire (cf. Dan. 8:21). Possibly the "raised on one side" may refer to

  1. the supremacy of Persia (see note at Dan. 5:28)
  2. preparing to attack again, even though it was still eating the last victim (imagery for unsatiated power and military destruction)

▣ "three ribs" The NRSV and NAB translate this Aramaic term as "tusks" (Hebrew BDB 854, Aramaic form BDB 1106). This probably comes from the basic meaning of the Hebrew counterpart, taken from the Arabic "curved." But also other usages of the Hebrew root are a play on the word "side" (i.e. rib of a hill, side chambers, rib of a tree or plank, BDB 854).

The controversy over the etymology of this term is related to its use in Gen. 2:21-22. The New International Dictionary of OT Theology and Exegesis, vol. 3, p. 811, gives an alternate possibility of the term "rib," as being confused with the Sumerian term for "life." How this would affect this verse in Daniel is uncertain.

This is a parallel to the ram of Dan. 8:4, where the ribs may relate to the three directions or areas of conquest: Babylon to the West, Lydia to the North, and Egypt to the South. Ben Ezra thinks they refer to three cities which were conquered. We know from historical records that Medo-Persia did not have many conquests to the East until the reign of Darius I Hystaspes.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF PERSIA

▣
NASB, NKJV, Peshitta  "thus they said to it"
NRSV, JPSOA  "and was told"
TEV  "a voice said to it"
NJB  "came the command"
REB  "the command was given to it"
LXX  "And thus it said"

This must refer to the personified "four winds of heaven" from Dan. 7:2 which symbolize God's omniscient presence throughout the earth (cf. Zechariah 1; 6).

▣ "Arise, devour much meat" The first Aramaic VERB (BDB 1110) is a Peal IMPERATIVE. The second VERB (BDB 1080) is also a Peal IMPERATIVE. Continuing with the predator imagery, God allows (cf. Dan. 7:6, "dominion was given to it") this second kingdom to conquer and spread its influence throughout the known world of the ancient Fertile Crescent.

entries.title: Daniel 7:6 "a leopard which had on its back four wings of a bird"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:6 "a leopard which had on its back four wings of a bird" This refers to the speed of the military conquest of Alexander the Great. Greece then is the third predatory Gentile Empire (cf. Dan. 8:21). The symbolic number "four" may refer to its conquest of the whole known world (cf. Dan.7:2). See chart in Contextual Insights to Daniel 8.

▣ "also had four heads" This specific detail about the number of Alexander's generals who succeed him, has caused many modern scholars to reject the predictive nature of Daniel. Yet, the affirmation of a supernatural God revealing to a faithful servant for the purpose of affirming His sovereignty to later generations seems perfectly adequate to explain this detailed description of history.

All of these details are not prophetic. Commentators must look to history to help interpret ambiguous apocalyptic passages. The four heads may refer to (1) extensive conquests in all directions or (2)four regional generals of Alexander the Great. Alexander died from a fever at the young age of 32 while in Babylon (or some say Egypt). His kingdom was initially divided among five generals, but four of them became dominant:

  1. Ptolemy in Egypt
  2. Cassender in Macedonia and Greece
  3. Seleucus in Syria and Babylon
  4. Lysimichus in Thrace

Antigonus ruled part of Asia Minor for a brief period, but was killed in 301 B.C. and was only of minor influence and importance.

entries.title: Daniel 7:7 "a fourth beast"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:7 "a fourth beast" By the sequencing of chapters 2, 7, and 8 of Daniel (see Textual Insights A., B., and C.) this refers to the Roman Empire. This would correlate with the iron and clay legs and feet of Dan. 2:33,41-43.

The fourth empire is characterized in several ways.

  1. dreadful, Dan. 7:7,19
  2. terrifying, Dan. 7:7
  3. extremely strong, Dan. 7:7
  4. iron teeth, Dan. 7:7,19 (dual in Hebrew, possibly two large teeth or two rows of teeth)
  5. devoured, Dan. 7:7,19
  6. crushed, Dan. 7:7,19
  7. trampled down the remainder with its feet, Dan. 7:7,19
  8. ten horns, Dan. 7:7,20
  9. a boastful little horn, Dan. 7:8,20
  10. claws of bronze, Dan. 7:19

Several of these terms are used in different senses in the book, which shows how context determines meaning.

  1. "dreadful" is used of
    1. the image in Dan. 2:31 and translated "awesome"
    2. Daniel's fears in Dan. 4:5 and the people's fear in 5:19
  2. "devour" is used
    1. literally in Dan. 4:33; 7:5,7,19
    2. as imagery for slander in Dan. 3:8; 6:25
  3. "crushed" ("broke in pieces") is used literally in Dan. 7:7,19,23
    1. also literally of the Messiah breaking the image in Dan.2:35,45
    2. also literally of the lions crushing those who falsely accused Daniel in 6:24

▣ "ten horns" This may speak of ten simultaneous kings (cf. Dan. 2:44). Because three of them are ripped out at the same time (cf. Dan. 7:8,24), they must be simultaneous. However, I believe them to be symbols of completeness or of power (cf. Zech. 1:18-21; Rev. 13:1), not literal kings which commentators try to fit into known history.

The term "horns" (BDB 1111) often stands for "kings" (Daniel 7 & 8) or "power" (OT imagery, i.e., the horns of the sacrificial altar and altar of incense).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #5

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALTAR OF SACRIFICE

entries.title: Daniel 7:8 "another horn, a little one, came up among them, and three of the first horns were pulled out by its roots before it"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:8 "another horn, a little one, came up among them, and three of the first horns were pulled out by its roots before it" The "little horn" of Daniel 7 may be

  1. Nero (Preterism)
  2. the Anti-Christ of the end-time because it comes from the fourth kingdom (Futurism, cf. H. C. Leupold, Exposition of Daniel, pp. 322-323 and E. J Young, The Prophecy of Daniel, p. 150).

This is somewhat confusing because the "little horn" of Dan. 8:9-14 seems to refer to the Seleucid ruler, Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175-164 B.C. who comes from the third kingdom during the Maccabean Period. He is a type of anti-christ which is always among us (cf. 1 John 2:18).

These "little horns" are both arrogant and boastful. They reject the worship of YHWH and try to destroy His people. They are both allowed by God to prosper and both will be destroyed by God. They come to epitomize rebellious, egocentric, fallen humanity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ANTICHRIST

entries.title: Daniel 7:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:9 Daniel 7:9-10 and 13-14 are set in poetic form (i.e., poetic lines) in NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NJB. This means that the verses must be interpreted in light of Semitic poetic parallelism (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY) Verses 9-10 and 13-14 are like a theological parenthesis. The vision about the Little Horn will resume at v. 11.

Synonymous parallelism in verses:

  1. Dan. 7:9b and c
  2. Dan. 7:9d and e
  3. Dan. 7:9f and g
  4. Dan. 7:10 a and b
  5. Dan. 7:10c and d
  6. Dan. 7:14e and f and g

Beginning in Dan. 7:9 the evil, suffering and chaos of the fallen earth is contrasted with the peace, calm, and purposeful actions of God in heaven (similar to Revelation 5). This section of chapter 7 is parallel to the crushing divine stone of chapter 2 that initiates God's eternal kingdom! God's judicial acts result in redemption, reconciliation, and lasting fellowship between the Triune God, faithful angels, and faithful humans! The purpose of original creation is restored through God's merciful character and redemptive intervention (cf. Gen. 3:15; see SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN).

Daniel 7:13 and 14 are one of the greatest Messianic texts in the OT (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIAH). One like a Son of Man is coming, riding on the clouds of heaven (see SPECIAL TOPIC: COMING ON THE CLOUDS) and the Ancient of Days gives Him the eternal kingdom (cf. Dan. 2:44; 4:3,34; 6:26; 7:14,27), but this involves a period of suffering and persecution of God's people. There is no victory without suffering (cf. Gen. 3:15; Psalm 22; Isaiah 53; Zechariah 12-14; Rom. 8:17,18-25; Phil. 3:10; 2 Tim. 2:11-13; 1 Pet. 4:13). Evil brings pain and suffering, but God transforms it into the path of growth and maturity (cf. Rom. 5:3-5; Heb. 5:8).

▣ "thrones were set up" The King James Version has "cast down," but the NKJV corrects this mistranslation by "the thrones were put in place" (i.e., arranged, BDB 1113, Peil PERFECT). There have been three major theories concerning who sits on these thrones:

  1. angels (cf. Ps. 89:7,8; see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS)
  2. saints (cf. LXX Dan. 7:22; Matt. 19:28; Luke 22:30; 1 Cor. 6:2; Rev. 20:4; see SPECIAL TOPIC: holy ones)
  3. some type of judges, identity unknown

Whomever these thrones represent, it is obvious that this is a court scene in heaven (cf. Revelation 4-5; 20:11-15; Matt. 25:31-46).

Option number one is best because of the OT recurrent mentioning of the concept of a heavenly angelic council (cf. 1 Kgs. 22:19; Job 1:6; 2:1; Ps. 82:1). The PLURAL term Elohim, translated God (cf. Gen. 1:1) may relate to God and the angelic council (see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.). This concept was developed in rabbinical Judaism as the seven angels of the presence (i.e., I Enoch).

▣ "the Ancient of Days took His seat" There is no definite ARTICLE with this unique Aramaic title "ancient of days" here, so it may emphasize the quality of timelessness ("one that was ancient of days"). This was a title used in Ugaritic literature for deity. The ARTICLE is present in Dan. 7:13 and 22. This title is related to the characterization of God as "living" in Dan. 4:34; 6:26; 12:7. The covenant name, YHWH, is from the Hebrew VERB "to be" (cf. Exod. 3:14), the Ever Living One!

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

▣ "His vesture was like white snow" This refers to the garments of heavenly beings.

  1. God (Dan. 7:9)
  2. Jesus (cf. Matt. 17:2; Mark. 9:3; Luke 9:29)
  3. angels
    1. OT (cf. Dan. 10:5-6)
    2. NT (cf. Matt. 28:3; Luke 24:4; John 20:12; Acts 1:10; Rev. 15:6)
  4. saints (cf. Rev. 3:4-5,18; 7:13; 19:8)

▣ "the hair of His head like pure wool" This refers to the wisdom of the aged (of Jesus in Rev. 1:14). The "white" and "pure" (NET Bible thinks it denotes "lamb's wool") of these two lines of poetry speak of both wisdom and holiness (cf. the Judgment scene of Isa. 1:18-20), which gives God the right and authority to judge (i.e., white throne judgment of Rev. 20:11; Jesus on a white horse as Judge in Rev. 19:11,14).

The following poetic lines speak of fire, which is another biblical image of holiness, cleansing, and judgment.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAIR

▣ "Its wheels were a burning fire" This is probably the portable throne-chariot of God, which Ezekiel saw in Babylon in Ezekiel 1 and 10. If this is truly a reference to the Ezekiel texts then Daniel must have known of Ezekiel's writings because this description of YHWH's chariot occurs only here and in Ezekiel 1 and 10. Daniel was in the palace in the city of Babylon; Ezekiel was in a concentration camp by the canal Chebar, while Jeremiah was in the city of Jerusalem (but forced to go to Egypt by renegade Jews). They must have known of each other's ministries, words or writings because Daniel makes allusions to both.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

entries.title: Daniel 7:10 "A river of fire was flowing"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:10 "A river of fire was flowing" The terms "flowing" and "coming out of" are parallel, possibly hendiadys. This is typical of Daniel's literary style. The imagery of fire coming from God is a biblical idiom of God coming to His creation for judgment (cf. Ps. 18:7-8; 50:3-6; 97:3; Isa. 30:27-28) as the phrases in

  1. Dan. 7:10e , "the court sat" (cf. Dan. 7:22,26)
  2. 10f, "the books were opened" (cf. Dan. 12:1)

imply.

These are imagery for the memory of a holy God. They form the documented basis used by the divine court for judgment and rewards (i.e., Dan. 7:9-10,26,27).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SECOND COMING, IV.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TWO BOOKS OF GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEGREES OF REWARDS AND PUNISHMENT

▣ "Thousands upon thousands were attending Him" If Dan. 7:10, c and d, are parallel (i.e., "10,000 x 10,000")

  1. Some have assumed that these were angels who serve God (cf. Dan. 7:10c) because of Dan. 7:16 and Deut. 33:2 (cf. Heb. 12:22; Rev. 5:11).
  2. Others have assumed that they are humans awaiting judgment (cf. Dan. 7:10d)>
  3. Perhaps saints because of Dan. 7:18, 22, and 27.
  4. This phrase is alluded to in Jude 1:14.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND

▣ "the books were opened" There is no DEFINITE ARTICLE. Here and in Rev. 20:11-15 there are two heavenly books mentioned related to God's memory:

  1. the Book of Life which records the names of God's people (i.e., saints/believers, cf. Exod. 32:32-33; Psalm 3; 69:28; Isa. 4:3; Dan. 12:1; Luke 10:20; Phil. 4:3; Heb. 12:23; Rev. 3:5; 13:8; 17:8; 20:15; 21:27)
  2. the Book of Remembrances (or deeds) which records the deeds of humanity, both positive and negative (cf. Ps. 56:8; 139:16; Isa. 65:6; Mal. 3:16; Rev. 20:12-13)

Being imagery for the memory of a holy God, they form and are used by the divine court as the documented basis for judgment and rewards (i.e., Dan. 7:9-10,26-27).

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEGREES OF REWARDS AND PUNISHMENT

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TWO BOOKS OF GOD

▣ "were opened" The United Bible Societies' A Handbook on the Book of Daniel, p. 188, mentions the interesting translation option of translating "the court sat" and "the books were opened" (both PASSIVE) as if they refer to the judges who sat on the thrones of Dan. 7:9b, "the judges sat down" ("to begin their work and opened the books").

entries.title: Daniel 7:11 "the sound of boastful words"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:11 "the sound of boastful words" This refers to the "little horn" of the fourth kingdom (cf. Dan. 7:7-8). Arrogance was Nebuchadnezzar's problem in Dan. 4:28-31; 5:20 and also Belshazzar's in Dan. 5:22-23. This arrogant attitude characterizes unbelieving Gentile powers (i.e., the little horn of the third kingdom of Dan. 8:11 and here the little horn of the fourth kingdom, cf. Dan. 7:8).

Paul discusses this very issue of human pride.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BOASTING

▣ "the beast was slain" Again God is in complete control of history (cf. Dan. 2:21; 4:17,32)! This boastful ruler is judged and destroyed, but apparently the kingdoms represented by the other beasts (cf. Dan. 7:3-6) continue in existence but without their previous power and glory (cf. Dan. 7:12, "their dominion was taken away").

This is a good place to admit that an interpreter is never sure when the details are to be taken as historical details or just part of the apocalyptic picture (much like the details of Jesus' parables). The issue is not one of truth, but one of literary presentation. Authorial intent, not literalness, is the interpretive key to figurative eastern language and literature!

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE

entries.title: Daniel 7:12 "As for the rest of the beasts. . .extension of life was granted to them for an appointed period of time"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 7:12 "As for the rest of the beasts. . .extension of life was granted to them for an appointed period of time" The phrases in Aramaic "for a season" and "and a time" are other examples of hendiadys. They mean the same thing. The nations continued to exist, but without their previous power and world influence. Their influence is limited and will be removed (cf. Dan. 2:21 and Dan. 7:18,22,27). This would therefore, refer to Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome. Notice the theme of God's sovereignty over the nations continues ("for an appointed period of time"). The Bible is teleological, not cyclical. History is moving toward a consummation!

entries.title: Daniel 7:13 "behold with the clouds of heaven"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:13 "behold with the clouds of heaven" The Septuagint has the PREPOSITION "on" (cf. Matt. 24:30; 26:64), but the Aramaic has the PREPOSITION "with" (cf. Mark 14:62; Rev. 1:7). Does this affect the theological aspect of this "one like a son of man" (human-like, cf. Phil. 2:7-8) being described with divine qualities (i.e., riding on the clouds of heaven)? Let us remember

  1. in a judgment scene (cf. Dan. 7:9-10) He is unjudged, even rewarded
  2. He is given the eternal kingdom
  3. all peoples serve (i.e., worship) Him
  4. parallel phrases are used in conjunction with the High One in Dan. 7:27
  5. NT authors used this text repeatedly for Jesus, who they believed was the promised Messiah

The phrase "The clouds of heaven" is used in several ways in the OT.

  1. God's physical, personal presence with His people by means of the Shekinah cloud of glory during the wilderness wandering period (cf. Exod. 13:21; 16:10; Num. 11:25; see SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH)
  2. a way to hide God's visible presence lest sinful humans see His holiness and glory and die (cf. Exod. 33:20; 1 Kgs. 8:10-11,12; Isa. 6:5; see SPECIAL TOPIC: CAN HUMANS SEE GOD AND LIVE?)
  3. imagery for expressing God's physical movements (cf. Isa. 19:1; Jer. 4:13; Dan. 7:13). This unique Messianic usage in Dan. 7:13 is alluded to over thirty times in the NT.
    1. the Messiah comes before God to receive the kingdom with clouds (Dan. 7:13)
    2. He leaves the earth on clouds (cf. Acts 1:9)
    3. He returns on clouds
      (1)
      for temporal judgment on Judaism (i.e., "this generation" and "those who pierced Him") ‒ Matt. 23; 24; Mark 13; Luke 21; Rev. 1:7).
      (2)
      for eschatological gathering ‒ 1 Thess. 4:7

SPECIAL TOPIC: COMING ON THE CLOUDS

▣ "One like" This Aramaic prefixed PREPOSITION meaning "like" has caused some commentators to reject this imagery as individual and Messianic. Theologically the "like" is parallel to Phil. 2:6-8, where even Paul is cautious about a complete and total identification of Incarnate Deity with fallen humanity. He is surely one with us and has faced the temptations of the flesh (cf. Heb. 2:18), but He was not affected by human rebellion and its pervasive consequences (i.e., not affected by the Fall, cf. Heb. 4:15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS' BAPTISM

▣ "a Son of Man was coming" The Aramaic phrase ("ben enosh," CONSTRUCT BDB 1085 and 1081) "son of man" is different from the similar Hebrew phrase ("ben adam") found in Psalms and Ezekiel. Both phrases are used in parallel in Job 25:6; Ps. 8:4; 90:3; 144:3; Isa. 13:12. This obviously refers to the Messiah and it links his humanity (cf. Dan. 8:17; Job 25:6; Ps. 8:4; Ezek. 2:1; see SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN), which is the meaning of the Aramaic and Hebrew phrases, "son of man" with his deity because the clouds are the transportation of deity (cf. Matt. 24:30; 26:64; Mark 13:26; 14:62; Rev. 1:7; 14:14).

Jesus uses the phrase to refer to Himself in the NT. It was not used of the Messiah in rabbinical Judaism. It had no exclusivistic, nationalistic, militaristic connotations. It uniquely describes the Messiah as fully human and fully God (cf. 1 John 4:1-3). Daniel's usage is the first which focuses on its divine aspect!

Jesus used the phrase for Himself in three senses.

  1. His suffering and death (e.g., Mark 8:31; 10:45; 14:21; Luke 9:22,44)
  2. His coming as Judge (e.g., Matt. 16:27; 25:31; John 5:27)
  3. His coming in glory to set up His kingdom (e.g., Matt. 16:28; 19:28; Mark 13:26-27; 14:62)

From The Jewish Study Bible, p. 1657 (also see George E. Ladd, A Theology of the New Testament, pp. 136-139), the later Jewish tradition about this text are listed.

  1. This context is Messianic (cf. I Enoch 46:1; 48:10; 4 Ezra [2 Esdras] chapter 13; b. Sanh. 98a)
  2. All predictions in this context are already fulfilled (cf. b. Sanh. 97b)
  3. This context does not refer to the end-time (cf. Gen. Rab. 98:2)
  4. This context represents corporate Israel (i.e., "holy ones," vv. 18,21,22,25,27, cf. Ibn Ezra and Rashi)

SPECIAL TOPIC: OT TITLES OF THE SPECIAL COMING ONE

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DEITY OF CHRIST FROM THE OT

▣ "was presented before Him" As the Messiah ("one like a son of man") is presented (BDB 1111, Haphel PERFECT) before the covenant-making YHWH, so Jesus introduces believers into the presence of God the Father (cf. 2 Cor. 4:14; Col. 1:22,28). Remember the Messiah receives the eternal kingdom, but in the same context it is the "saints" (holy ones) who receive the eternal kingdom (cf. Dan. 7:13-14 versus Dan. 7:18,22,27).

entries.title: Daniel 7:13-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:13-14 If it is true, and I think it is, that vv. 9-10 and 13-14 are a vision of what is happening in heaven (i.e., Revelation 5), then a human person is being brought before God. This "special" (i.e., incarnate Messiah) is being given the eternal, universal, non-ending Kingdom (i.e., given dominion, glory, kingdom). It must be added that progressive revelation, particularly 1 Cor. 15:24-28, clearly states the ultimate Kingdom belongs to the Father (also note 1 Cor. 3:23; 11:3).

The poetic parenthesis (i.e., vv. 9-10,13-14) is a cricial theological perspective of human history. The purpose of God from Gen. 3:15; 12:1-3 is being fulfilled through a child of a woman (i.e., Mary).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIANIC ERA

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: TITLES FOR THE SPECIAL COMING ONE

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

entries.title: Daniel 7:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:14 As the five empires of chapter 2 are parallel, so too, here. The first four are successive Gentile kingdoms of the known world of Daniel's day. The fifth is the eternal Messianic Kingdom, which was the stone that struck the image in chapter 2. The eternal Kingdom of God has been the goal since Genesis 1! This is the reign of God spoken of so often by Jesus as "the Kingdom of God" or "the Kingdom of Heaven." It is the ultiimate purpose and plan of God for unlimited fellowship with His creatures, made in His image.

All things that Gentile rulers sought in power, glory, and the extent of their kingdom, the God of Judah has freely given to the Messiah (cf. Rev. 11:15). This contrast magnifies God's sovereignty, as well as His merciful character and eternal purpose in redemption through the Messiah.

  1. The Covenant-making God, YHWH, gives the eternal kingdom to the Son of Man (Dan. 7:14; Isa. 9:6; 11:1-5; Micah 5:4-5a).
  2. The Son of Man gives the eternal kingdom to "the saints of the Highest One," which denotes all peoples (Dan. 7:14,18,22,27; Rev. 5:9; 7:9; 14:6).
  3. It is possible that the Great Commission of Matt. 28:19-20 is parallel in imagery to this text.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: IMMANUEL'S PERSON AND REIGN

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "glory" See SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (OT)

▣ "serve Him" Daniel 7:27 adds "and obey Him" (both "serve" and "obey" are Peal IMPERFECTS)! The OT uses the king and kingdom imagery to describe the appropriate relationship between God and humanity (cf. Zech. 6:15), but the NT picks up on the rare family imagery of Father (or parent) and children. The goal is an interpersonal and dependent relationship between the Creator and those made in His image and likeness (cf. Gen. 1:26-27).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

SPECIAL TOPIC: WORSHIP

entries.title: Daniel 7:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:15 These powerful visions of God's power and human evil distressed Daniel (cf. Dan. 4:19; 7:28; 8:27).

▣ "my spirit" This Aramaic NOUN (BDB 1112) is parallel to the Hebrew ruah "spirit" (BDB 924, KB 1197). It denotes a person, similar to "heart."

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

▣ "was distressed" This Aramaic VERB (BDB 1097, NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 610-611) is used often to denote the human response to divine revelation.

  1. Saul ‒ 1 Sam. 28:21
  2. Daniel ‒ Dan.4:5,19; 7:15,28
  3. Belshazzar ‒ Dan. 5:6,9,10,

The Hebrew parallel can denote

  1. fear, usually of judgment
  2. haste, rapid action

Remember, context determines meaning, usually within linguistic boundaries (i.e., the semantic field of a Semitic root).

▣ "within me" The marginal note of NASB, "in the midst of its sheath" (BDB 1102) is a Semitic idiom that later translators did not understand. Daniel had both "a spirit of the holy gods" (cf. Dan. 4:8,9,18; 5:11,14), as well as an anxious human spirit.

▣ "visions See SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

entries.title: Daniel 7:15-28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:15-28 This is the angelic interpretation of Daniel's vision. The same literary pattern is in the vision of Dan. 8:1-14 and the interpretation in Dan. 8:15-27. This is typical of apocalyptic literature.

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

entries.title: Daniel 7:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:16 One characteristic of apocalyptic literature is interpreting angels (e.g., Dan. 8:16,17; 9:22; Zech. 1:9,19; 2:2,3; 4:4,5,13; 6:4; Rev. 5:5; 7:13). This is another way to show God's sovereignty. No human can know the true interpretation without heaven's help! These visions and dreams are given to communicate inspired truths from God, but they are still under God's control. Only some understand (cf. Isa. 6:9-10; 43:8; Jer. 5:21; Ezek. 12:2; Matt. 11:15; 13:9,43; Mark 4:9,23; Luke 8:8; 14:35; Acts 7:51; 28:27; Rev. 2:7,11,29; 3:6,13,22; 13:9). This is revelation for God's people!

For a good discussion of dream interpretation involving both Joseph and Daniel, see NIDOTTE, vol. 3, pp. 722-724.

entries.title: Daniel 7:17 "these great beasts, which are four in number, are four kings who will arise from the earth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:17 "these great beasts, which are four in number, are four kings who will arise from the earth" This is the angel's interpretation of the successive nature of the kingdoms mentioned in the vision. The first had already come and gone (i.e., Nebuchadnezzar, Neo-Babylon).

▣
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NJB, Peshitta   "kings"
REB. JPSOA, LXX   "kingdoms"
TEV   "empires"

The MT has "Kings" but the UBS Text Project, p. 207, gives it only a "C" rating (considerable doubt). This doubt comes from

  1. the similarity of the Hebrew words
    1. "Kings" ‒ מלכין (MT)
    2. "kingdoms" ‒ מלכון (LXX)
  2. "kingdoms" appears in v. 23

entries.title: Daniel 7:17-18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 7:17-18 This is a historical and theological summary of Daniel's visions recorded in Daniel 1-6. The kingdoms of this world have become the eternal Kingdom of God, His Messiah, and His faithful followers. There will be problems and persecution along the way (i.e., human history of anti-God empires), but victory is coming!

entries.title: Daniel 7:18 "But the saints of the Highest One will receive the kingdom and possess the kingdom forever for all ages to come"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:18 "But the saints of the Highest One will receive the kingdom and possess the kingdom forever for all ages to come" This shows the fluidity of this chapter as well as the nature of apocalyptic literature between

  1. the Highest One (cf. Dan. 7:27)
  2. the Messiah (cf. 7:13)
  3. His people (cf. 7:18,22,27)

Notice again the emphasis on the eternal nature of the kingdom (cf. Dan. 7:27; 12:2-3). This cannot refer to a millennial kingdom unless it, itself, is imagery of the eternal kingdom!

The identification of the Aramaic phrase "saints" or "the holy ones" (BDB 1110) has been disputed.

  1. angels
    1. the Hebrew counterpart phrase almost always refers to angels (cf. Dan. 4:13,17,23; 8:13; Job 5:1; Ps. 89:5,7; see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS)
    2. the term "people" in Dan. 7:27 can mean "hosts of," which would remind one of the common OT angelic description "the hosts of YHWH"; see SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS
  2. believers
    1. in the OT they are rarely called "saints" or "holy ones" (cf. Dan. 8:24; Ps. 16:3; 34:9). The designation probably comes from Exod. 19:5-6; Deut. 14:21; 26:19.
    2. they receive the eternal kingdom (cf. Dan. 7:18,22,27)
    3. they suffer persecution and defeat (cf. Dan. 7:21,25)
  3. The real problem is the GENITIVE phrase used with "people" in v. 27, "to the people of the saints of the Highest One." This looks like "people" and "saints" are distinct groups.

Also notice the Aramaic ADJECTIVE "Most High" is PLURAL in Dan. 7:18,22,25,27, while the SINGULAR is in Dan. 3:26,32; 4:21,22,29,31; 5:18,21. Notice in Dan. 7:25 both forms occur as a title for the God of Judah. This same fluctuation is found with the Hebrew ADJECTIVE. This does not relate to polytheism, but probably to the Semitic grammatical feature called the PLURAL OF MAJESTY (see full exegetical notes at Gen. 1:26).

SPECIAL TOPIC: holy ones

▣
NASB  "forever, for all ages to come"
NKJV  "even forever and ever"
NRSV, TEV, JPSOA  "forever and ever"
NJB, REB, Peshitta  "for ever and ever"
LXX  "forever,  forever and ever"

This phrase is the threefold use of 'olam (BDB 1106) with the PREPOSITION "until" (twice) used of time (BDB 1105, cf. Dan. 2:20; 6:15,27; 7:18,26). It is an Aramaic superlative! The concept of "eternal future" is expressed often in Daniel using 'olam (and in other ways also, cf. Dan. 6:26) in its various forms and phrases (cf. R. B. Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament, pp. 316-317).

  1. "everlasting kingdom," Dan. 4:3; 7:27
  2. "forever, for all the ages to come," Dan. 7:18
  3. "forever and ever," Dan. 2:20
  4. "live forever" (Nebuchadnezzar), Dan. 2:4; 3:9 (Belshazzar), 5:10; (Darius), 6:6,21, "lives forever" (YHWH), 4:34
  5. "which will never be destroyed," Dan. 2:44a; 7:18
  6. "endure forever," Dan. 2:44c; 6:26
  7. "everlasting dominion," Dan. 4:34; 7:14

The kingdoms of men come and go, but God's Kingdom is eternal because God is eternal.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

7:19
NASB  "the exact meaning"
NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta  "the truth about"
TEV  "more about"
NJB  "about"
REB  "really signified"
JPSOA  "the true meaning"
LXX  "accurately"

This PREPOSITION and the VERBAL Pael INFINITIVE (BDB 1096), are used several times in Daniel in two senses.

  1. certain or sure, Dan. 2:8,45; 3:24
  2. true, Dan. 6:12; 7:16,19

Daniel wanted to know truthfully and with certainty the identity of

  1. the fourth beast
  2. the ten horns
  3. the boastful little horn (cf. Dan. 7:20)
7:20
NASB  "which was larger in appearance than its associates"
NKJV, Peshitta  "whose appearance was greater than his fellows"
NRSV  "that seemed greater than the others"
TEV  "It was more terrifying than any of the others"
NJB  "it sooked more impressive than its fellows"
JPSOA  "which was more conspicuous than its fellows"

This little horn suddenly looked larger:

  1. its boasting arrogance (cf. Dan. 7:8,11)
  2. its overthrow of three other horns (cf. Dan. 7:8)
  3. it grew as Daniel watched from a little horn to the largest horn, showing its extended kingdom (cf. Dan. 7:20)
  4. the fact that it attacked and overcame the saints of the Highest One (cf.Dan. 7:21)

entries.title: Daniel 7:21 "and the horn was waging war with the saints and overpowering them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 7:21 "and the horn was waging war with the saints and overpowering them" This shows the historical setting of the time of the little horn of the fourth empire will be the severe persecution of God's people. God allows this to happen for His ultimate purposes (cf. Rev. 13:7). I have come to think this refers to Nero.

entries.title: Daniel 7:21-22 "and I kept looking"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:21-22 "and I kept looking" It seems that Dan. 7:21-22 are part of Daniel's vision (cf. Dan. 7:2) and not part of the angels' explanation. If so then Daniel's questions in Dan. 7:19-20 are not answered until Dan. 7:23.

The new information about the suffering of the saints ("holy ones") is addressed in Dan. 7:25,27.

entries.title: Daniel 7:22 "until the Ancient of Days came, and judgment was passed in favor of the saints of the Highest One"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:22 "until the Ancient of Days came, and judgment was passed in favor of the saints of the Highest One" We must remember that this chapter had a word for those in exile in Babylon as well as for believers of every age who suffer persecution for their faith in YHWH and His Messiah and do not always understand why! God is in control even amidst suffering and persecution (the book of Revelation).

Notice that the titles "the Ancient of Days" (cf. Dan. 7:9,13) and "the Highest One" (cf. Dan. 7:18,25,27) are synonymous. This is also true of "the Most High" and "the Highest One" of Dan. 7:25.

Daniel's titles for Judah's God are much more traditional in chapter 9, where he prays for himself and his nation's sins (adon, YHWH, Elohim).

Verse 22 seems to imply the final judgment (cf. Matt. 25:31-46; Rev. 20:11-15). If this is correct, then "the Little horn" of Daniel 7 must be the anti-Christ of 2 Thessalonians 2, who Paul calls "the man of Lawlessness." This would also link up with the triune evil of Revelation (i.e., Satan, the land beast, and the sea beast) being totally overthrown and permanently defeated and removed. I think there is confusion because

  1. Daniel's visions apply to the first coming, not the Second Coming
  2. "Coming" in the Olivet Discourse and the book of Revelation refers to the fall of Jerusalem (A.D. 70) and the later fall of the Roman Empire (A.D. 476).
    SPECIAL TOPIC: SECOND COMING, IV.
  3. There are two "little horns"
    1. chapter 7 ‒ first century A.D.
    2. chapter 8 ‒ Maccabean period (second century B.C.
  4. Daniel's visions are not chronological; chapter 8 occurs before chapter 7.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D. (YHWH)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C. (Elohim)

entries.title: Daniel 7:23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:23 The NKJV, NRSV, and NJB print Dan. 7:23-27 as poetry, but the NASB and TEV treat it as prose. This same problem is also found in Dan. 7:9-10, 13-14. It is difficult to know if these verses are poetic or elevated prose.

▣ "he said" This refers to the interpreting angel of Dan. 7:16.

▣ "which will be different from all the other kingdoms" Notice the fourth kingdom is different by its ferocity (cf. Dan. 7:19) and extent (cf. 7:23), but the little horn is different by being

  1. more arrogant than its predecessors (cf. Dan. 7:8,11)
  2. larger in extent (cf. 7:20,24)
  3. but most of all in its persecution of God's people (cf. Dan. 7:21,25)

▣ "will devour the whole earth" The VERB (BDB 1080) is a Peal IMPERFECT. See Dan. 4:1 for the use of this same hyperbole, which refers to the known world.

entries.title: Daniel 7:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:24 The specificity of this verse has caused problems for commentators who try to take it literally. Apocalyptic literature is notoriously ambiguous and uses a form of hyperbolic stylized language (see D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, IVP, 2002).

It is quite possible that "ten" is used symbolically for a complete number. Notice the time sequence and progression.

  1. ten kings of the fourth kingdom
  2. then the eleventh comes, who is different from the others
  3. the three kings are
    1. part of the ten kings (i.e., horns, cf. Dan. 7:8)
    2. "pulled out" of Dan. 7:8 and "subdue" of 7:24 refer to the influence, policies, or remembrances of these three kings are being removed. The interpretive issue is, are the ten horns
       (1) sequential kings of the fourth empire (cf. 7:24)
       (2) somehow simultaneous kings of different parts or regions of the fourth empire (cf. Dan. 7:8)
  4. apocalyptic details not meant to be historically specific (the exception is Daniel 11)
  5. the eleventh king (the little horn) is allowed to persecute the people of God (cf. Dan. 7:21,25)
  6. God passes judgment and the little horn is destroyed (cf. Dan. 7:26)
  7. sovereignty and the eternal kingdom is given to the people of God (cf. Dan. 7:18,27)

I have come to believe Daniel's prophecy relates primarily to the first coming of the Messiah (Preterism) and not a future world ruler (Futurism). The authors who have helped me come to this conclusion are

  1. Josephus, Wars of the Jews
  2. Kenneth Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell
  3. John Bray, Matthew 24 Fulfilled
  4. Jay Adams, The Time Is At Hand
  5. Four Views of the Book of Revelation, several authors, pp. 35-92

entries.title: Daniel 7:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:25 Joyce G. Baldwin, Daniel, p. 146, points out the four characteristics of the fourth kingdom

  1. blasphemy
  2. persecution
  3. alteration of annual religious holidays
  4. an altered morality

But all four deal with the anti-God bias of this kingdom and its leaders. Like Belshazzar they despise YHWH and His covenant people because they demand complete personal freedom and independence from all authorities, especially YHWH.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣
NASB, REB, LXX  "wear down"
NKJV  "persecute"
NRSV  "wear out"
TEV  "oppress"
NJB  "torment"
JPSOA  "will harass"
Peshitta  "plot against"

Brown, Driver, Briggs (BDB 1084, Pael IMPERFECT) has "figurative for harass continually." The Hebrew counterpart is used similarly in 1 Chr. 17:9. It is normally used for wearing out clothing. The same surprising divine permission to persecute and overcome the saints ("holy ones") is found in Rev. 11:7 (the two witnesses are a symbol for the whole people of God) and Rev. 13:7! God allows evil to fully reveal itself (by also revealing true faithful followers) and its intentions so that its judgment, punishment, and removal/isolation is understood as fair and just.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ETERNAL PUNISHMENT

▣ "to make alterations in times and in law" These two terms may be a hendiadys (refer to one thing, not two). This phrase is not limited to religious laws, but the context seems to demand this. This ruler will try to overcome the worship of YHWH by changing the religious calendar (cf. Leviticus 23).

This text is the reason why many modern commentators speculate that the fourth kingdom refers to Greece and that this phrase specifically reflects Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175-164 B.C., cf. I Maccabees 1:41-53; II Maccabees 6:2,6,7) trying to force the Jews of Palestine to become more Hellenistic by drastically changing and modifying their religious traditions and worship practices.

Personally I think, because of Dan. 2:38 and 8:20-21, that the third sequenced empire is Greece. What Antiochus did has a multiple significance (i.e., multi-fulfillment prophecy) as do the phrases "the abomination of desolation" and "virgin."

SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: VIRGIN

▣
NASB, REB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "a time, times, and a half time"
NKJV  "a time and times and a half time"
NRSV, NJB  "a time, two times, and a half a time"
TEV  "three and a half years"

This same phrase is used in Dan. 12:7 and Rev. 12:14. Its exact meaning is uncertain. Many assume "time" refers to years, however; this is not spelled out in the text. But because of related time phrases.

  1. Dan. 8:14, "2300 evenings and mornings"
  2. Dan. 12:11, "1290 days"
  3. Dan. 12:12, "1335 days"
  4. Rev. 11:2, 13:5, "42 months" or "1260 days

The understanding of "3.5 years" seems to be the best interpretation. This is the length of the period of the Jewish War (A.D. 66-70).

Another way to look at this enigmatic phrase is to see it as a sequence: one, two, but not a third; therefore, a divinely limited amount of time under which Gentile kingdoms persecute God's people. God, in the book of Daniel, is in complete control (cf. Dan. 2:21; 4:17,32; 7:4,6,11,12,18,22,25,26,27)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: FORTY-TWO MONTHS

7:26
NASB, NKJV, REB, Peshitta  "But"
NRSV, TEV, NJB, JPSOA  "Then"
LXX  "And"

This CONJUNCTION shows the contrast. Gentile empires and their arrogant rulers are under God's control and guidance (cf. Dan. 2:21). As there was a stark contrast between Daniel's vision of the four beasts and their destructive power (cf. Dan. 7:1-8) with the calmness and dignity of the heavenly court (cf. Dan. 7:9-14), the same chaos/calm is found here.

▣ "the court" This is the court described in Dan. 7:9-12,13-14,18,22,27.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF DIVINE BEINGS

▣ "his dominion will be taken away, annihilated and destroyed forever" The first Aramaic VERB (BDB 1105) is a Haphel IMPERFECT and the next two (BDB 1116 and 1078) are Haphel INFINITIVES. This deals with the ultimate judgment and complete destruction of all powers that are opposed to God! There is both temporal judgment and eschatological judgment (see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SECOND COMING).

Verses such as this are what cause some (me included) to assert the eventual annihilation of the wicked. The following YouTube videos have helped me think through this issue.

  1. Edward Fudge, "The Fire That Consumes"  YouTube One Hour Lecture
  2. Steve Gregg, "Hell, Three Christian Views"  YouTube Lecture - 1:34:57
  3. My Special Topics online
    1. SPECIAL TOPIC: ETERNAL PUNISHMENT
    2. SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?
    3. SPECIAL TOPIC: DESTRUCTION (apollumi)

These lectures and my personal study have caused me to rethink what I have believed for over 50 years.

  1. I am still bothered by the imagery of eternality in Dan. 12:2; Matt. 25:46; John 5:29; Acts 24:15; Rev. 14:11
  2. The verses that caused me to begin thinking were John 3:16 (perish) and Romans 6:23 (death).

The area of theology is characterized by the term "limited mortality," which asserts that humans were not created immortal (i.e., the need for the tree of life). Only those who trust in Jesus are given immortality by the only eternal Triune God (cf. John 3:1,16,36; 5:24; 6:27,40,47,51,58; 8:51-52; 11:26; Acts 13:46,48; Rom. 2:7; 5:21; 6:23; Gal. 6:8; 1 John 5:11.

Thank God, those of us who believe can think about this issue but we will never experience separation from God!

entries.title: Daniel 7:27 "all the kingdoms under the whole heaven"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:27 "all the kingdoms under the whole heaven" This sounds very much like Rev. 11:15b.

▣
NASB  "will be given to the people of the saints
  of the Highest One"
NKJV  "shall be given to the people, the saints
  of the Most High"
NRSV, NJB, JPSOA, LXX, Peshitta  "shall be given to the people of the holy
  onesof the Most High"
TEV  "will be given to the people of the
  Supreme God"
REB  "will be given to the holy people of the
  Most High"

The Aramaic VERB (BDB 1095) is a Piel PERFECT. This shows the two ways this phrase is understood (cf. a similar Hebrew phrase in Dan. 8:24).

  1. The NKJV, REB, and TEV translations make "people" and "saints" parallel (appositional).
  2. If the NASB is followed then angels seem to be the referent of "holy ones" or "saints" in this verse, which would relate it to the national angels of Deut. 32:8 (LXX), in this case, to Michael and Gabriel and other angels (cf. Daniel 10) that serve God and His people.
  3. Some commentators even see "Son of Man" in Dan. 7:13 as referring to these same angels. Daniel, as all apocalyptic literature, pictures angels as intimately involved with God's dealings with humanity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

SPECIAL TOPIC: holy ones

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

▣ "His kingdom" Notice the continuing fluidity between the kingdom as belonging to:

  1. God, Dan. 7:9-10, 27
  2. His Messiah, "Son of Man," Dan. 7:13
  3. His people, Dan. 7:18,22,27
  4. some would see Dan. 7:27 as referring to faithful angels (i.e., Michael, Gabriel, angel of Daniel, chapter 10, etc.)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KINGDOM OF GOD

▣ "and all the dominions will serve and obey Him" This term "dominion," "have power," or "sovereignty" (BDB 1115) is used in Daniel for

  1. God (cf. Dan. 4:3,34; 6:26)
  2. the Gentile kingdoms (cf. Dan. 4:22; 6:26; 7:6,12,26)

It is used of the "Son of Man" in Dan. 7:14, which may reflect Gen. 1:26,28-30, where Adam (and thereby mankind) is given authority or dominion over this planet. One wonders if the phrase "all the dominions" refers to

  1. the PLURAL "kingdoms" in Dan. 7:27
  2. the believers of the OT and NT (cf. Isa. 45:20-25)
  3. possibly angelic realms (cf. Heb. 1:13-14; Dan. 7:10)

This concept of complete cosmic allegiance may be expressed in Phil. 2:10-11 and Col. 1:16-20 or even 1 Cor. 15:24-25!

The first Aramaic VERB (BDB 1105) is a Pael IMPERFECT and the second (BDB 1116) is a Hithpael IMPERFECT.

SPECIAL TOPIC: IMMANUEL'S PERSON AND REIGN

entries.title: Daniel 7:28 "At this point the revelation ended"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:28 "At this point the revelation ended" Daniel 7 is a literary unit. It is linked to chapter 6, but the vision is complete in itself and covers

  1. the entire history of mankind from Daniel's day to the eschaton (Futurists)
  2. from Daniel's day specifically to the judgment of A.D. 70 (Preterists)

▣ "my thoughts were greatly alarming me and my face grew pale" See note at Dan. 4:19 (also 7:15,28; 8:27; 10:16-17). There is so much pain, suffering, and persecution still ahead for the people of God.

▣ "I kept the matter to myself" How would he communicate these visions and to whom? This is when and how apocalyptic literature becomes so helpful!

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. How are chapters 2, 7, and 8 related?
  2. Why is there such a problem in identifying these four nations?
  3. Who is
    1. the Ancient of Days?
    2. the Son of Man?
    3. the little horn?
  4. What does Dan. 7:25 say about the time element of this occurrence?

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Daniel 8:1 "In the third year of the reign of Belshazzar"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:1 "In the third year of the reign of Belshazzar" This shows that the vision of chapter 8 came after a time span of two years from the vision of chapter 7. We do not know when or how long Belshazzar served as co-regent under his father, Nabonidus, before the fall of the Neo-Babylon Empire by the army of Cyrus II, known as Cyrus the Great (cf. Daniel 5). Chapter 8 restarts the Hebrew section of the book of Daniel (i.e., Dan. 1:1-2:3; 8:1-12:13).

▣ "vision" In chapters 2 and 4 Daniel receives from God the interpretation of dreams that Nebuchadnezzar II had, but in chapters 7; 8; 10; 11, he is directly addressed by God in his own vision. In chapter 7:1, this divine revelation is called both "a dream" and "a vision." In Daniel there seems to be no distinction made between these two means of revelation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣
NASB  "previously"
NKJV  "the first time"
NRSV, Peshitta  "at first"
TEV  "I saw a second vision"
NJB  "originally"
REB  "my earlier vision"
JPSOA  "appeared to me earlier"
LXX  "the first one"

This is literally "at the first" (BDB 321, e.g., 9:21; Gen. 13:3; 2 Sam. 21:9,10; 2 Kgs. 17:25; Neh. 11:17), which is idiomatic for the vision Daniel received earlier in Belshazzar's reign (i.e., Daniel 7).

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Chapters 2, 7 and 8 of Daniel are related as they reveal a sequence of four coming kingdoms and a fifth eternal divine kingdom.

    PREDICTED SEQUENCE OF WORLD EMPIRES
