      Steve Gregg, Revelation: Four Views, Revised and Updated, pp. 35-36, has a good list of the out of sequence or repeated visions in the book of Revelation.
      You can hear my four audio tapes on the recapitulation model for understanding Revelation. Click on "Worldwide Voices" (yellow box) on my homepage, then my name, and A. #3.

  2. As in his first vision Daniel was compelled to focus on the fourth kingdom; two years later (compare Dan. 7:1 with 8:1) God further revealed information about the second and third kingdoms in another vision. Daniel's visions are not chronological.
     The little horn of the third kingdom is focused on because it (he) will impact the lives and worship of Israel more than any other previous Gentile ruler.
     The little horn of the fourth kingdom will also impact God's people in the future.
    1. first coming temporal judgment of
      1. Jerusalem and the temple (Preterism)
      2. Nero
      3. Roman Empire
    2. an end-time world ruler (Futurism)

  3. The language has switched back to Hebrew because Daniel, chapters 8-12 are messages for God's people. This vision is primarily about the future suffering and domination caused by the little horn(s) against God's people. For them, the vision is about a limited time of suffering and desecration followed by a divine intervention.
     The twenty-three hundred evenings and mornings (cf. Dan. 8:14) were a sure promise of the deliverance and restoration of the temple/Jerusalem (i.e., the small rebuilt temple of Zerubbabel, Joshua, and Haggai).
    SPECIAL TOPIC: POST EXILIC CHART
    SPECIAL TOPIC: FORTY-TWO MONTHS

  4. The book by D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, has been very helpful and I recommend it to all who attempt to understand Daniel 7-12. He even gives a whole chapter on the interpretation of the apocalyptic imagery of Daniel 8, pp. 101-128.
     The other book that has been so helpful in understanding the different genres of the Bible is How to Read the Bible For All Its Worth by Gordon Fee and Doug Stuart.
     As interpreters our worst enemies are:
    1. western culture and evangelical Christianity's over-emphasis on literalism
    2. a systematic eschatology (usually personally unexamined), which has been given to us by sincere, godly, well-meaning parents, pastors, denominations, and authors (Futurism)

  5. Satan does not know God's plans; therefore, he must have an anti-God leader prepared and active in every age (cf. 1 John 2:18) to carry out his bidding (Idealist). Antiochus IV is one example of a selfish, self-centered, atheistic individual who wants, not only political and military power, but also adoration, even worship, and there have been many others throughout human history like him. Fallen humanity regularly produces this type of individual. Yet, God is still sovereign and He even uses these kinds of persons to accomplish His will, as He does Satan.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: SATAN

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Daniel 8:2 "I was in the citadel of Susa"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:2 "I was in the citadel of Susa" Susa later became the capitol of the kingdom of Persia (cf. Neh. 1:1); but at this time it was simply a large, fortified city in the province of Elam (i.e., east of the Tigris River, cf. Isa. 22:6; Jer. 49:34-39). It would later be called Shushan (cf. Neh. 1:1; Esther 1:2,5). The Greek name was Susa.

Was Daniel physically in Susa, or was this part of the vision? He could have been in Susa on governmental business (cf. Dan. 8:27). There seems to be no integral part of the vision linked to this locality.

Several visions in the Bible involve some type of mental or physical transport.

  1. Ezekiel, from Babylon, to the temple in Jerusalem, Ezek. 8 (cf. Ezek. 3:14; 11:1; 43:5)
  2. Philip, in Gaza, taken to Azotus, Acts 8:39-40
  3. John, on Patmos, taken to heaven, Rev. 4:2 (cf. Rev. 17:3; 21:10)

▣ "I looked in the vision, and I myself was" Daniel sees himself in his vision for the first time.

▣ "Ulai Canal" This was a 900 foot wide man made irrigation canal north of the city (BDB 19 I), which connected two rivers. The ancient Bible versions in Greek, Aramaic, and Latin translate this rare Hebrew word "canal" or "river" (BDB 385).

entries.title: Daniel 8:3 "a ram which had two horns"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:3 "a ram which had two horns" This seems to refer to Medo-Persia (cf. Dan. 8:20) and is analogous to the bear with one side lifted of Daniel 7 and the breast and arms of silver in chapter 2.

The horns are described by several features.

  1. two horns
  2. one longer than the other
  3. the longer one came up after the other was in place

They probably represent the historical fact that Cyrus (1/2 Median descent) first conquered Media and then later became the king of Persia after the fall of Neo-Babylon. The two horns may also be parallel to the bear of chapter 7, raised on one side (showing the dominant kingdom of Persia in the Medo-Persian Empire (cf. Dan. 8:20). See chart in Contextual Insights, A., B.

entries.title: Daniel 8:4 "I saw the ram butting westward, northward and southward "
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:4 "I saw the ram butting westward, northward and southward " Many use this as parallel to the three ribs in the bear's mouth, Dan. 7:5, to describe the three directions of Medo-Persian conquest.

The nations that Greece conquered by compass direction were:

  1. westward ‒ Neo-Babylon, Syria, and Asia Minor
  2. northward ‒ Armenia and the area of the Caspian Sea
  3. southward ‒ Egypt and Ethiopia

▣ "nor was there anyone to rescue from his power; but he did as he pleased and magnified himself" There are several aspects to this phrase that characterize the arrogance of these Gentile kings and kingdoms (i.e., "no rescue," cf. Dan. 8:8,11,25).

  1. They thought no nation, army, or god could thwart their desires (i.e., "rescue," cf. Dan. 2:21).
  2. The essence of human rebellion is "I did it my way" ("he did as he pleased," Dan. 8:4,7).
  3. The king magnified himself (like the little horns of chapters 7 and 8), which attracts God's notice and judgment (this phrase could be understood as relating to the power and size of his kingdom as in Dan. 8:9, but this Hebrew word (BDB 152) has a negative connotation in this chapter).
  4. He did as he pleased, which is a recurrent theme (cf. Dan. 5:19; 11:3,16,36-37).

This prediction is a good place to remind all interpreters of the fuzzy nature of apocalyptic literature. The details are often for effect, not to be interpreted as literal historic events (cf. D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares & Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, pp. 117-128). In fact, Greece did repel Persia's advance several times (490 B.C. and 480 B.C.). Apocalyptic literature cannot be interpreted or evaluated by the details. Often, which of the details have significance can only be known after the fulfillment in history!

entries.title: Daniel 8:5 "a male goat was coming from the west over the surface of the whole earth without touching the ground"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:5 "a male goat was coming from the west over the surface of the whole earth without touching the ground" This refers to Greece (cf. Dan. 8:21; 11:3). Notice the speed of the victory (334-331 B.C.) and direction from which Alexander III, known as Alexander the Great, came. This parallels the leopard with four wings of Dan. 7:6.

▣ "the surface of the whole earth" This is a hyperbolic statement which refers to the known world of that day.

▣ "a conspicuous horn between his eyes" This refers to Alexander III, known as Alexander the Great, who conquered the whole known world and died at the age of 32 (cf. Dan. 8:8,21-22; 11:4).

The term "conspicuous" (BDB 303) is very similar to the term "vision" (BDB 302) in Dan. 8:1. In Isaiah it is used for a vision or oracle several times (cf. Isa. 21:2; 29:11). It means "conspicuous" only in this context (Dan. 8:5,8).

entries.title: Daniel 8:6-7 "rushed at him in his mighty wrath. . .and he was enraged at him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:6-7 "rushed at him in his mighty wrath. . .and he was enraged at him" We know that Persia, under Darius III, attacked Greece several times over the Hellespont (490 and 480 B.C.). This made Greece so angry that when Alexander III finally crossed this narrow gap of water in 334 B.C. with thirty thousand soldiers and five thousand cavalry, he engaged the Persian army with over 600,000 soldiers and soundly defeated them several different times. Alexander would not make a peace treaty with Persia!

If one reads Daniel 8 alone, he would expect one decisive battle, but in fact, there were three major decisive battles. The prediction is true, but fuzzy (as are all apocalyptic details, see note at Dan. 8:4).

entries.title: Daniel 8:8 "the male goat magnified himself exceedingly"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:8 "the male goat magnified himself exceedingly" See note at Dan. 8:4,5.

▣ "the large horn was broken and in its place came up four conspicuous horns toward the four winds of heaven" This refers to the death of Alexander the Great (323 B.C.) in Babylon at the age of 32 or 33 caused by swamp fever. The unexpected, sudden death of Alexander caused great and prolonged conflict throughout his kingdom. The governors or generals who were dominant as separate regional satraps throughout his kingdom continued to maintain their control.

  1. Peucestas in Persia
  2. Peithon in Media
  3. Ptolemy in Egypt
  4. Lysimachus in Thrace
  5. Antigonus in Phrygia
  6. Leonnatus in Hellespontine
  7. Laomedon in Syria
  8. Lumenus in Cappadocia
  9. Stasonor in Bactria
  10. Philotas in Cilicia
  11. Asander in Lycia
  12. Menander in Lydia

The ones that impacted the Jews were #3 and #7, which are discussed in detail in Daniel 11.

I agree with E. J. Young that the "four conspicuous horns toward the four winds of heaven" may be an idiom of universal rule not relating specifically to any of the four major generals. Apocalyptic literature is designed to give an emotional general impression, not detailed facts of history. For a good discussion of the biblical use of the number "four," see:

  1. SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #2
  2. NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 495-496
  3. Biblical Numerology by John J. Davis

entries.title: Daniel 8:9 "a rather small horn which grew exceedingly great toward the south, toward the east and toward the Beautiful land"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:9 "a rather small horn which grew exceedingly great toward the south, toward the east and toward the Beautiful land" This refers to the fourth Seleucid ruler known as Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175-164 B.C.). We learn from history that he gained, through craftiness (cf. Dan. 8:24), a rather extensive kingdom and was especially a problem to the Jewish people of Palestine (i.e. "the beautiful land," cf. Dan. 11:16,41; Jer. 3:19).

The Hebrew term gdl (BDB 152, KB 178, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) appears in Dan. 8:8, 9, 10-11. In 8:8 it means "magnified himself"; in 8:9 it means "grew exceedingly great," as it does figuratively in 8:10, "it grew great." It is obvious that at least two senses are possible.

  1. arrogance, Dan. 8:8,10,11
  2. size, extent, Dan. 8:9.10

It is hard to know which is the intent of the original author.

▣ "south. . .east. . .in the Beautiful Land" It is possible from secular history to document the nations that Antiochus IV attacked.

  1. south ‒ Egypt (Daniel 11)
  2. east ‒ Parthia
  3. Beautiful Land ‒ Canaan/Palestine (cf. Dan. 11:16,41)

entries.title: Daniel 8:10 "to the host of heaven"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:10 "to the host of heaven" The PREPOSITION "to" is translated in poetry as "as far as," "even to," or "up to" (cf. Dan. 8:11).

The term "host" often applies to YHWH"s angelic army (TEV, cf. Josh. 5:14,15; 1 Sam. 1:3; Neh. 9:6), but in this context (cf. Dan. 8:12) it refers to

  1. the people of God ("saints," cf. Dan. 7:18,22,27)
  2. imagery for the little horn's ambition to rival God (e.g., Isa. 14:13, the kings of Babylon), in which case the stars would refer to angels or heaven

It is problematic that in the span of four verses this term (BDB 838) is used in several senses.

  1. "the host of heaven," Dan. 8:10 (faithful believers or angels)
  2. "the commander of the host," Dan. 8:11 (angels)
  3. "the host," Dan. 8:12 (believers)
  4. "the host," Dan 8:13 (believers or temple worshipers and temple servants)

Here is where context is crucial. Hebrew, being such an ancient language, uses terms in several ways (semantic field). Our problem as modern interpreters is that we demand specific historically verifiable details and consistent, lexical usage. The genre and our distance in time from the actual events make these demands impossible. This is a faith document, not a history book!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

SPECIAL TOPIC: holy ones

▣ "and some of the stars to fall to the earth" Who does this refer to?

  1. Usually in Jewish extra-biblical apocalyptic literature falling stars refer to angels coming to earth, but in this context "stars" is a parallel to "hosts" (the people of God, cf. Dan. 8:24a; 12:3; see SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS); therefore, this idiom is referring to the earlier promises of God that Israel will be like the stars of heaven (in number, cf. Gen. 15:5; Jer. 33:22; in glory, cf. Dan. 12:3).
  2. This verse refers to the little horn of the third kingdom attacking God's people (i.e., those faithful Jews who opposed Antiochus' laws), as did the little horn of the fourth kingdom in Dan. 7:21,25. There is an anti-God force loose in creation. It can be identified by its attack on God, God's Messiah, and God's people! Here, "stars" could refer to "the holy ones" (i.e., the faithful).

entries.title: Daniel 8:11 "It even magnified itself to be equal with the Commander of the host"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:11 "It even magnified itself to be equal with the Commander of the host" One characteristic of these Gentile kings has been their arrogance. The influence of the fall (cf. Genesis 3) continues!

The phrase "to be equal" is the same PREPOSITION as "up to the hosts" in Dan. 8:10.

"The Commander" is the Hebrew word (BDB 978) for "chief," "ruler," "official," "captain," or "prince." This could refer to:

  1. YHWH, Dan. 8:11c, 25
  2. Messiah, possibly Dan. 8:11; 7:13-14
  3. a powerful angel, Dan. 8:13; 10:1-9
  4. Michael, Israel's national angel, Dan. 10:13,31; 12:1

The next few phrases seem to imply either #1 or #2.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣ "it removed the regular sacrifice from Him and the place of His sanctuary was thrown down" This seems to refer to something involving the daily morning and evening sacrifices in the temple ritual called "the continual" (cf. Exod. 29:38-42; Num. 28:1-8) and/or all the sacrificial system. This daily ritual was stopped ("removed," BDB 926, KB 1202, Hophal PERFECT; which is the Qere reading.

The second VERB, BDB 1020, KB 1527, Hophal PERFECT, may refer to the same event) by Antiochus IV Epiphanes and he further defiled the temple by regularly offering a swine on the altar and placing an image of Zeus in the Holy Place (cf. Dan. 11:31; 12:11). Antiochus IV tried to Hellenize the Jews (cf. I Macc. 1.54-61; II Macc. 4.11-6.11) by forcing them to eat the flesh of swine. This caused the rebellion led by the priest of Moden, whose son, Judas Maccabees, through an extended guerilla warfare, finally succeeded in defeating the Seleucid army and, in 165 B.C., cleansed and restored the temple. In modern times, this is known as the Festival of Lights (Hanukkah) , and is celebrated in December (the date changes each year because the Jews use a lunar calendar).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SACRIFICIAL SYSTEMS OF THE ANE

entries.title: Daniel 8:12 "on account of transgression"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:12 "on account of transgression" Some see this as:

  1. the sins of the Jewish people (cf. Dan. 9:24) which God allowed to be punished by a foreign leader (cf. Isa. 10:5; Jer. 51:20)
  2. the sins of Jewish leadership which helped Antiochus
  3. or more probably in this context, Antiochus IV Epiphanes' sin (cf. Dan. 8:13,23)

I think #3 fits best.

▣ "the host" This seems to refer to the people of God. See note and Special Topics at Dan. 8:10.

▣ "the regular sacrifice" See note at Dan. 8:11.

▣ "it will fling truth to the ground" The "it" here refers to the actions of the little horn. The same VERB (BDB 1020, KB 1527) appears in v. 11 and in Ezek. 19:12, but the concept is expressed in Isa. 59:14. In general it refers to the worship of God or the word of God. Notice the little horn is allowed by YHWH to do this evil.

"Truth" is a significant theological term (BDB 54). It denotes the trustworthiness and faithfulness of God that can be seen in His faithful followers. Therefore, this could refer to Antiochus' persecution and murder of faithful Jews during his reign.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: TRUTH/TRUE

▣ "perform its will and prosper" This refers to fallen humanity's independent attitude, which is a recurrent theme in Daniel (cf. Dan. 5:19; 8:4; 11:3,16,36). It will succeed (by God's will) but only for a designated period of time (cf. Gal. 6:7).

entries.title: Daniel 8:13 "I heard a holy one"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:13 "I heard a holy one" This is translated "saint" in Dan. 7:18,21,22,25 and refers to faithful believers. Here it must refer to the conversation between two angels (cf. possibly Dan. 7:27) for Daniel's benefit. Other OT titles for angels are

  1. "sons of God" (cf. Gen. 6:2; Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7; Ps. 29:1; 89:6-7; see
    SPECIAL TOPIC: "sons of God" IN GENESIS 6)
  2. "holy ones" (cf. Dan. 4:13; Ps. 89:5, 7; Zech. 14:5; see SPECIAL TOPIC: holy ones)
  3. "watchers" (cf. Dan. 4:13, 17, 23; see SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE)
  4. sometimes "man" or "men" (cf. Dan. 8:15,16; 9:20; 10:5,16,18; 12:6-7; Zech. 1:8,10,19; 2:1,3)

▣ "How long" This does not refer to Jeremiah's prophcy about a seventy year exile (cf. Dan. 9:2; Jer. 25:11,12; 29:10; Zech. 7:5). It is connected to the "little horn" of the third empire (i.e., Greece, cf. Dan. 8:21), which is being discussed in Dan. 8:9-14. Therefore, this time frame is related to the atrocities of Antiochus IV (175-164 B.C.), who desecrated the temple and attempted to force individual, faithful Jews to become Hellenists.

  1. The TEV translates this so that the three aspects of the question stand out.
    1. How long will these things that were seen in the vision continue?
    2. How long will an awful sin replace the daily sacrifices?
    3. How long will the army of heaven and the temple be trampled on?
  2. H. C. Leupold, Exposition of Daniel, p. 352, says that the Hebrew text has four items in apposition to "vision."
    1. the regular daily offerings
    2. the crime-causing horror
    3. the sanctuary to be trodden under foot
    4. the host to be trodden under foot
▣
NASB  "while the transgression causes horror"
NKJV  "the transgression of desolation"
NRSV  "the transgression that makes desolate"
TEV  "the awful sin"
NJB  "of horrifying iniquity"
REB  "impiety causes desolation"
LXX  "the sin of desolation"
Peshitta  "iniquity and corruption"

This probably refers to the idol of Zeus Olympius, that Antiochus IV placed in the temple (II Maccabees 6:2). This VERB, "makes desolate" (BDB 1030, KB 1563, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) may be a word play from the Canaanite deity, Ba'al Shamem ("Lord of Heaven"), because "heaven" has the same Hebrew consonants as "makes desolate." Zeus was the Greek counterpart of Ba'al.

This same phrase appears in Dan. 9:27; 11:31; and 12:11. It refers to different atrocities, but all are connected by rebellion against God and His people. In the Bible it can refer to

  1. Antiochus IV
  2. Titus' destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70 (Preterists)
  3. the end-time antiChrist (Futurists)

It is obviously a multiple fulfillment prophecy.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION

▣
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta  "the host"
TEV  "the army of heaven"
NJB  "the army"
NEB, REB  "the fairest of all lands"
JPSOA  "the (heavenly) hosts"

The MT has the NOUN "hosts" (BDB 838, cf. vv. 10,11,12,13), which means "army," "war," or "warfare." BDB suggests this refers to Michael, the angel-prince of Israel (cf. Dan. 12:1) because the Hebrew is MASCULINE SINGULAR.

However, it could be a collective use of Judah's military (i.e., hosts).

The NEB, REB have a similar Hebrew root, "and of the beauty."

  1. and of the army ‒ וצבא
  2. and of the beauty (cf. v. 9) ‒ וצבי

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

8:14
NASB, NKJV, JPSOA, Vulgate  "He said to me""
NRSV, LXX, Peshitta  "he answered him"
TEV  "the other angel answered"
NJB  "the first replied"
REB  "the answer came"

The MT has "and he said to me," but context seems to require "him" (i.e., two interpreting angels speaking to one another, cf. v. 13).

  1. to me ‒ אלי
  2. to him ‒ אליו

The UBS Text Project, p. 312, suggests "to me," but gives it a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

▣ "For 2,300 hundred evenings and mornings" This phrase has been interpreted in three ways:

  1. 2300 full days (E. J. Young, pp. 173-175; NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 420, 1. b.)
  2. a number equivalent to three years, 55 days; this calculation seems to follow the usage in Genesis 1 ("evenings and mornings") and the phrase related to persecution in Dan. 7:25
  3. refers to the number of times "the continual" sacrifice was not given

Context favors #2 because of the use of a similar period of time in Daniel and Revelation. See note at Dan. 7:25.

Differing commentators choose one. I like #2, but H. C. Leupold, Exposition of Daniel, p. 355, quotes a German commentator, Meinhold (1889), ". . .an entirely satisfactory computation has neither been found here nor for the kindred periods in chapters nine and twelve." The problem is that we forget that this is apocalyptic/prophetic literature, not history.

If one assumes this portion of Daniel is related exclusively to the atrocities of Antiochus IV, then this identifies the period of time of his persecution of the faithful (i.e., holy wars).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FORTY-TWO MONTHS

▣
NASB, REB  "the Holy Place will be properly restored"
NKJV, JPSOA  "the sanctuary shall be cleansed"
NRSV  "the sanctuary shall be restored to its rightul state"
TEV  "the Temple will be restored"
NJB  "the sanctuary will have its rights restored"
LXX  "the sanctuary shall be purified"
Peshitta  "then righteousness shall prevail"

This VERB, Niphal PASSIVE (BDB 842, KB 100, PERFECT WITH WAW) is used in this form only here in the OT. The basic meaning is "to be made just or righteous," so here it would imply, "shall be put in right or properly pure condition." December 12, 165 B.C. was the date of the cleansing and restoration of the temple in Jerusalem by Judas Maccabeus. See note at Dan. 8:11.

entries.title: Daniel 8:15 "I sought to understand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:15 "I sought to understand" As the Gentile kings needed Daniel's God-given gift to understand their dreams, so Daniel needs heavenly beings to help him. Angelic mediation and interpretation is one of the characteristics of apocalyptic literature. Humans cannot discover truth. It must be revealed!

▣ "who looked like a man" This is the Hebrew word gbr, (BDB 149) which makes up Gabriel's name. This has nothing to do with Dan. 7:13. Angels often appear in human form (cf. Zech. 1:8,10; 2:1,4). This does not describe their true essence, simply how they appear to us. See note at Dan. 8:13.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

entries.title: Daniel 8:16 "Gabriel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 8:16 "Gabriel" Only two angels are named in the Bible, Gabriel and Michael. Michael is called the Archangel of Israel (cf. Dan. 10:13,21; 12:1; Jude 1:9; Rev. 12:7), while Gabriel seems to be God's messenger angel (cf. Dan. 9:21; Luke 1:19,26). His name means "man of God" or "strong man of God" (BDB 150).

entries.title: Daniel 8:17 "I was frightened and fell on my face"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:17 "I was frightened and fell on my face" Humans are shocked at the presence and awesomeness of the spiritual realm (see NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 692).

  1. God, Gen. 17:3; Job 13:11,21; Ezek. 1:28; 3:23; 44:4
  2. angels, Dan. 8:17; 10:9,10,12,15,19; Rev. 1:17
  3. visions, Job 7:14 (4:13-14); Dan. 7:28; 8:27

▣ "Son of man" Here "man" simply refers to Daniel as a human being (Adam, cf. Dan. 8:16), as in Ezek. 2:1; 3:1; 4:1; 5:1; 6:2; 7:2; 12:2,8; and Ps. 8:4. The angel Gabriel is addressing Daniel.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

▣ "understand" This is a Hiphil IMPERATIVE (BDB 106, KB 122), as it is in Dan. 8:16 (cf. John Joseph Owens, Analytical Key to the Old Testament, vol. 4, p. 737). Gabriel is commanded by the man above the Ulai Canal (i.e., an angel) to help Daniel understand the conversation (cf. Dan. 8:15), spoken in the dialogue between the two holy ones (i.e., angels) in Dan. 8:13-14.

There are authoritative levels in the angelic world.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

▣ "the vision pertains to the time of the end" This vision seems to refer not to the far future, but the relatively near future (i.e., Empires of Persia and Greece). This should give modern interpreters a warning about trying to define the phrase "the time of the end" (cf. Dan. 8:19) as always eschatological (i.e., Dan. 12:4,6; NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 955). In Dan. 11:35,40 "the end time" is used of the period of Greek rule involving the kingdoms of the Ptolomies and Seleucids (323-165 B.C.).

entries.title: Daniel 8:18 "I sank into a deep sleep"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:18 "I sank into a deep sleep" The presence of the spiritual realm causes humans to be frightened and pass out (BDB 922, KB 1191, cf. Gen. 15:12; Job 4:13; Dan. 10:9). In Rev. 1:17 John looked as if he had died!

▣ "he touched me" The angel's touch was a great comfort (cf. Dan. 10:10,16,18; possibly 9:21; 1 Kgs. 19:7; Rev. 1:17). The spiritual realm can manifest physicalness.

Just an added thought about angels in the physical realm. In modern times there have appeared physical forms of flying objects (i.e., UFOs). I have become convinced these are fallen angels' attempt to lead modern naturalists away from God and His unique revelation (i.e., in His book, and in His Son). Modern secularists ask, "Are we alone in the universe?" No, we are not! The angelic world has several levels and categories (see SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE). Some are supportive of mankind, made in God's image and likeness, but some are not (see SPECIAL TOPIC: DEMONS [fallen angels]).

Let me list some helpful books in this area of modern deception.

  1. William M. Alnor, UFO in the New Age (1992)
  2. William M. Alnor, UFO Cults and the New Millennium (1992)
  3. Gary Bates, Alien Intrusion (updated and expanded), (2010)
  4. a good YouTube video by Walter Martin, "UFOs ‒ Friend, Foes, or Fantasy"

▣ "made me stand upright" Exactly why the angel wanted Daniel to stand up (BDB 763, KB 840, Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw) is uncertain, but it happens again in Dan. 10:11 (Qal IMPERATIVE). Perhaps it has to do with the dignity of faithful followers made in God's image. Angels seem so powerful to humans in this time period and this fallen reality, but in truth, humans have great dignity and worth. See full exegetical note at Hebrews 1:14 online.

entries.title: Daniel 8:19 "the final period of the indignation"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:19 "the final period of the indignation" This term (BDB 276) is used often in Isaiah of YHWH's indignation against His people for their covenant faithlessness; therefore, He punishes them by means of foreign nations (cf. Isa. 10:5-6,25; 13:2-16 [esp. v. 5]). However, His indignation will pass (cf. Isa. 26:20; 30:27; 66:7-24 [esp. v. 14]). This theme is continued in Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 21:31; 22:24,31). It is foreshadowed in Deut. 28:49-57.

In the context of the book of Daniel, this indignation (BDB 276) has to do with the independence and arrogance of the Gentile nations who God used to judge His people. Their arrogance is projected into the distant future (i.e., Greece for Dan. 8:19 and a future (at least future to Daniel) antichrist for 11:36 [cf. Dan. 7:8,20-22,23-26; 2 Thessalonians 2; Revelation 12-13]). Now He will judge these Gentile nations (cf. Dan. 11:36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SECOND COMING, IV.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTICHRIST

▣ "for it pertains to the appointed time of the end" This phrase (BDB 417) is found here and in Dan. 11:27,29,35, which all refer to events relating to Greece, especially Antiochus IV, who aggressively attacks God's people.

The confusion so common in interpreting Daniel is the failure to:

  1. recognize its genre and to try to identify all details historically
  2. recognize its near future symbols and its far future symbols
    1. the little horns of Dan. 7:8
    2. Dan. 9:1-23 vs. 9:24-27
    3. Dan. 11:1-35,40-45 vs. 11:31-39
  3. recognize its merging of anti-God kingdoms. The fourth kingdom is Rome (Preterism), but more, it is all Gentile world-dominating powers (Idealism).

entries.title: Daniel 8:20 "the ram. . .Media and Persia"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 8:20 "the ram. . .Media and Persia" The ram was the sign of Persia (Aries, the Zodiac sign), but the ram was also the guardian spirit of Persia and the king wore the ram's emblem to battle.

entries.title: Daniel 8:21 "the shaggy goat. . .Greece"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:21 "the shaggy goat. . .Greece" In Dan. 8:5 there is a Hebrew CONSTRUCT for male goat (BDB 862 and 777). In Dan. 8:21 there are two words which the Handbook on the Book of Daniel, from the Untied Bible Societies, says is made up of the Hebrew word for male goat (BDB 972 II) and the Aramaic word for he-goat (BDB 862), which are in opposition, p. 222. The ADJECTIVE form of this term means "hairy," therefore, the additional word "shaggy" in Dan. 8:21. This additional term usually refers to the goats offered as a sin-sacrifice (cf. Lev. 4:23,24; 9:15; 16:5,7-8; Num. 7:16).

The goat was the Zodiac sign of Greece, Capricorn, and it was the national symbol of the Macedonian coat of arms. These two verses are very historically specific in the identification of the second and third Gentile kingdoms of Daniel's vision.

▣ "the first king" This is obviously Alexander the Great.

entries.title: Daniel 8:22 "although not with his power"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 8:22 "although not with his power" None of the rival Greek generals (satraps) ever equaled the power and extent of Alexander's kingdom!

entries.title: Daniel 8:23 "A king will arise, insolent and skilled in intrigue"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:23 "A king will arise, insolent and skilled in intrigue" This seems to describe Antiochus IV Epiphanes' rise to power. Therefore, in this context, "in the latter period" must refer to the latter time of the Greek Empire.

▣
NASB  "insolent and skilled in intrigue"
NKJV  "who understands sinister schemes"
NRSV  "skilled in intrigue"
TEV  "stubborn, vicious and deceitful"
NJB  "ingenious-minded man"
REB  "a master of strategem"
JPSOA  "impudent and versed in intriuge"
LXX, Peshitta  "who understands obscure sayiings"

This is literally "strong of face" (CONSTRUCT BDB 738 and 815) and "one who understands riddles" (CONSTRUCT BDB 106 and 295). Antiochus IV applied wisdom in a negative way, only to achieve his own ends!

The non-canonical, interbiblical books of I, II Maccabees record this periof of history.

entries.title: Daniel 8:23-26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:23-26 These verses are in poetic form in the NASB, NRSV, NJB, and REB translations. This means interpreters should note the parallelisms.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

entries.title: Daniel 8:24 "his power will be mighty, but not by his own power"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:24 "his power will be mighty, but not by his own power" Here again, is the recurrent theme of God's control and direction of human history (cf. Dan. 8:25f; 2:20-23). God used Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece, Rome, and will use whomever He chooses to accomplish His will (cf. Romans 9)! Often humans, even redeemed humans, do not understand (cf. Isa. 55:8-11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SECOND COMING, IV.

▣
NASB  "he will destroy to an extraordinary degree"
NKJV, LXX  "he shall destroy fearfully"
NRSV  "shall cause fearful destruction"
TEV, Peshitta  "will cause terrible destruction"
NJB  "will plot incredible schemes"
REB  "he will work havoc untold"
JPSOA  "he will be extraordinarily destructive"

The first VERBAL (BDB 810, KB 927) is a Niphal PARTICIPLE and the second VERB (BDB 852 II, KB 1026) is a Hiphil PERFECT with waw. This word is often used for the wonders and marvelous works of God (cf. Exod. 15:11; Isa. 25:1; 29:14; Dan. 12:6). Here, however, it speaks of the terribly destructive acts of this king of the third empire (cf. Dan. 8:11-13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW GRAMMAR

▣ "And prosper and perform his will" See note at Dan. 8:12.

▣
NASB  "will destroy mighty men"
NKJV, JPSOA, Peshitta  "shall destroy the mighty"
NRSV, NJB, LXX  "shall destroy the powerful"
TEV  "will bring destruction on powerful men"
REB  "will work havoc on the mighty nations"

The VERB means

  1. "corrupt" (BDB 1007, KB 1469, Hiphil PERFECT with waw, cf. Gen. 6:12; Deut. 4:16; 31:29; Ezek. 16:47)
  2. "ruin" (cf. Mal. 3:11)
  3. "destroy" (cf. Dan. 8:25; Isa. 36:10; Jer. 51:20)

The ADJECTIVE "mighty" usually means numerous (BDB 783, cf. "many" of Dan. 8:25d). Because of Daniel's literary style it is surely possible

  1. that "the mighty men" and "the holy people" are parallel
  2. The other option would be to see "mighty men" as the army of national or political rivals.
  3. The full phrase denotes the king's (i.e., little horn) complete success.

This phrase "the holy people" is literally "the people of the holy ones," which is very similar to Dan. 7:27. Many scholars believe that the phrase in Dan. 7:27 is parallel to "holy ones" of Dan. 7:18,22, and 25. In context Dan. 8:24 cannot refer to angels.

SPECIAL TOPIC: holy ones

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

entries.title: Daniel 8:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:25 This fits what we know of Antiochus IV. See also I Maccabees 1:29-41,44-50; 4:38-39.

▣ "He will magnify himself in his heart" The VERB (BDB 152, KB 178) is a Hiphil IMPERFECT (i.e., continuing action). This has been the recurrent problem of fallen humanity and especially of tyrannical dictators and potentates. This activity always attracts God's attention (cf. Genesis 11; Isa. 9:9; 10:12; Dan. 5:20; 8:11; 11:36-37).

▣
NASB  "while they are at ease"
NKJV  "in their prosperity"
NRSV, TEV  "without warning"
NJB, JPSOA  "taking them unawares"
REB  "when they least expect it"
LXX  "be deceit"
Peshitta  "suddenly"

The term "at ease" (BDB 1017) means quietness in the sense of security, but without warning at such a time and in such a place (probably "the Beautiful Land," i.e., Palestine, cf. Dan. 8:9,11,16,41), they will be attacked (cf. Dan. 11:21,24).

The attacker will be the king of Dan. 8:23 and those attacked will be "the mighty men and the holy people" of Dan. 8:24.

▣ "he will even oppose the Prince of princes" The VERB, "will even oppose" (BDB 763, KB 840) is a Qal IMPERFECT.

This same word, "prince" (BDB 978, cf. Dan. 8:11,25; 10:13,21; 12:1) is translated "commander" in 8:11 and seems in context to refer to YHWH (cf. Josh. 5:12-15). The Hebrew word does not imply a crown prince, co-regent, or ruler in waiting as it does in English, but the chief leader. It is used of

  1. the Messiah in Isa. 9:6,7
  2. Michael the Archangel (cf. Jude 9)
  3. Israel in Dan. 10:13,21; 12:1

The redundant "Prince of princes" is a Hebrew SUPERLATIVE, "the greatest of all rulers" (i.e., King of Kings, cf. 2:37,47; Ezek. 26:7; or [God of gods]; Ezra 7:12).

▣ "But he will be broken without human agency" The VERB (BDB 990, KB 1402) is a Niphil IMPERFECT. This is the recurrent theme of God's sovereignty and control of history (cf. Dan. 2:20-23).

entries.title: Daniel 8:26 "evenings and mornings"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:26 "evenings and mornings" This refers to the offering of a lamb in the temple each morning and evening (i.e., "the continual," cf. Dan. 8:11-14,19). The Jewish culture starts the new day at evening, following the order of Gen. 1:5,8,13,19,23,31.

The vision and prophecy of chapter 8 is future to Daniel, but past to us. This gives us a great opportunity to evaluate prophetic/apocalyptic language in a known event (cf. D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, pp. 103-128). We can read I Maccabees, Josephus, and secular histories to compare how the event was recorded in the Bible and outside the Bible. The differences show us

  1. the stylized language of Hebrew prophecy
  2. the over-the-top emotional hyperboles of apocalyptic symbolism

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

▣ "Which has been told" See Dan. 8:15-25.

▣ "is true" This (BDB 54) should possibly be understood as certain to happen just the way it was revealed in Dan. 8:15-25. For a good discussion of meaning and truth in Scripture see Kevin. J. Vanhoozer, Is There a Meaning in This Text? and C. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: TRUTH/TRUE

▣ "But keep the vision secret" This secrecy is seen in Dan. 7:28 and 12:4,9. This is literally, "stop us" or "shut up" (BDB 711, KB 771, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. 2 Kgs. 3:19; 2 Chr. 32:4,30; the PASSIVE in Dan. 12:9). This means that the phrase may mean to

  1. conserve the vision
  2. keep it secret (NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 301, #2)
8:27
NASB  "I was exhausted and sick for days"
NKJV  "fainted and was sick for days"
NRSV  "was overcome and lay sick for some days"
TEV  "I was depressed and ill for several days"
NJB  "lost consciousness; I was ill for several days"
REB  "having been weak many days my strength failed and
  I lay sick for some days"
JPSOA  "I was stricken, and languished many days"
Peshitta  "trembled and was troubled for some days"

The vision of both Dan. 7:28 and 8:27 made Daniel physically ill.

▣ "there was none to explain it" This phrase is surprising in light of Dan. 8:15-19! Interpreting angels are common elements of apocalyptic literature. Humans cannot understand without divine help!

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. What two kings are mentioned in chapter 8?
  2. Should we identify the little horn of chapter 7 with the little horn of chapter 8? Why or why not? Who are these little horns?
  3. Who are the transgressors in Dan. 8:12, 23?
  4. To whom does the prophesy relate: to Daniel's time; to the Maccabean period, to Jesus' time, or to the end time? Why?
