entries.title: Daniel 12:1 "Now at that time"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:1 "Now at that time" The Septuagint begins this chapter with "unto that place." It is obvious that Dan. 12:1-4 are connected with the message of chapter 11. The time of Dan. 12:1 links up with the events of Dan. 11:40-45.

The real issue is the time frame.

  1. The use of "the king of the South" (Dan. 11:40) and "the king of the North" (Dan. 11:40) implies that it refers to the second century B.C.
  2. However, the use of "at the end-time" (Dan. 11: 40) could imply a future period (cf. Dan. 12:4,9).
  3. But not necessarily because a similar phrase is used in Dan. 12:27 and 35.

The only reason that a second century context is questioned is because of

  1. the accuracy of Dan. 11:2-35 compared to known secular history
  2. the possible accuracy of Dan. 11:36-39
  3. the total inaccuracy (based on known secular history) of Dan. 11:40-45

▣ "Michael" His name means "who is like God" (BDB 567). There are only two angels mentioned by name in the Bible: Gabriel, apparently a messenger angel, and Michael, apparently the guardian angel of the nation of Israel or the people of God. This angel is mentioned in Dan. 10:13, 21 and in the book of Jude, v. 9, where he is called the archangel. His name occurs often in the DSS literature and intertestamental literature, such as I Enoch. John Calvin thought that Michael was the pre-existent Christ.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

▣ "the great prince" This same term "prince" (BDB 978) is used several times in Daniel.

  1. Babylonian official in charge of the four Jewish youths, Dan. 1:7,8,9,10,11,18
  2. Jewish political (royal) leaders, Dan. 9:6,8
  3. God Himself or the Messiah, Dan. 8:11,25
  4. powerful national angels
    1. Persian, Dan. 10:13,20
    2. Greek, Dan. 10:20
    3. Jewish, Dan. 10:13,21; 12:1

Another term (BDB 617) translated "prince" is used in

  1. Dan. 9:25 for the Messiah
  2. Dan. 9:26 for the leader of the opposition against the Messiah
  3. Dan. 11:22 possibly for the priest, Onias III, who was betrayed and killed in Antiochus IV's attempt to take over the Jewish priesthood (see full note there)

▣ "who stands guard over the sons of your people" Many believe that this refers only to the Jews because of the context of chapter 11. However, the quote in Matt. 24:21, 22 seems to imply that Jesus was referring to "the elect." From Rom. 2:28,29; 4:16; Gal. 6:16 we know that this promise refers to all humans who have the faith of Abraham.

▣
NASB, NRSV, NJB  "will arise"
NKJV  "shall stand up"
TEV, REB, JPSOA  "will appear"
LXX  "will pass by"
Peshitta  "arisen"

This word's basic meaning (BDB 763, KB 840, Qal IMPERFECT) is "stand" or "take a stand." It is used often in Daniel

  1. present oneself, Dan. 1:5
  2. come on the scene, Dan. 8:22,23; 11:7; 12:1
  3. stand against, Dan. 8:25; 10:13; 11:14
  4. stand for, Dan. 10:21; 11:1
  5. stand up, Dan. 8:18; 10:11
  6. rise from the dead, Dan.12:13

BDB asserts option #3 best fits this context, but A Handbook on the Book of Daniel by Peter Contesse and John Ellington, UBS, p. 323, thinks option #4 fits best (cf. Esther 8:11; 9:16). Remember, context determines meaning, not lexicons or dictionaries.

▣ "And there will be a time of distress such as never occurred since there was a nation until that time" The OT prophets (cf. Jer. 2:27-28; 14:8; 30:7; Joel 1:5-18; Zeph. 1:14-18) reveal that because of Israel's and Judah's idolatry that a future time would be a time of divine judgment (i.e., both temporal and eschatological). God tried to use the covenant blessings and cursings of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-29 to bring His people back, but they would not; then He allowed foreign nations to exile them (e.g., Isa. 10:5; Jer. 51:20), but still they did not turn to Him and keep His covenant. However, even amidst judgment there is hope in the merciful character of God (cf. Hosea 11; 13:14).

This seems to refer to the Messianic woes referred to by Jesus in Matt. 24:21, 22 (cf. Mark 13:19-20). The Septuagint has "nations written in the book." In Matt. 24:21 Jesus changes the word "nations" to "world," which is the NT universal understanding of the extension of covenant love to all humans through the gospel.

The context of Daniel 10-12 surely links this phrase to national Israel. Daniel experienced one time of distress (i.e., Babylonian exile) and was told about another (i.e., the time of Antiochus IV and the Maccabean period). However, this immediate context points toward an even more future period. Since the final resurrection is mentioned, then this context must be widened from national Israel into a "fulfilled" period of the Gentile mission.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "everyone who is found" There has been much discussion among commentators because of this universal element implied by "everyone" but contrasted with the word "many," found in Dan. 12:2 and 10 (cf. Dan. 11:33,39). Daniel 12:10 helps to interpret the "many" of 12:2. They both refer to the redeemed, the faithful, the followers of Messiah.

This will seem confusing, but

  1. the Hebrew term (BDB 912 I) for "many" means "all" in Deut. 7:1; Isa. 52:14,15
  2. Isa. 53:11,12 compare with 53:6 as well as the parallelism of Rom. 5:18-19
  3. this same concept of "many" being used for "all" can be found in Matt. 20:28; and 26:28
  4. Jesus seems to allude to Dan. 12:2 and changes "many" to "all" in John 5:28-29

The Hebrew term for "all" is parallel to "many" in Isa. 2:2. This same confusion of "all" versus "many" has sometimes degenerated into denominational conflict between Calvinists and Arminians. There is enough fluidity in the Scriptures that we cannot be dogmatic in this area. Compare Rom. 5:15, 16 with 5:12.

It is sad to acknowledge that not everyone of the lineage (Hebrew idiom, "sons of your people") of Abraham had his faith. As one reads the OT it becomes obvious that most Jews were not faithful followers of YHWH; many were idolaters. It is only the faithful remnant who will be saved. Being the covenant people involves more than who your mother was; it involves personal faith and a faithful life.

SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (three senses)

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

▣ "written in the book" This same book of 1ife is referred to in Dan. 7:10. There are two books mentioned in the Bible (cf. Rev. 20:12-15).

  1. One is the "Book of Remembrances" where the deeds of both the godly and ungodly are recorded, Ps. 56:8; 139:16; Isa. 65:6; Mal. 3:16.
  2. The other is the "Book of Life" where only the names of the redeemed are mentioned, Exod. 32:32; Ps. 69:28; Isa. 4:3; Dan. 12:1; Luke 10:20; Phil. 4:3; Heb. 12:23; Rev. 3:5; 13:8; 17:8; 20:12,15; 21:27.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TWO BOOKS OF GOD

▣
NASB, JPSOA  "will be rescued"
NKJV, NRSV, REB, Peshitta  "shall be delivered"
TEV, LXX  "will be saved"
NJB  "will be spared"

This Hebrew term (BDB 572, KB 589, Niphil IMPERFECT) is also used in Dan. 11:41. It denotes physical deliverance (cf. Dan. 11:41), but like its NT counterpart, it has the connotation in some contexts of spiritual salvation (cf. Dan. 12:1).

In Daniel, as in all of history, many faithful believers are killed, but they will be ultimately rescued and restored (cf. Dan. 12:2-3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT)

entries.title: Daniel Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
DANIEL 12

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB (MT Versing)
The Time of the End Prophecy of the End-Time The Final Consummation The Time of the End The End of the Persecutor
        11:40-12:1
12:1-4 12:1-4
    (1-3)		 12:1-4 12:1-3 Resurrection and Retribution
      12:2-4 12:2-3
        12:4
        The Sealed Prophecy
12:5-13 12:5-13 12:5-13 12:5-6 12:5-13
      12:7  
      12:8  
      12:9-10  
      12:11-12  
      12:13  

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

BACKGROUND

  1. Daniel 12 concludes the literary unit of chapters 10-12, which has one unified message.

  2. Interestingly, Dan. 12:1-3 are written in poetic lines in the NAB translation. The Jerome Biblical Commentary, vol. 1, p. 459, says, "12:1-3, magnificent poetic conclusion of the revelation given in chapters 10-11." This poetic form it is not followed in other English versions (NEB, REB, NET).

  3. The interpretations vary as to which historical context the interpreter assumes is addressed.
    1. Many see it as Antiochus IV.
    2. Others see it as Titus in A.D. 70.
    3. Others project it into the end time.

      Possibly the text is ambiguous enough to refer to all three and possibly more. This is a good example of "multi-fulfillment prophecy" (i.e., "abomination of desolation," Dan. 9:27; 11:31; 12:11).
      SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Daniel 12:2 "those who sleep"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:2 "those who sleep" There are several terms in Hebrew for sleep.

  1. yashen (BDB 445, NIDOTTE, vol. 2, pp. 553-555), which is normally used of natural sleep, but in Dan. 12:2, of death
  2. shenah (BDB 446), also used of natural sleep, Dan. 2:1; 6:18
  3. shakab (BDB 446), which is used in the books of 2 Samuel, 1 and 2 Kings, and 2 Chronicles for death (2 Sam. 11:9) and normal sleep (2 Sam. 7:12)

The concept of death as sleep is also found in the NT (e.g., Matt. 27:52 [note resurrection]; John 11:11 [note resurrection in John 11:25-26; 13:36; Acts 7:60; 1 Thess. 4:13 [note resurrection in 4:14-17]; 5:10).

▣ "in the dust of the ground" This Hebrew idiom is

  1. a play on the word "ground," adanah (BDB 9) and dust (BDB 779) from which the first man, Adam, is created and to which he will return at death from Gen. 2:7 and 3:19 (cf. Job 10:9; Ps. 90:3; 104:29)
  2. used as imagery for the grave (i.e., buried in dirt, cf. Job 7:21; 17:16; 20:11; 21:26; Ps. 22:15,29; 30:9; Isa. 26:19)
  3. the holding place of the dead (i.e., Sheol, e.g., 1 Sam. 2:6; Job 14:13; 17:16; Ps. 30:3; 49:14-15; 139:8; Isa. 38:10; Hosea 13:14; Amos 9:2; NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 269-274)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?, I. #2

▣ "will awake" This VERB (BDB 884, KB 1098) is a Hiphil IMPERFECT. This is another Hebrew idiom of life from death (cf. 2 Kgs. 4:31; Jer. 51:39,57; Job 14:12). In Isa. 26:19 and here it denotes resurrection (see SPECIAL TOPIC: RESURRECTION). This is exactly the implication of Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones (corporate, cf. Ezekiel 37), but here in an individual sense. Some will awake to everlasting joy (cf. Isa. 66:22-23) and others to everlasting contempt (cf. Isa. 66:24).

For a good discussion see

  1. Millard J. Erickson, Christian Theology, 2 ed., pp. 1200-1210
  2. Dictionary of Jesus and the Gospels, IVP, pp. 673-688
  3. The Zondervan Pictorial Encyclopedia of the Bible, vol. 5, pp. 70-75
  4. Edward Fudge, The Fire That Consumes (book and YouTube video)

SPECIAL TOPIC: ETERNAL PUNISHMENT

▣ "these to everlasting life, but the others to disgrace and everlasting contempt" This refers to a general resurrection (cf. John 5:28,29; Matt. 25:46; and Acts 24:15-16). This is one of the earliest Scriptures which discusses the developing understanding of the need for an afterlife in order for God to set straight the evil which has been done in this world (cf. Job 14:7-12,13-14; 19:25-26; Ps. 16:10; 49:15; 73:24; Isa. 25:8; 26:19; 38:11). Apparently the rabbinical understanding of a divided Sheol/Hades into "paradise" and "Tartarus" developed from these early texts related to resurrection (see notes at Luke 23:43).

▣ "everlasting. . .everlasting" This is the Hebrew word 'olam (BDB 761, KB 798), which must be interpreted in light of the intent and perspective of this permanent division in Matt. 25:46 (i.e., heaven ‒ hell). There has been a recent study on annihilationism that brings up some interesting points.

  1. Edward Fudge, The Fire That Consumes: A Biblical and Historical Study of the Doctrine of Final Punishment (also YouTube video)
  2. Millard J. Erickson, Christian Theology, 2nd ed., pp. 1244-1247
  3. Steve Gregg, "Hell: Three Christian Views" (YouTube video)

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

▣ "contempt" This Hebrew term (BDB 201) is used only here and in Isa. 66:24. Jesus used this Isaiah text to describe Gehenna (cf. Matt. 3:12).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GEHENNA

entries.title: Daniel 12:3 "Those who have insight"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:3 "Those who have insight" This is a recurrent theme. This same phrase (BDB 968) is used in Dan. 11:33,35 (the faithful during the reign of Antiochus IV). Daniel 12:10 shows that this does not refer to degrees of intelligence, but the distinction between the saved and the lost. "Those who have insight" is used in Dan. 11:33,35 to note those who understand and act on the truth revealed by God. In Dan. 11:33 the insight is meant to be passed on to others (i.e., the wise become teachers so others can be "wise"), but they will be killed for their actions.

▣ "will shine brightly" There is a word play between "shine" (BDB 263) and "those who lead the many to righteousness" (cf. Isa. 53:11), based on the parallel of the actions of those in Dan. 11:33. The concept of illumination (i.e. light and teaching) links "shine" and "giving understanding." Those who know God share Him with others!

The verse is quoted by Jesus in Matt. 13:43, which is in the context of eschatological judgment.

It is possible that this verse denotes degrees of rewards.

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEGREES OF REWARDS AND PUNISHMENT

▣ "like the brightness of the expanse of heaven" These are parallel images. The first one may refer to

  1. the height of God's portable throne (cf. Ezek. 1:22)
  2. the Hebrew word (BDB 956) means "an extended surface"

It is used to describe the vault of the sky in Gen. 1:6,7,8 and in v. 14 to the great lights (sun, moon, stars, comets, etc.).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN, #4

▣ "and those who lead many to righteousness" Notice the two qualifications.

  1. those who know and act on a knowledge of God
  2. those who share that knowledge with others

▣ "star" The term "stars" (BDB 456) was used in many ways in the ANE.

  1. members of God's people ‒ Gen. 15:5; 22:17; 26:4; Exod. 32:13, ect.
  2. members of Joseph's family ‒ Gen. 37:9
  3. Israel's king ‒ Num. 24:17
  4. part of astral worship ‒ Deut. 4:19 (also note Ezek. 8:16; NIDOTTE, vol. 2, pp. 609-614)
  5. agents of God's will ‒ Jdg. 5:20
  6. angels ‒ Job 38:7; Dan. 8:10 (i.e., "the host of heaven" ‒ 1 Kgs. 22:19)
  7. God's people ‒ Dan. 12:3
  8. idolatrous image ‒ Amos 5:26
  9. imagery of extension ‒ Obadiah v. 4; Nahum 3:16

▣ "righteousness" See SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

▣ "forever and ever"This Hebrew phrase combines the word for "long duration" (BDB 761) with the word for "perpetuity" (BDB 723 I), which means "longevity" (cf. Isa. 30:8; 45:17). God's promises and judgments are sure and everlasting (cf. Matt. 5:17-19).

For a good discussion of 'olam and other words for duration see Robert B. Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament, pp. 312-319.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

entries.title: Daniel 12:4 "conceal these words and seal up the book until the end of time"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:4 "conceal these words and seal up the book until the end of time" The TEV and NJB translations make this verse a separate paragraph. This concept of "seal up the words" (BDB 367, KB 364; NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 324) is found in Dan. 8:26 and 12:9.

The "sealing" seems to refer to

  1. protection for future reading (cf. Jer. 32:11-14)
  2. spiritual understanding (cf. Isa. 29:9-12)
  3. security (cf. Dan. 9:24)
  4. certainty of the predictions
  5. for end-time (cf. Dan. 12:9)

It helps me to know that these words were not easily understandable to Daniel, nor his contemporaries. I think that suffering, persecuted generations of believers will understand some texts that the preceding generations have never fully understood.

There are two interpretive questions.

  1. To what period of time was Daniel's message (1) sealed from and (2) revealed to? Was it for
    1. the sixth century B.C.
    2. the second century B.C.
    3. the first century (cf. Rev. 22:10)
    4. or the end-time?
  2. Is the main purpose the detailed prediction or the revelation of the sovereign God fully in control of history and redemption?
▣
NASB  "many will go back and forth"
NKJV  "many shall run to and fro"
NRSV  "many shall be running back and forth"
TEV  "many people will waste their efforts"
NJB  "many will roam about, this way and that"
REB  "Many will rush to and fro"
JPSOA  "Many will range far and wide"
Peshsitta  "Many shall want to know the end"

This Hebrew term (BDB 1001, KB 1439) means moving about quickly. This idiom of frantic activity is used in several senses, all related to God's judgment.

  1. Jer. 5:1 ‒ The frantic search to find one righteous person in Jerusalem so that God may spare its judgment by Neo-Babylon's invasion and exile.
  2. Jer. 49:3 ‒ Frantic activity inside the walls of Heshbon (Ammon) at the approach of the Assyrian invasion.
  3. Amos 8:12 ‒ Frantic seaarch for God in apostate Israel as God brings the Assyrian army to invade, destroy, and exile.
  4. Zech. 4:10 ‒ Imagery for God's knowledge of the activities of humans. He especially knows and watches over those who trust Him (cf. 2 Chr. 16:9).
  5. Dan. 12:4 ‒ In Daniel it could refer to either God's knowledge of
    1. the end-time judgment events
    2. end-time believers amidst hard times

The term "the many" can refer to

  1. faithful Jews (cf. Dan. 11:33,39)
  2. the rebellious Jews who supported the Seleucid dynasty (cf. Dan. 11:14)
  3. all humans (cf. Dan. 12:2)
▣
NASB, NKJV, JPSOA  "and knowledge will increase"
NRSV, LXX  "and evil shall increase"
TEV  "trying to understand what is happening"
NJB  "and wickedness will continue to increase"
NIV  "to increase knowledge"
REB  "trying to gain such knowledge"
Peshitta  "and knowledge shall be increased"

Many commentators see this as secular knowledge (the modern world), but others see it as knowledge of God's actions in history related in Dan. 12:3a ("those who have insight").

The UBS Text Project, p. 225, lists two options.

  1. knowledge ‒ הדעת
  2. evil ‒ הרעה

It picks option #1 (MT) with a "B" rating (some doubt).

entries.title: Daniel 12:5 "Then I, Daniel, looked and behold, two others were standing"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 12:5 "Then I, Daniel, looked and behold, two others were standing" This chapter is a continuation of the literary context which began in chapter 10. In Dan. 10:4 two angelic beings were seen standing by the Tigris River. However, the term "river" in Dan. 10:4 (BDB 625) is the Tigris, and the one here in Dan. 12:5 (BDB 384) is a different Hebrew word. The one here is most often used for the Nile River. However, there is an exception to this in Isa. 33:21, where it is used of canals.

entries.title: Daniel 12:6 "And one said to the man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:6 "And one said to the man" The Masoretic text has "and he said," while the Septuagint and the Vulgate have "I said." In Dan. 8:13,14,16 Daniel hears two angels discussing the vision that Daniel had just seen, so too, here. Angels are often referred to as "man." See note at Dan. 8:16.

▣ "dressed in linen" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LINEN

▣ "How long will it be until the end of these wonders" This is exactly the same question the angelic being asked in Dan. 8:13. The word "wonders" (BDB 810) could have a negative connotation here (cf. Dan. 12:7) and a positive one (cf. Dan. 12:1-3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WONDERFUL THINGS

entries.title: Daniel 12:7 "as he raised his right hand and his left toward heaven"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:7 "as he raised his right hand and his left toward heaven" This is an OT oath gesture (cf. Deut. 32:40; Isa. 62:8; Ezek. 20:5 and in the NT, Rev. 10:5, 6). Both hands being raised must denote intensity or solemnity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

▣ "and swore by Him who 1ives forever" This is another use of the term 'olam (BDB 761), which must be interpreted in light of its context. Notice its usage in Daniel.

  1. everlasting righteousness, Dan. 9:24
  2. everlasting life, Dan. 12:2
  3. everlasting contempt, Dan. 12:2
  4. those who lead the many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever, Dan. 12:3
  5. Him who lives forever, Dan. 12:7

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

▣ "a time, times, and half a time" There has been much discussion over this phrase. This exact phrase is used in Dan. 7:25 (and Rev. 12:14). It seems to be an apocalyptic idiom for a time of persecution (half of seven, cf. Milton S. Terry, Biblical Hermeneutics, p. 445; also see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 764-767).

There are several other phrases in Daniel and the Book of the Revelation that use this basic time frame:

  1. Dan. 8:14,26 ‒ 2300 evenings and mornings; this has been interpreted as either
    1. 1150 days
    2. 6 years, 110 days
  2. Dan. 9:27 — reference to half of seven
  3. Dan. 12:11 — 1290 days
  4. Dan. 12:12 — 1335 days
  5. Rev. 11:2-13:5 42 months or 1260 days (Rev. 11:3; 12:6)

This seems to refer to about three and one-half years in the lunar calendar. These numbers are more symbolic than literal because of their similarity, yet their difference.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FORTY-TWO MONTHS

▣ "they finish shattering the power of the holy people" Does this refer to

  1. some kind of persecution of the Jewish people (cf. Dan. 7:21,25; 8:23-26; 9:24-27; 11:36-45)
  2. of the Christian church by both Jews and the Roman government (cf. Matthew 24; Mark 13; Luke 21; 2 Thessalonians; Revelation; see Kenneth Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell)

There is a third option that goes back to Dan. 11:14, 34; God will accomplish the victory in His own time, in His own way, and for His purposes (the book of Daniel's emphasis on God' sovereignty, which is such a common element in apocalyptic literature).

There has been much discussion about this period of time, but it is obvious that it refers to a historical occurrence when the evil one seems to be gaining an advantage (cf. Dan. 8:23-26; Luke 21:24). The Septuagint totally changes the thought of this verse and must be ruled out as a realistic option. The future time setting (cf. Dan. 12:4) will see things getting worse and worse for the people of God (cf.Dan. 12:1).

Apocalyptic literature is pessimistic about the possibility of historical process accomplishing anything positive or righteous. Therefore, the power of humans, even redeemed humans, must be shown to be inadequate. Only a powerful, climatic coming of God into fallen history can restore and accomplish the plans and purposes of God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTAUGINT

SPECIAL TOPIC: SECOND COMING

entries.title: Daniel 12:8 "As for me, I heard but could not understand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:8 "As for me, I heard but could not understand" Daniel had been given special gifts of wisdom and dream (vision) interpretation (cf. Dan. 1:17). In Dan. 8:16 the powerful angel orders Gabriel to give Daniel understanding (cf. Dan. 9:22; 10:21). However, this does not mean to imply that Daniel understood everything about these visions.

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

▣ "My lord, what will be the outcome of these events" Although the godly man, Daniel, asked, his curiosity would not be answered. These events are for a future generation (cf. Dan. 12:9).

The term "lord" here is not a title for deity, but the general term for respect, "adomi" (cf. Dan. 10:16).

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

entries.title: Daniel 12:10 "Many"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:10 "Many" See note at Dan. 12:1 ("everyone").

▣ "will be purged, purified and refined" Some will respond to God's messengers and it will radically change their lives! The goal of God for every believer is a godly, self-giving, new heart, mind, spirit. Eternal life has observable characteristics.

Persecution is a means of purging.

  1. "shall purify themselves" ‒ BDB 140, KB 162, Hithpael IMPERFECT
  2. "make themselves white" ‒ BDB 526, KB 517, Hithpael IMPERFECT
  3. be refined" ‒ BDB 864, KB 1057, Niphal IMPERFECT

Notice there is both human will (i.e., #1,2) and God's actions (i.e., #3).

Persecution

  1. separates the true believer from the pretend believer
  2. separates the believer from that which displeases God
  3. separates the believer into God's service (cf. v. 4)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY DO CHRISTIANS SUFFER?

▣ "but the wicked will act wickedly, and none of the wicked will understand" There will be a huge division among humans. Those who do not know God will be completely surprised by the events of history. Evil will show itself for what it is!

▣ "those who have insight will understand" If this refers to a future time, and if the New Testament is true, then these must be believing Jews and Gentiles because in Christ there are no more racial, sexual, or social distinctions in salvation (cf. Rom. 2:28-29; Gal. 3:28; Eph. 2:11-3:13; Col. 3:11).

entries.title: Daniel 12:11 "From the time that the regular sacrifice is abolished"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:11 "From the time that the regular sacrifice is abolished" This obviously refers to a historical event. The "regular sacrifice" (BDB 556) refers to the daily sacrifice of a lamb, every morning and evening in the temple ("the continual"). There has been a diversity of opinions based on the time frame in which the passage is viewed:

  1. Antiochus IV (cf. Dan. 8:11-13)
  2. the Roman general, Titus, in A.D. 70 (cf. Dan. 9:25-27; Matt. 24:15)
  3. the end-time Antichrist (cf. Daniel 7; 11:36f-40)

▣ "the abomination of desolation is set up" Some see this phrase (BDB 1055, 1030) as referring to

  1. Antiochus IV setting up an altar to Zeus in the temple during the Macabbean period (cf. Dan. 8:11-13; NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 169, #6 and p. 245)
  2. divine judgment on apostate Judaism in the fall of Jerusalem and the complete destruction of the temple
  3. Others see it as referring to the anti-God world ruler of the end-time (cf. Dan. 7:21,25; 8:23-26; 9:25-27; 11:36-45).

The phrase is ambiguous enough to fulfill several historical situations.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SECOND COMING, IV.

▣ "1290 days" See note at Dan. 12:7.

entries.title: Daniel 12:12 "How blessed is he who keeps waiting and attains to the 1,335 days"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:12 "How blessed is he who keeps waiting and attains to the 1,335 days" This seems to be a bit longer than most of the prophetic dates (cf. Dan. 12:7). Those who know God's wisdom and remain faithful (i.e., "blessed," BDB 80) to God even in the midst of an extended persecution will be rewarded and blessed. Perseverance is crucial.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSEVERANCE

SPECIAL TOPIC: FORTY-TWO MONTHS

entries.title: Daniel 12:13 "go your way. . .enter into rest"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:13 "go your way. . .enter into rest" Daniel is told to quit wrestling with this, to leave it alone, and to live out his normal life until his death (i.e., "to the end," cf. Dan. 12:9). But the great hope of Dan. 12:13 is the assumption that he (and all who believe) will rise again unto an end-time reward (i.e., "your alloted place" with YHWH, cf. Ps. 16:5). Hallelujah!

The term "rest" (BDB 628) has several connotations. Here, it seems to mean "wait quietly" (cf. 1 Sam. 25:9; Hab. 3:16). God will act in His time to bring the period of human rebellion and shame to an end. God's people will inherit the world.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. What is the historical reference of the literary unit Daniel 10-12?
  2. Why are there so many diverse interpretations of this passage of scripture?
  3. Is this the only place in the OT where a resurrection is mentioned?
  4. What is the central truth of Daniel 12:5-13?
  5. Explain the concept of multiple fulfillment prophecy.

Additional note ‒ The LXX includes two non-canonical books which are denoted as Daniel chapters 13 and 14.

  1. chapter 13 ‒ "The story of Susanna"
  2. chapter 14 ‒ "Bel and the Dragon"
